Adviser to the National Command Authority (NCA) and former director general of the Strategic Plans Division (SPD) retired Lieutenant General Mazhar Jamil has warned of the “risky” outcome for South Asia and beyond of a “dangerous ideology” shaping the Indian military mindset. “Indian military thinking is being shaped by a dangerous ideology, which conflates mythology with national power.

The outcome is very risky and delusional Indian military doctrines with a poor strategic sense of nuclear realities are endangering South Asia and beyond,” he said in his key note address at a workshop titled ‘Nuclear Deterrence and Strategic Stability in South Asia’.
The workshop, held last week in London, was organised by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, which shared a transcript of Jamil’s address late on Monday.
He began by saying that a strategic stability model for a region must take into consideration the political beliefs and strategic thinking of states, which formed the basis of policies.

And that shaped the strategic and security environment in the region, he explained. “The political and strategic thinking of states, therefore, should prefer [a] political approach because military adventurism, hegemonic ambitions are highly risky and unaffordable in the South Asian nuclearised environment,” Jamil stressed, before specifically talking about India and Pakistan.
The two South Asian rivals, he said, had outstanding disputes, Kashmir being the core one. “It needs to be resolved as per the United Nations Security Council resolutions.

But, what we are seeing, on the contrary, is [an] Indian political approach of avoiding the resolution of conflict, because perhaps the Indian leadership believes it has no locus standi on Kashmir when it is presented on the multilateral forums,” Jamil said.
He added that India “tries to manage [the] Kashmir conflict with military violence within occupied Kashmir and through military aggression against Pakistan.
This has not worked, and therefore Kashmir remains a nuclear flashpoint, seriously impacting the South Asian strategic and security environment”.

The security perceptions in South Asia had not evolved in a vacuum, Jamil continued. “Indian revisionist and hegemonic political aspirations have [a] long history of Indian coercion and militant violence against all [of] its neighbours.

Jamil said Bharat was essentially a “revisionist concept that is rooted in reclaiming [the] vast landmass of South Asia and its domination by Hindu civilisation”. “Indian political forces, interestingly, do not shy away anymore in projecting what previous governments pursued covertly.
Very surprisingly, the map of Mahabharat, the greater Bharat, as they call it, covering [the] entire landmass of South Asia, is on the display in the Lok Sabha.

That’s the parliament of India, clearly giving the political direction to the state and the state organisations. “So, no wonder, beyond [the] core nuclear diet of India–Pakistan, India’s conflict with all other countries serves as a perpetual driver of [the] evolving security dynamics in South Asia,” he added.

He also mentioned a recent “political transformation, led by the extremist Hindutva doctrine, that seeks to marginalise and delegitimise [the] non-Hindu population of the state, especially the Muslims”, in India. “This has introduced an additional layer of complexity to the regional security environment.

This marks a significant shift towards a nationalism, which is prejudiced by extreme theological principles,” Jamil said. “So, what we see is that we have a nuclear-armed neighbour whose political and strategic thinking is subordinated to a revisionist, mythological outlook with an overconfidence to subdue its neighbours.

This dangerous political philosophy has trickled into the Indian political, strategic, organisational and even societal culture.” The NCA adviser went on to say that this mindset had also, “unfortunately, penetrated deeply into Indian military thinking”.

He said the first of those lessons was that conflicts outlasted military adventurism and wars, unless they were resolved politically. “The resolution of the Kashmir conflict, therefore, needs a political approach and dialogue to achieve stability at [the] higher political planes,” he asserted.
The second lesson, he said, was that any military misadventurism between two nuclear powers could only escalate the crisis to undesirable consequences and could not serve any purpose to the policy.

In this connection, he added that the Indian leadership needed to understand that it “cannot dictate its unjustified and illegal policy objectives through military aggression to another nuclear power”.
Moving on to the third lesson, Jamil said it was “pivotal to the crisis dynamics of South Asia”.
He then cited military scholar Carl von Clausewitz, who Jamil said had warned that “war is the realm of uncertainty and escalation is really a control ladder”.
Elaborating further, he said: “War is the realm of uncertainty and the lesson from the history of warfare and theory alike is clear.
The Indian strategic approach, he said, sought political and military dominance to be a “regional hegemon with a revisionist political thinking”.
This, however, gave India a false sense of hegemony in the region,” he said.

The second outcome, Jamil said, pertained to the support by Indian technology partners and, “very strangely, also allowing India to get a Nuclear Suppliers Group waiver, in spite of its irresponsible nuclear behaviour”. “Resultantly, India, now, is running one of the fastest-growing nuclear and missile programmes.
This has been done with no regard and concern to arms control, a key factor in the strategic stability for the region.

I think what [we] should now worry about is this ambitious and revisionist state reaching to most of their capitals with no restraints and transparency, even to its own technology partners,” Jamil said.

He said the third outcome was about the policy of appeasement by “certain powers that has made India think that its exceptionalism will always be acceptable to the world”. “Indian propaganda and [its] disinformation campaign was accepted without scrutiny and responsibility.
The case in point is the intentional BrahMos missile attack on Pakistan on 9 March 2022.
Strangely, it took India 48 hours to tell its nuclear neighbour about this incident,” Jamil recalled.
In the 2019 crisis, he pointed out, Modi had bragged at an election rally that India was “not storing nuclear weapons for Diwali”.
India then launched a military offensive despite Islamabad calling for an independent investigation into the incident.

Jamil said that India’s strategy aimed for “escalation domination” and that it planned to intimidate Pakistan via sheer force and the tempo of the operation; however, “Indian planners closely underestimated Pakistan’s resolve and capability”. “The crisis of India’s making could have taken South Asia to the brink of nuclear catastrophe, saved only by the strategic restraint of Pakistan,” he stressed.
He added that Indian leadership had dismissed Pakistan’s nuclear deterrent as “mere nuclear bluff” and boasted about being able to “break Pakistan apart”.
He emphasised that when “rhetorics and confidence” became policy, blunders were likely.

On the other hand, he said, Pakistan’s retaliation was not impulsive but rather had clear political direction and strategic restraint, denying India the space to “normalise coercive conventional aggression”.

He added that Pakistan made the responsible choice not to escalate and to agree to a ceasefire, noting, “I think in all fairness, India owes a thanks to (US) President Trump.” However, he highlighted that this responsible behaviour was being “deliberately misrepresented” by India as a bluff.
Strategic landscape post-2025 Jamil stressed that in the wake of the May 2025 conflict, there was an increased risk of escalation in the region.

He highlighted the “revisionist agenda” of Modi that had “dangerously enhanced the conflict profile” of South Asia by holding the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance, adding to the flashpoint of Kashmir, and continuing with “threats and compellence to another nuclear power”.

He added that India also supported terrorist organisations such as the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), “exporting terrorism as an instrument of policy” to engineer instability in Pakistan. “The space is shrinking between Indian aggressive posturing and Pakistan’s restraint,” he said.

He called on India to shun the policy of supporting terrorist organisations such as the TTP and BLA, noting that Pakistan had presented “irrefutable evidence” of Indian state support to these organisations to the international community and the UNSC.

He also called for the international community to hold India accountable for its involvement in supporting terrorism. “It should be realised that the restraint and strategic patience of Pakistan has its own thresholds,” Jamil stated, adding that “in any future military aggression, the aggressor will have to bear a heavy cost”.
He stressed Pakistan’s readiness to move towards a political dialogue to resolve conflicts, including that of Kashmir, as a responsible nuclear state.

He added that Pakistan offered to establish a robust crisis management mechanism as a first step towards this. “Bharatiya leadership should not be allowed to hold hostage the welfare of two billion people of South Asia, in favour of their hegemonic and delusional revisionist aspirations,” he concluded.

KARACHI: A judicial commission formed to investigate the circumstances and possible negligence in businessman Mir Raza Ali’s murder case has pointed out the police’s “epic failure” in their investigation.
The Sindh cabinet decided to make the report public during a meeting chaired by Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah earlier in the day.

While acknowledging that the initial police response when they were informed of the presence of a body was prompt, the report noted that subsequent events “left a lot to be desired”. “It was a murder,” the report declared.

It explained that the bullet trajectory, the unusual location of the wound if it had been a self-inflicted injury, the “absence of blood, the state of the body, the principles of medical jurisprudence, acid burns and the anaesthesia detected in the blood all clearly excluded suicide as the cause of death”.

The commission determined that releasing the police findings before a proper investigation was “premature and fell short of professional standards”. “Even if the death had been a suicide, the police should have established who was responsible for driving a young man to that point, including whether coercion, blackmail, or instigation was involved.
They made no such effort.” It said the police investigation “failed in its most basic duty: to establish the truth”.

It further observed that “incessant public criticism of the police created problems” as the police “went into a shell, completely broke down communication channels, and took a position based on ego rather than on cogent, solid reasons”.
The report pointed out specific issues with the police conduct: “Lack of leadership, seriousness, and supervision, and, in some cases, negligence by the senior officers.

The handling of this case has been like a rudderless ship, not aware of its destination. “Ranging from negligent to criminally negligent, inexplicable, casual, and unprofessional investigation.” According to the commission, an active cover-up in the initial stages of the investigation cannot be conclusively ruled out.
It noted that senior police officers swept clear investigative lapses under the carpet, without acknowledging them, addressing them, or even attempting to do so. “Too many cooks spoil the broth.

The inquiry said there was a need to mitigate public speculation by an “honest and timely briefing on the investigation”, but this was not done, and the family or the public were not updated through official disclosures. “The police did not follow the commission’s recommendation to appoint a focal person for this reason.
The meeting was attended by Medico-Legal Officer (MLO) Dr Osama Sheikh, who conducted Ali’s first autopsy, the Karachi police chief and other senior officials.

Observations on officials Listing its observations for certain police officials involved in the case, the judicial panel identified “criminal negligence” on the part of Station House Officer (SHO) Adeel Afzal of Ferozabad police station. “Initiate a comprehensive inquiry into him, leading to dismissal from service.
He should be suspended in the interim.
He must also be questioned to determine whether he has facilitated the destruction of key evidence,” the report read.
It also found criminal negligence by Sub-inspector Shabbir Leghari, the first investigating officer (IO) in the case, and called for disciplinary proceedings against him and his suspension.
The report also determined criminal negligence of Inspector Ghaus, but did not recommend any action against him.
Regarding DIG Farukh Lanjar and Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Samiullah Soomro, the commission noted a “lack of leadership and supervision”.

The judicial panel also called out “extreme immaturity” and “childish behaviour” of MLO Sheikh, who conducted the first medico-legal examination, whose findings were later proven incorrect after a second autopsy. “Overconfidence.
Unprofessional conduct not befitting a medical professional.

Must not be assigned medico-legal duties unless he has undergone at least two years of rigorous academic and practical training.” The report said he was “possibly influenced” and called for the angle to be “conclusively determined”.
Suicide vs murder The report also said a voice note provided by Alishaz Mushtaq to police was “one of the most suspicious parts of this case”.
It said that Mushtaq and ASP Nida Junaid, “played a very important role in supporting the police narrative that the death was due to suicide”.
It said that the person Mushtaq named as his source did not corroborate the information he provided, raising suspicion regarding his conduct.

It further said that the WhatsApp messages Ali sent to Sarim Bin Tahir asking for Rs30m, which was “full of uncharacteristic grammatical errors and truncated spellings and read as acute panic”, suggested the deceased was being “blackmailed or threatened”.

It also noted that while CCTV footage showed Ali with a pistol on the night he was killed, this was “unusual”. “All his close friends and associates told the Commission that Raza did not possess or use pistols.
They said he would probably not even know how to handle one.
Witnesses also vouched for his peace-loving, calm, and gentle demeanour.
Why he took the pistol remained a mystery.
The pistol, however, has not been found to date,” it said.
It further said: “The known financial distress was also not of such a nature that would lead a person to suicide.

Ali’s behaviour, until the ride-hailing service dropped him off, did not suggest he was ready to take an extreme step for this reason.” Recommendations Suggesting the next steps, the judicial commission said accommodating the family’s request for a joint investigation team (JIT) was the “most viable path to mitigate ongoing reputational damage to the Government of Sindh”.

It recommended that a JIT be constituted under the leadership of Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Irfan Baloch to “balance the need for public accountability with preserving Sindh Police morale and reputation”.

The report said the team should “integrate senior representatives from the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), Intelligence Bureau (IB), Pakistan Rangers (Sindh), and the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) to ensure an impartial, comprehensive, and credible resolution. “This extreme step is necessary to restore public trust and end speculation,” it stressed.

The commission contended that any subsequent police actions will inevitably face heavy public speculation, determining that the police department “bears responsibility for this profound trust deficit between itself and society”. “Even an accurate conclusion or the apprehension of the true culprit is unlikely to be accepted by the public,” it added.
The report pointed out that the case could now “only be resolved through a rigorous, intelligence-based investigation as a “significant portion of physical evidence has been compromised”.

It called for the police to “transparently acknowledge and apologise for past operational lapses”, as well as immediately initiate formal inquiries against the responsible officers in light of the report.

While stating that it did not have investigative powers and that it was difficult to conclude conclusively that an active cover-up occurred, the commission noted that “certain inexplicable actions are difficult to justify and raise the possibility that one may have occurred”.

Therefore, it suggested that a high-level committee, preferably led by the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA), be constituted to initiate criminal action against any police officials it finds culpable.
The judicial commission also called for initiating police reforms, particularly to address and modernise the investigation protocol.

It suggested forming a committee of “seasoned professionals” to “specifically address first response, crime scene handling, medico-legal dynamics, collection, safekeeping, and analysis of evidence, and recording the entirety of the investigation in written or digital form”.
While it proposed a three-month timeframe for the exercise, the commission said the Sindh government will make the final decision.
Another suggestion was to consider an increase in the investigation budget, with a protocol in place to monitor the fund’s use.
The panel further suggested steps regarding training of investigators and enhancing the capacity of Crime Scene Units.

Panel formed to ensure implementation The judicial panel’s primary mandate was to determine the facts and circumstances of the case; assess whether police and medico-legal investigations were impartial; identify professional negligence, misconduct, evidence manipulation, or cover-ups; review digital/forensic evidence; and recommend further investigation, forensic analysis, or legal/departmental action.
According to a handout issued by the Sindh chief minister’s spokesperson, the judicial inquiry report was presented in seven separate sealed envelopes.
It will be uploaded on the website of the provincial home department on Tuesday, while a copy will also be provided to the aggrieved family.
Further, CM Shah also constituted a four-member sub-committee to ensure the implementation of the report.
The committee comprises Home Minister Ziaul Hassan Lanjar, Local Government Minister Nasir Hussain Shah, Labour Minister Saeed Ghani and the Sindh advocate general.

Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon also took to X to announce that the report would be made public on Tuesday. “The government of Sindh remains committed to transparency, accountability and ensuring that due process of law is upheld,” he said.
Last week, the commission handed over the sealed report to the provincial government after examining 49 witnesses during 15 hearings.

The inquiry report, along with associated documents, was handed over to the focal person of the provincial government and Home Department Additional Secretary Javed Ahmed Abro by the commission registrar, Abdul Majid, on the premises of the SHC.

After receiving the record, Abro told reporters that he would hand over the sealed report along with other records to the provincial government and it was the prerogative of the government to decide whether the inquiry report was to be brought into the public domain or otherwise.

In August, the provincial government formed the commission, which was tasked with making recommendations for further investigation and forensic analysis or legal/departmental action, and it was required to submit its findings and recommendations to the Sindh government within 30 days.
However, the commission had struggled to meet its deadline and sent an application last month to the Sindh government for an extension in its tenure till Oct 15.
Therefore, the provincial cabinet granted an extension.

Besides examining 49 witnesses and available record, the commission had also sent questionnaires to Karachi police chief Azad Khan, head of current investigation team DIG Amir Farooqui and DIG East Farrukh Lanjar after dismissing an application by the aggrieved family to summon the senior police officers to testify before the commission.

The minister underscored the importance of private sector patronage in promoting sports and supporting athletes, saying financial security would enable players to focus entirely on their performance rather than personal expenses. “A player’s primary concern should be how to score the next goal rather than how to meet personal expenses,” he said.
Ahsan Iqbal stressed that excellence in modern sports required more than talent and physical ability, highlighting the growing role of sports science, technology and data-driven performance analysis.
Physical fitness, mental resilience, discipline and sustained concentration were also essential for success at the international level, he added.
Referring to leading athletes worldwide, he said their achievements were built on consistent practice, discipline and an unwavering focus on performance.

The minister also highlighted the vision behind establishing the National Sports City in Narowal, saying it offered international-standard infrastructure for 14 sports at one location to provide athletes with modern training facilities.

He offered the National Sports City in Narowal as a permanent training centre for the Pakistan national hockey team, reaffirming the government’s commitment to providing players with a conducive environment to improve their performance.

Describing the PHF-Vital Group partnership as an important step towards strengthening hockey and engaging young people in sports, Ahsan Iqbal expressed confidence that sustained collaboration among sports institutions, the private sector and young talent would help Pakistan rebuild its hockey legacy and restore its standing in international competitions.

ISLAMABAD: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) on Monday rejected the recent imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, terming the measures an unconstitutional assault on the public mandate, and vowed to resist them through legal, parliamentary and peaceful public mobilisation.

In a unanimous declaration issued after a two-day joint meeting of its political committee and core committee, the party condemned the actions taken on October 11, including the establishment of a council and measures it said were intended to render the elected provincial government ineffective or dissolve it.

PTI argued that politically undermining an elected government would revive authoritarian practices associated with the country’s past, drawing parallels with the repealed Article 58(2)(b) of the Constitution.
It said the measures violated constitutional supremacy, provincial autonomy, federalism and democratic principles, and declared it would not accept them.

PTI condemned the alleged abduction and illegal detention of the KP chief minister, assembly speaker, ministers and lawmakers, demanding their immediate recovery, protection of their legal rights and action against those responsible.

PTI also raised concerns over the treatment of Imran Khan’s three sisters, alleging that their grievances had remained unresolved for a month and demanding protection of their fundamental, constitutional and legal rights.

The declaration accused authorities of conducting a nationwide crackdown on PTI leaders, office-bearers, workers and supporters through raids, arrests, harassment and politically motivated detentions.
According to figures presented at the meeting, more than 1,500 party workers were arrested during the street movement in Punjab.
Hundreds were subsequently detained under the Maintenance of Public Order (MPO), particularly Section 3, while several remained imprisoned, the party claimed.
PTI alleged that workers whose MPO detention periods were expiring were being rearrested under fresh orders instead of being released.
It termed the practice an abuse of legal powers, a violation of civil liberties and an organised campaign of political retaliation.
The party also condemned continued detentions of workers arrested during the movement in Sindh, alleging that supporters remained imprisoned or held under MPO orders.
It extended its condemnation to arrests in KP, Balochistan and Islamabad, as well as raids on the homes of party leaders, workers and their families.

The meeting reviewed what PTI described as violations of the fundamental rights of incarcerated party chairman Imran Khan and other political prisoners, demanding protection of their constitutional and legal entitlements.
The party alleged that arrests and harassment had intensified after the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP, linking the actions to political retaliation.
PTI vowed to challenge the measures on all constitutional, legal, parliamentary and peaceful public platforms.

Pakistan is a federal parliamentary republic, with powers shared between the Federal government and the provinces.
Relations between federation and provinces are defined in Part V(Articles 141–159) of the constitution.
Many Pakistani parties support a federalist and regionalist agenda advocating for increased powers to be held by the provinces.

The Ministry of Inter Provincial Coordination manages federal relations between provinces while the Senate of Pakistan is an important body giving representation of the provinces of Pakistan in national governance.
Legislative powers The power of the provinces and the Federal government were defined by the constitution and the legislative powers are divided into two lists.
The Concurrent List was abolished after the 18th amendment, and most powers were transferred to provinces.
Council of Common Interests Council of Common Interests or CCI was established as a body to solve disputes between the federation and the provinces.
The membership of CCI consisted of the Prime Minister, Provincial Chief Ministers and three members nominated by federal government.
The 18th Amendment The federal framework of Pakistan was significantly reformed by the 18th Amendment.
The amendment adjusted the formula for sharing finance between the provinces.
The amendment was followed by significant devolution of administrative responsibility to the provinces.

Advocacy for further reform A number of political movements support expansion of the federation, to give provincial status to Gilgit-Baltistan for example, or to create new units out of existing provinces.

The Baloch Yakjehti Committee (BYC; Balochi: بلۏچ یکجهتی کمیٹی; lit. 'Baloch Unity Committee') or Balochistan Yakjehti Committee ('Balochistan Unity Committee'), is a human rights movement established in response to alleged state human rights abuses in Balochistan, Pakistan.
The organisation has been confronted by Pakistani government as proxy of terrorist organisations and criminal smuggler groups.
This organization was formed in 2020.
Background In December 2020, it campaigned against the alleged murder of Karima Baloch in Canada, who was believed by the activists to have been assassinated by the Pakistani state.

In 2023, the BYC launched campaigns to protest the detention of Mahal Baloch by the Counter Terrorism Department of the police in Quetta, the assassination of Rauf Baloch by religious extremists in Turbat, and the state's alleged use of religious extremism.
Protests 2023 Baloch long march The protest was sparked by the extrajudicial killing of Balach Mola Baksh, a 20-year-old from Turbat.

Balach was abducted from his home on the night of October 29 by men in civilian clothes, suspected to be security officials, and was later killed in custody after a staged encounter by the Counter Terrorism Department (CTD) of Pakistan.
Najma Mola Baksh, Balach's sister, also participated in the protest to seek justice for her brother and others.
Amnesty International condemned the severe crackdown on peaceful protesters.
Authorities imposed blockades and a public assembly ban in Quetta to restrict movement.
The next day, security forces killed at least three protesters and injured dozens more in Gwadar and Talar.
On July 29, police used tear gas to disperse crowds and detained organizers, including Sammi Baloch, Sibghatullah Shah, and Dr.
Balochistan's Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti criticized the protests, claiming they aimed to disrupt development in the province.

Human rights groups including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan condemned the violent crackdowns and called for the release of detained protesters.
Controversy The Baloch Yakjehti Committee (BYC), while advocating for Baloch unity and rights, has faced criticism for allegedly backing separatist movements and promoting anti-state sentiments.
It is believed that anti-Pakistan groups have significantly supported the BYC to destabilize Balochistan and undermine Pakistan-China economic cooperation.
Through coordinated social media campaigns, BYC and Mahrang Baloch are accused of spreading narratives against the state, the military, and China.

Critics have noted that Mahrang Baloch, the primary leader of Baloch Yakjehti Committee (BYC), has not publicly addressed or condemned the killings of civilians by militant groups such as the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) and Baloch Liberation Front (BLF).
These groups, while claiming to advocate for Baloch rights, have been responsible for attacks on civilians, public infrastructure, and dissenting voices.
Observers argue that the lack of condemnation from activists like Mahrang undermines the credibility of their advocacy and overlooks the victims of militant violence.

Following the killing of 23 civilians in Musakhel/Loralai criticism has been directed at groups such as the Baloch Yakjehti Committee (BYC) for not condemning the attack, which was attributed to the banned Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA).
Observers have questioned the silence of these groups, as well as of certain journalists and human rights advocates, who are otherwise vocal on issues of enforced disappearances.
Critics argue that this selective condemnation raises concerns about potential bias and the overlooking of human rights violations committed by militant groups.

Allegations have also surfaced regarding the use of women and children by groups like BYC to shield militants, and claims that individuals linked to armed outfits are portrayed as human rights defenders.

On 23 May 2025, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry stated that the Baloch Yakjehti Committee (BYC) is not a legitimate Baloch movement but a campaign allegedly backed by Indian intelligence agencies.
In a press briefing, he accused the BYC of acting against Pakistan's national interests and promoting narratives aligned with hostile foreign entities.
He urged the media to critically examine the group's leadership and activities.
Additionally, he declared BYC leader Mahrang Baloch as a terrorist proxy.

Former senator and head of the Pakistan People's Party’s Human Rights Committee Farhatullah Babar warned against labeling Mahrang Baloch or her group as terrorists without due process, calling such actions problematic and potentially counterproductive.

• Industrial, services sector slowdown drags down economic growth in FY26 • Per capita income ‘lowest in region’; economy reaches $450.4bn ISLAMABAD: The government on Monday revised the gross domestic product (GDP) growth slightly downward to 3.65 per cent for the outgoing fiscal year (FY26), attributing the adjustment to a mild slowdown in the industrial and services sectors.

The country’s GDP registered modest growth alongside an increase in per capita income in dollar terms, reflecting a sluggish pace of recovery in the country’s overall output compared with the previous year, the government said.
In May 2026, the government had projected the economy to grow by 3.70pc in FY26, revising its earlier estimate of 4pc.
The downward adjustment now indicates that the country fell short of its GDP target.
The revised growth rates in agriculture, industry and services in FY26 are 3.50pc, 3.34pc and 3.81pc, respectively, compared with earlier growth rates of 2.89pc, 3.51pc and 4.09pc.
The revision came during the 118th meeting of the National Accounts Committee (NAC), which was held on Monday at the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics.
The NAC estimate places Pakistan broadly in line with the outlook of multilateral lenders, though with some variation.

The International Monetary Fund has projected GDP growth at 3.6pc for FY26, the World Bank at 3.7pc and the Asian Development Bank at 3.7pc, while the State Bank of Pakistan expects growth to remain close to 3.7pc.

The committee approved the incorporation of revised imports data in the national accounts estimates from FY21 to FY25, quarterly GDP growth rates for Q1 (revised), Q2 (revised), Q3 (revised), and Q4 during FY26 and updated annual growth rates for FY25 and FY26.
The size of the economy rose to $450.4 billion in FY26 from $410.96bn in FY25, mainly driven by growth in the services sector, followed by industry and livestock.
Per capita income slightly increased to $1,896 in FY26, the lowest in the region, up from $1,824 in FY25.
The projection is based on the 2023 census.
However, it was $1,551 in FY23, $1,766 in FY22 and $1,677 in FY21.

This suggests a deterioration in the standard of living and well-being across almost all segments of society, with no tangible increase in personal incomes due to unprecedented inflationary pressures, which reduce disposable income and limit individuals’ ability to afford goods and services, save, or invest.

Updated growth rates Meanwhile, the NAC also approved the updated growth rates for Q1, Q2 and Q3 of 2025-26 at 3.89pc, 4.31pc and 4.42pc, respectively, compared with 3.92pc, 4.05pc and 3.99pc, presented at the 117th meeting of the NAC.
The fourth quarter of FY26 recorded a 2pc growth in GDP.
The committee approved the updated annual growth of 3.11pc for FY25, which was estimated at 3.18pc in the previous meeting.

In agriculture, important crops improved from 0.65pc to 1.59pc due to wheat and maize, other crops have witnessed significant improvement from 2.43pc to 4.28pc due to higher production of pulses (6.3pc), fruits (1.3pc), tomato (44pc), oilseed (5.4pc), and green fodder (2.4pc).
Livestock decreased slightly from 3.75pc to 3.71pc because of increased fodder inputs.
Updated growth rates in forestry and fishing are 10.80pc and 1.39pc, respectively.
The committee revised growth in industry during FY26 to 3.34pc from 3.51pc estimated previously.
The mining & quarrying industry has improved from 0.38pc to 1.52pc due to improvement in gas (2.84pc), crude oil (5.12pc), and coal (2.73pc).
Large-scale manufacturing (LSM), which is measured through the Quantum Index of Manufacturing (QIM), has declined from 6.11pc to 5.01pc.

The major LSM groups with positive contributions are food (7.03pc), tobacco (12.61pc), petroleum products (9.7pc), rubber products (14.19pc), electrical equipment (14.25pc), automobiles (57.77pc), transport equipment (42.36pc), furniture (22.69pc), and other manufacturing (football) (16.62pc).
The construction industry has improved from 5.73pc to 6.30pc because of increased construction-related expenditure in the public sector.
However, some LSM groups posted negative growth, e.g., pharmaceuticals (-8.87pc), iron & steel products (-7.84pc), chemicals (-2.53pc), and leather products (-1.95pc), electricity (-10.24pc) in FY26.
The services industry has declined from 4.09pc to 3.81pc in FY26, with positive contributions from all the constituents.
The growth in wholesale and retail trade posted at 2.37pc as against the previous growth of 3.71pc due to decrease in manufacturing and imports.
Transport and storage industry growth improved to 3.23pc from 2.31pc due to upward revisions reported in railways, water transport, and air transport.
Similarly, information & communication growth increased from 7.52pc to 9.53pc, the finance & insurance also improved from 0.32pc to 4.23pc in FY26 due to improvement in the insurance industry.
The slowdown was also reported in public administration and social security to 5.67pc from 8.54pc, education 4.17pc from 5.23pc, and human health and social work 5.52pc from 6.85pc.

As reported by Reuters, the World Bank's president Ajay Banga said is in discussions with 30 to 40 countries about potential crisis aid to help them manage energy shocks and price increases triggered by the war in the Middle East, its president.

Banga stressed the global economy had proven fairly resilient, in part due to big AI investments and adjustments in supply and demand for oil, which meant that few countries had sought the initial issues in crisis funds that the World Bank had made available when the war began in late February.

"There is pressure, and so I think maybe over the coming months, more countries will come for some slice of that first $50 to $60 billion." World Bank President Ajay Banga said the institution initially made $25 billion available for crisis financing but could mobilise as much as $100 billion if economic conditions worsen.
Many developing countries are already struggling with heavy debt repayments while higher diesel and fertiliser prices threaten transport costs, food production and household budgets.

Banga did not identify all the countries seeking assistance, but Reuters reports that capital flows to Africa have increased, with Nigeria among major recipients of World Bank-supported private investment.
The discussions come ahead of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, where energy prices, debt and slowing economic growth are expected to dominate talks.

World Bank President announced that while the global economy has shown unexpected resilience—partly cushioned by major technology investments and supply adjustments mounting geopolitical tensions and volatile energy costs continue to threaten vulnerable nations.

Speaking ahead of joint international financial meetings, Banga noted that many governments are currently opting to retool existing project portfolios rather than immediately tapping specialized emergency windows.
However, the institution remains prepared to deploy substantial financing if economic conditions deteriorate further.
The ongoing talks also focus heavily on tackling soaring public debt levels that have constrained fiscal space across the developing world.

The World Bank and the International Monetary Fund are concurrently advancing initiatives—including debt-for-development swaps and portfolio-backed guarantees—to help emerging markets restructure high-priced legacy debt into sustainable funding for education, healthcare, and infrastructure.

Officials stress that agile, proactive policy responses will be critical as nations grapple with the compounding pressures of regional conflicts, shifting commodity markets, and tightening global liquidity.

Published October 17, 2026 Clashes broke out between police and protesters in cities across France on Saturday as tens of thousands of people took to the streets in some of the country's most violent protests in years over rising costs and declining public services.

Some 272 people had been arrested by mid-afternoon after violent incidents involving hooded individuals, including in Paris, Marseille in the south, Rennes in the northwest, Toulouse in the southwest and Angers in the west, the Interior Ministry said.

"Such actions include attempted looting, confrontations with law enforcement, the setting of fires to street furniture and the targeting of seats of power and media outlets," it said, blaming the unrest on what it described as the "ultra-left".
In Lyon, in east-central France, protesters also set ablaze a tourist office.

The protests began last month at high schools in Paris' poor northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending and living standards.

"We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," said Lola, a 19-year-old protester in Paris.

A large police presence was visible in central Paris, especially near landmarks such as the Champs-Elysees and the Arc de Triomphe, which were excluded from the routes of two authorised demonstrations.
Protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, recalling the Yellow Vest movement that marked President Emmanuel Macron's previous term in office.
In Marseille, the mayor said the town hall had been vandalised and that additional police were being sent to the city following talks with the prime minister and interior minister.
About 100 people walked towards the start of the protests shouting "All cops are bastards", according to a Reuters witness.
Macron, who urged calm on Friday, is entering the final stretch of his presidency amid a fragmented political landscape and growing pressure over the economy.
France's efforts to reduce public debt have failed to reassure investors, pushing government borrowing costs to their highest levels in more than two decades.
Police tactics have drawn criticism following a series of injuries among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking up a stun grenade.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said more than 900 police officers had also been injured in previous protests.
The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence.
France suspended the use of stun grenades during the student demonstrations, but Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said they could be used on Saturday.
Calls on social media for veterans of previous protest movements to join the demonstrations appeared to have broadened participation, raising the prospect of larger.
The Yellow Vest movement emerged in 2018 in opposition to diesel taxes before expanding into a wider protest against living costs and inequality.
The movement subsided after Macron announced billions of euros in tax cuts.

Yannick Maillou, a teacher from La Creche in western France who participated in the Yellow Vest movement, said several gathering points had been organised locally for Saturday's protests, with labour unions also encouraging participation.

Azma Bokhari wins defamation case against Moeen Qureshi - By Abid Khan - - Oct 20, 2026 LAHORE: Punjab Information and Culture Minister Azma Bokhari has won a defamation case against Punjab Assembly Opposition Leader Moeen Ud Din Riaz Qureshi, with the Lahore Defamation Tribunal ordering him to pay Rs3 million in damages.
The tribunal issued a brief written judgment in the case, directing Qureshi to pay Rs3 million to the provincial minister over allegations he made against her during a television programme.

The case stemmed from remarks Qureshi made following the visit of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi to the Punjab Assembly.
Qureshi had alleged that Bokhari facilitated the entry of 150 to 200 paid individuals into the provincial assembly during the visit.
He also claimed that journalists who questioned Afridi were paid employees of the provincial information minister.
According to the tribunal’s judgment, Qureshi admitted that he had made the statements during a television programme but failed to produce evidence substantiating his allegations.
The tribunal further observed that his lawyers could not establish the claims during their arguments.
Bokhari approached the Lahore Defamation Tribunal in January 2026 under Section 3 of the Punjab Defamation Act 2024, seeking damages over the allegedly defamatory remarks.

Her petition stated that the allegations had been broadcast on television and circulated on social media, including through the official Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) social media account, reaching millions of people.
The minister maintained that the statements had seriously harmed her reputation, dignity and credibility.
Afridi visited Lahore on December 26, 2025, for a three-day trip that included political engagements and a visit to the Punjab Assembly.
His visit to the provincial legislature was marked by altercations between members of his delegation and security personnel.
Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah on Tuesday said the federal government was ready to invite all political parties and build consensus on counterterrorism.
Speaking in the Senate, the PML-N leader also urged the opposition to “set other demands aside”.

The PM’s aide’s remarks come after the Centre imposed emergency and governor’s rule in KP on October 11, citing the PTI-led provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism.
Sanaullah then turned his attention to the rise in terrorism in the country, expressing sorrow at the martyrdom of an army officer a day earlier.
Chaudhry said political differences should not be allowed to compromise the national interest, adding that peace and prosperity required a collective effort.

Pragmatism over polarity When Pakistan’s first shipment of rare earth minerals quietly departed for the US in October, it drew immediate attention across Asian commentary circles.
Some in China saw betrayal, others in Washington viewed it as an opportunity.

However, in reality, Pakistan’s decision to export rare earths and receive its first crude oil shipment from Houston around the same time signals something more pragmatic than ideological: a bid to regain economic relevance through strategic balance.
Rare earth minerals sit at the heart of today’s technology race.
They power everything from electric vehicles to precision-guided missiles, making them a symbol of strategic dependence.
For years, China has dominated this supply chain, controlling nearly 70 per cent of global production.
Against that backdrop, any new entrant supplying the US naturally raises geopolitical eyebrows.
But Pakistan’s export should not be read as a pivot away from China.
Instead, it reflects Islamabad’s growing recognition that surviving in the current world order requires diversification.
China remains Pakistan’s largest investor and infrastructure partner through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC).
Yet the economic stagnation of recent years, combined with the IMF’s tight fiscal conditions, has forced Islamabad to broaden its options.
Selling minerals to the US and importing energy from Houston are acts of necessity.
For decades, Pakistan’s economic narrative has been shaped by dependency, first on US military and economic aid, then on Chinese loans and projects.
Both relationships brought short-term relief but long-term vulnerability.
The rare earth shipment, though small in volume, reflects an emerging understanding in Islamabad: that sustainability requires trading with everyone and depending on no one.
Pakistan sits atop untapped reserves of copper, lithium and other critical minerals in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
These assets, however, remain trapped under poor infrastructure and limited investment.
Unlike China, Pakistan lacks the capital, refining technology, and logistics network to process these resources domestically.
Partnering with US companies allows the country to monetise what would otherwise stay underground while avoiding over-reliance on a single partner.
In this sense, Pakistan’s rare earth exports are less a geopolitical signal than a developmental strategy.

By opening trade lanes westward, Pakistan aims to attract the type of high-value investment it has historically lacked, investment that generates jobs, builds infrastructure and earns foreign exchange rather than merely incurring debt.
That same pragmatism explains why a crude oil shipment from Houston docked in Karachi almost simultaneously.
This is an experiment in energy diversification driven by affordability.
The fact that the US has now entered Pakistan’s energy matrix underscores how Islamabad is learning to manoeuvre in a multipolar world where ideology matters less than supply security.
It also aligns with Washington’s broader strategic considerations.
The US is actively seeking to ‘de-risk’ its critical mineral supply chain from Chinese dominance.
Engaging with smaller partners like Pakistan serves both strategic and symbolic purposes: it signals that resource security is no longer confined to alliances but open to pragmatic partnerships.
For the US, importing from Pakistan offers limited volume but valuable diversification.
For Pakistan, it provides recognition and leverage.
Beijing’s discomfort with Pakistan’s move is understandable but perhaps overstated.
China has long viewed Pakistan as its strategic partner and buffer in South Asia, not its exclusive economic client.
In fact, a more economically stable Pakistan benefits China’s regional ambitions, particularly the viability of CPEC.
If US engagement helps stabilise Pakistan’s currency, infrastructure and security, Beijing indirectly gains from it.
Moreover, Pakistan’s rare earth exports to the US are unlikely to threaten China’s global dominance in this sector.
The volumes are small, the refining capacity is minimal and the technology gap is wide.
What Islamabad offers instead is optionality, a signal to both great powers that it can cooperate with each without being consumed by either.
Pakistan’s history is littered with moments where it leaned too far towards one power and paid the price.
In the cold war, US aid flowed when Pakistan was useful and dried up when it wasn’t.
In the post-9/11 era, counter-terrorism partnerships brought dollars but also dependency.
More recently, reliance on Chinese loans exposed fiscal vulnerabilities when projects stalled and debt repayments mounted.
This latest round of trade with the US reflects a course correction.
Islamabad appears to be rediscovering a fundamental principle of foreign policy: balance is power.
By trading across geopolitical divides, Pakistan can reassert agency over its economic future.
The move also speaks to a broader trend in global politics.
As the US and China compete for strategic dominance, middle economies like Pakistan, Vietnam and Indonesia are finding room to manoeuvre.
They can extract value from both sides.
Pakistan’s rare earth shipment to the US will not upend global power dynamics, but it does mark a subtle shift in Islamabad’s approach: from ideological alignment to strategic maturity.
Rather than choosing between Washington and Beijing, Pakistan is learning to pick itself, leveraging its geography, resources and partnerships for its own development.

The next step should be to transform these one-off transactions into a coherent national resource policy, one that encourages transparent investment, ensures environmental safeguards and fosters local refining capacity rather than merely exporting raw materials.
That is how Pakistan can convert this moment from symbolism into substance, and from survival into strength.
The writer is a non-resident fellow at the CISS.

Muhammad Aatif Ismail Multan, Oct 18 (APP):For a few weeks each year, ordinary agricultural fields in the villages of South Punjab undergo a remarkable transformation.

The land that usually waits for the next crop becomes a cricketing arena, where makeshift pitches are prepared, boundaries are marked and young players gather with dreams far bigger than the fields on which they play.

In villages where proper cricket grounds remain scarce, temporarily … Lack of cricket grounds spurs new trend of tournaments on agricultural land Muhammad Aatif Ismail Multan, Oct 18 (APP):For a few weeks each year, ordinary agricultural fields in the villages of South Punjab undergo a remarkable transformation.
In villages where proper cricket grounds remain scarce, temporarily vacant farmland has become an unlikely home for the sport.
With permission from farmers and landowners, young enthusiasts transform agricultural plots into makeshift grounds, organize local tournaments and invite teams from neighboring villages.
When the competitions end, the wickets are dismantled, the crowds disperse and the land returns to its agricultural purpose.
He added that young players in many parts of South Punjab faced similar challenges.
His concern echoes the frustration of countless aspiring cricketers whose ambitions often collide with the absence of basic playing facilities.

In villages where suitable grounds are unavailable, even regular practice becomes a challenge, leaving talented youngsters with limited opportunities to sharpen their skills, compete at higher levels and earn recognition.
Muhammad Dilawar, a resident of Basti Nau, Multan, said village youngsters had found a practical way to keep their sporting dreams alive.
They approach farmers, landowners and influential community members to seek temporary permission to use vacant agricultural land.
With their cooperation, they prepare pitches, mark boundaries and arrange tournaments that generally last 15 to 20 days, sometimes extending beyond a month.
What begins as a makeshift arrangement often grows into a celebration of village life.
Teams arrive from surrounding settlements, spectators gather along the boundaries, and the sound of bat striking ball brings the fields alive.
For a brief period, these otherwise quiet stretches of farmland become centers of excitement, rivalry and collective pride.

Dilawar said such competitions gave young players an opportunity to display their abilities, test themselves against unfamiliar opponents and experience organized cricket without travelling long distances in search of suitable grounds.
Muhammad Naveed, another cricket enthusiast, said community cooperation had become essential to sustaining the game in areas lacking permanent facilities.
Village elders, nambardars and influential landowners often helped by making land available until farming activities resumed.

Similar tournaments have recently been held in Chak 31 of Vehari district, while competitions in Chak 69 of Mailsi tehsil have become a regular annual feature, according to Muhammad Ramzan, a coach and sponsor of a local cricket club.
These events demonstrate how rural communities are mobilizing their limited resources to keep cricket alive despite the absence of dedicated playing fields.
Tennis-ball cricket has further strengthened the popularity of these tournaments.
Its relatively low cost and flexible arrangements allow youngsters from different economic backgrounds to participate without the expense associated with more formal competitions.
Local businesses and individual sponsors frequently contribute towards equipment, prizes and other tournament expenses.
Overseas Pakistanis who retain close ties with their hometowns also play an important role in supporting these activities, helping village competitions continue despite limited financial resources.
Beyond the boundaries, however, the tournaments offer something even more valuable than sporting entertainment.
They bring communities together, encourage teamwork and healthy competition, and give youngsters a constructive outlet for their energy.
Representing one’s village before an enthusiastic crowd can build confidence, strengthen friendships and inspire players to pursue the game more seriously.

But when the final ball is bowled and the temporary wickets are pulled apart, an uncomfortable question remains: why should young cricketers in a region so passionate about the game have to depend on borrowed agricultural land to play it?.
Temporary grounds may provide an immediate solution, but they cannot replace permanent facilities that remain accessible throughout the year.
Without reliable playing surfaces, aspiring cricketers struggle to practice consistently, improve their performance and participate in structured competitions.
Their talent may be visible to an entire village, yet remain beyond the reach of coaches, talent scouts and formal cricket pathways.
The responsibility now rests with the government and local administrations to turn this grassroots enthusiasm into a lasting sporting opportunity.
Suitable public land could be identified for village-level cricket grounds, with basic facilities developed in consultation with local communities.
Schools, sports departments, local governments and private sponsors could work together to establish affordable playing spaces.
Transparent partnerships could also encourage overseas Pakistanis and local philanthropists to invest in village sports projects.
Even modest improvements to playing surfaces and basic facilities could benefit generations of youngsters, replacing temporary arrangements with permanent opportunities.
For now, the cricket grounds of South Punjab remain temporary creations carved out of agricultural land.
When the tournaments end, spectators return home, the wickets disappear and farmers prepare their fields for the next crop.
The cheers fade, the boundaries vanish and the game gives way to the demands of the soil.
But the dreams born on those fields do not disappear with the last match.
Behind every makeshift pitch stands a generation of young players waiting for a fair chance to prove itself.
Providing permanent cricket grounds would mean more than laying a pitch or marking a boundary.
It would mean recognizing rural talent, investing in young people and ensuring that a shortage of facilities does not decide the limits of their ambitions.
South Punjab’s youngsters have already shown that passion can turn farmland into a sporting arena.
The challenge now is for the authorities to ensure that their dreams no longer have to depend on the next vacant field.
Ahmedpur East (also known as Ahmadpur Sharqia) is a city located in Bahawalpur District in Punjab province of Pakistan.
As of the 2023 census, the city has a population of approximately 196,618, making it the 69th most populous city in Pakistan.
The city is situated near the Cholistan Desert, offering a hot desert climate with extreme summers and mild winters.
Ahmedpur East was built by Ahmed Khan son of Qadir Din Khan and grandson of Piruj Khan, in 1748.
The city was badly damaged by heavy floods from the Ghara River in 1758.
A new city on a mound half a mile to the south of the previous site was selected for the present city.
Demographics Population According to 2023 census, Ahmedpur East had a population of 196,618.
Languages Culture The city of Ahmedpur East is a tourist destination for not only locals but provides an important hot spot for historians and archaeologists due to its rich heritage.
The city contains the Sadiq Garh Palace and many old buildings which were built by Nawab Sadiq I.
The Derawar Fort is also in Ahmedpur East Tehsil.
Ahmedpur East is also known for its cotton, silk, embroidery, carpets, and extraordinarily delicate pottery.
Nuclear power plant According to The Wall Street Journal, Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission (PAEC) plans to install three Chinese nuclear reactors at Ahmedpur East and the site is now being prepared.
The Ahmedpur East nuclear power complex would have 1100 MW nuclear reactor.
2017 oil tanker fire disaster In 2017, Ahmedpur East was the site of a major disaster, when over 200 villagers collecting fuel from an overturned truck were killed in an accidental explosion.
More than 70 among the injured died in burn centers.
Updated numbers indicate that at least 200 people died in the explosion.
The death toll of Ahmadpur East oil tanker tragedy reached to 219 when another victim died at the Nishtar Hospital, Multan.
As many as 94 victims died in different hospitals, including 18 at Jinnah Hospital, Lahore, 11 at Burns Ward of CMH, Bahawalpur, and 10 at Bahawal Victoria Hospital.

However, 34 injured persons were under treatment at different hospitals, including 22 at BVH, five at THQ Hospital, Ahmadpur East, three at Nishtar Hospital, Multan, and four at Jinnah Hospital, Lahore.
According to the focal person appointed for giving details about the tragedy Dr.
Amir Mahmood, 31 injured persons had been discharged after recovery.

Meanwhile, relatives of several Ahmadpur East tragedy victims alleged that their financial aid cheque issued by the district government on the order of Punjab CM Shahbaz Sharif had been bounced by the banks concerned.
The DC Office spokesman through the Information Department said that the claim was not true.
The spokesperson said that if any cheque did not cash then the concerned families should immediately contact the DC Office.
Education Facilities in Ahmedpur East Apart from the Abbas Higher Secondary School and Army Public School at Dera Nawab Sahib, the city has two government postgraduate colleges.
The city also has a government commerce college, Government Sadiq Abbas Degree College and a college for individuals who require special education.

Many private colleges such as Punjab College, Nimz College, Allama Iqbal College, United College, Millat College, Laurel College, City College, Oxford College, Amal College and many more are working there.
A campus of the Virtual University of Pakistan is also situated here.
There are about ten government high schools in the city and nearby area.
The city contains hundreds of private schools.

Some of them are Allied School, Islamic Model Higher Secondary School, Country School System, The Educators, Dr AQ School System, The Smart School, Dar-e-Arqam School, EFA School System, The PACE School System and many more.
Shrines of Sufi saints Syed Mohammad Abdullah Shah Madni Jilani, great grand son of Abdul Rehman Jilani Dehlvi and a descendant of Sheikh Abdul Qadir Gilani.
Born and raised in Medina, he walked miles between Mecca and Medina in the heat.

Makhdoom Bahauddin Akbar, belonging to Bahauddin Zakariya's 18th generation of descendants.

Azmat Sultan, a descendant of Sultan Bahu.

Abdul Asad Khan Afghan: There is a khanqah by the name of Abdul Asad Khan in Ahmadpur East.

His family lineage and biography is preserved in his writing Takmala Sharif.
Khawaja Muhammad Abdul Malik Siddique was the Peer-e-Tariqat of Naqshbandi-Haqqani Golden Chain.
Khawaja Muhammad Abdul Malik Siddique was the khalifa of Peer Shaikh Mufti Muhammad Fareed Sahib and of Peer Fazal Ali Qureshi of Miskeen Pur Sharif, Muzaffargarh District.
Now his son Khawaja Abdul Majid Siddiqui is the Sajjada Nashin of Khanqah Malikia.
Molana Manzoor Ahmed Faizi was a scholar and Sufi from the Chishtia order.
Abbasi Mosque Abbasi Mosque, situated nearby, is a historical and significant mosque.
This mosque was established in the year 1804 by Haji Allah Ditta Khoker, who laid its foundation stone.
The design of Abbasiya Masjid closely resembles that of the famous Derawar Mosque, which is renowned for its grandeur and unique structure.
The mosque is known for its architecture and intricate details that make it a place of both spiritual significance and aesthetic appeal.
Its spacious prayer hall is designed to accommodate a large number of worshippers, making it a central hub for the local Muslim community.

In addition to the prayer space, the mosque features several important facilities, including a madrasa (Islamic school), where students are taught religious education, and a wuzu (ablution) area, which allows worshippers to perform the necessary ritual washing before prayers.
There are also modern washrooms available for the convenience of the visitors.
Abbasiya Masjid has the capacity to accommodate almost 20,000 people for prayer.
The mosque is led by its imam, Qari Bashir Ahmed.
Ghalla Mandi The Ghalla Mandi in Ahmedpur East is a major agricultural marketplace, where farmers, traders, and vendors come together to buy and sell various commodities, particularly cotton.
Located in the central region of the city, it plays a vital role in the local economy, serving as a hub for the agricultural community.
The mandi is known for its bustling atmosphere, with a diverse range of goods being exchanged, including cotton, grains, and other produce.

US officials have portrayed resource-rich Central Asia — the region between China, Russia and Iran — as worthy of more attention than it received from US President Donald Trump's predecessors.

Trump hosted C5 leaders at the White House last November, when Kazakhstan agreed to join the Abraham Accords, a series of agreements under which Muslim-majority countries have normalized or deepened relations with Israel.
Separately, Trump met with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev at the United Nations General Assembly last September.

Regional politics aside, the trip fits an emerging pattern in which Rubio often visits regions not at the center of the news cycle, while leaving some more fraught foreign-policy portfolios to other Trump aides, including special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Vice President JD Vance.
More than 200 business executives will accompany Rubio to Uzbekistan, the State Department said.
The Central Asian diplomat said the Trump administration has focused its commercial efforts on expanding access to the area's rare earth mineral resources.

After Uzbekistan, Rubio will visit the Indian cities of Mumbai and Jamnagar to meet with business leaders, including Reliance Industries, Chairman Mukesh Ambani, who earned the Trump administration's favor earlier in the year by backing a new refinery in Texas.
As reported, the trip is due to wrap up on Thursday, October 22, 2026.
Rubio's previous foreign trip, in early October, took him to Greece, Portugal and Iceland.

Effective measures are being taken in line with the vision of Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz to ensure the uninterrupted supply of wheat and flour, stabilize prices, and prevent illegal transportation of the commodities.

Wheat quotas, flour supplies to mills to be monitored closely BAHAWALPUR, Oct 20 (APP):Effective measures are being taken in line with the vision of Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz to ensure the uninterrupted supply of wheat and flour, stabilize prices, and prevent illegal transportation of the commodities.

In this regard, a divisional-level meeting was held under the chairmanship of Commissioner Bahawalpur Division Irfan Ali Kathia to review ongoing operations against the illegal transportation of wheat and flour.
Officials of the Food Department briefed the commissioner on measures being taken to prevent illegal transportation, ongoing enforcement operations and the overall situation in the division.

Commissioner Irfan Ali Kathia directed the concerned authorities to intensify action against those involved in the illegal transportation of wheat and flour and initiate legal proceedings against violators without delay.
He also ordered regular inspections of wheat quotas allocated to flour mills and stressed strict compliance with the prescribed regulations.
The commissioner emphasized the need for effective monitoring of flour dispatches from mills to ensure transparency and continuity in the supply chain.
He directed the relevant departments to strictly enforce the prescribed procedures for wheat transportation and flour distribution, making it clear that violations would not be tolerated.
He further instructed the concerned departments to adopt a coordinated strategy to curb illegal wheat transportation.
The Food Department, Agriculture Department, Industries Department, and other relevant agencies were directed to maintain continuous monitoring of wheat transportation and flour supplies.
He stressed the importance of regularly reviewing field operations to identify illegal transportation activities and ensure their immediate prevention.

The commissioner directed all concerned officials to maintain the momentum of enforcement operations and perform their duties diligently to ensure the uninterrupted availability of flour to consumers at affordable prices.
Deputy Commissioner Bahawalpur Syed Hasan Raza and officials from the Food Department, Agriculture Department, Industries Department and other relevant departments attended the meeting.
Deputy Commissioner Bahawalnagar Syed Muhammad Abbas Shah and Deputy Commissioner Rahim Yar Khan Zehir Anwar Jappa participated in the meeting through video link.

Published October 20, 2026 KARACHI: The Sindh cabinet has approved an increase in the upper age limit for the Combined Competitive Examination (CCE) from 30 to 33 years, while also increasing the number of attempts allowed for the examination from three to five.
The decisions were taken at a Sindh cabinet meeting chaired by Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah at the CM House in Karachi, according to a spokesperson.

The cabinet approved a series of reforms to the Sindh Public Service Commission (SPSC), including changes to the age limit, the number of attempts permitted and the minimum qualifying marks for the CCE.
Under the approved changes, candidates will be allowed to appear in the competitive examination up to five times instead of the existing three attempts.
The upper age limit for appearing in the examination has also been raised by three years, from 30 to 33 years.
The provincial cabinet further approved reducing the minimum qualifying marks for CCE 2026 from 40% to 33%.
In another decision, the cabinet approved the introduction of computerised testing for examinations comprising a single paper, the spokesperson said.
During the meeting, CM Shah also briefed the cabinet on his recent visit to China, the spokesperson said.
The meeting also discussed 29 agenda items relating to various provincial departments, according to the chief minister's spokesperson.
Provincial ministers, advisers, special assistants, the chief secretary and other senior officials attended the meeting.

Real Madrid's rough Diomande starting to shine as Leipzig visit - By AFP - - Oct 20, 2026 When Real Madrid splashed a club record 140 million euros ($157m) to sign Yan Diomande from RB Leipzig this summer, it was because of his clear potential to become one of the game’s stars, as showcased at the 2026 World Cup.

That talent has begun to unveil itself in recent matches, with Diomande lashing in a spectacular strike against Sevilla on Sunday in La Liga ahead of a reencounter with his former side Leipzig in the Champions League on Wednesday.
Diomande’s sheer potential was not, however, the only reason Madrid forked out.

President Florentino Perez pledged to fans during his campaign for reelection in June that he would pay a fee of that magnitude for a new star as Madrid tried to rebuild following two seasons without a major trophy.
Diomande had demonstrated exciting promise, shining with Leipzig during just one season in Germany after emerging at Spanish side Leganes.
The 19-year-old did not join Madrid to fill an obvious vacancy, with his arrival actually exacerbating an overbooking in attack.
On the same day Diomande’s transfer was announced, Brazilian winger Vinicius Junior signed a new deal until 2032 with Los Blancos.

Madrid struggled last season to find a balance with Kylian Mbappe, Jude Bellingham and Vinicius on the pitch together, let alone throwing a new attacking star carrying a record price tag into the mix.
For a combination of those factors, it should not come as a surprise that Diomande is still finding his footing in the Spanish capital.
The youngster has shown flashes of his great quality, without yet firmly establishing himself as an essential figure for coach Jose Mourinho, although he is improving.
Diomande scored his first goal for the club against Villarreal on October 10, securing Real Madrid a 1-0 win.
The winger’s superb finish was not the main talking point though, after Vinicius was dismissed later in the game and subsequently banned for four matches.
That further opened the door for Diomande to settle in, with the winger starting on the left wing in Sunday’s 4-1 rout of Sevilla, in which he lashed home from long range in the final stages.
Diomande also assisted the opener for Arda Guler, in his best performance for the club thus far.
He suffered rejection after leaving the Ivory Coast to go to school in Florida in the United States, unable to reach a deal with MLS sides Charlotte FC and Colorado Rapids.
Eventually the winger’s senior debut came with Leganes against Real Madrid in March 2025, and in 10 games for the club he netted twice, earning himself a move to Germany.
Diomande helped Leipzig reach the Champions League with 12 goals and eight assists, and he was named “rookie of the year” in the Bundesliga, before his Madrid move.
The winger said he is spurred on by tragedy from his life.

Imran Khan’s sisters released after brief detention in Rawalpindi Imran Khan’s sisters stage protest on Adiala Road after being denied meeting with their brother RAWALPINDI: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder Imran Khan’s sisters — Aleema Khan, Noreen Khan Niazi and Uzma Khanum — were taken into custody after refusing to end their sit-in near Central Jail Rawalpindi, but were released shortly.
During the crackdown against the PTI’s sit-in at Gorakhpur picket, the police also took several activists of the former ruling party.
Later, the police released Khan’s sister near Chakri Interchange.
The sisters of the incarcerated PTI founder, along with dozens of party workers, staged a sit-in on Adiala Road after being denied permission to meet him and his wife, Bushra Bibi.
Meanwhile, the police asked Khan’s sister to clear the road, but the talks failed, and Aleema refused to call off the sit-in.
After that, police sprayed water on the road and detained around 8 to 10 PTI activists, including Khan’s sisters.
Talking to journalists after being released, Aleema said that her sister Noreen was dragged on the road by the women police personnel.
Aleema has been visiting her incarcerated brother at Adiala and has served as a key channel for conveying Khan’s messages to PTI workers through the media.
Last month, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) Chief Minister Sohail Afridi was denied permission to meet the jailed PTI founder.
The KP chief minister had arrived outside the Adiala jail in Rawalpindi alongside PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Khan and Secretary General Salman Akram Raja.
However, CM Afridi returned without a meeting with the PTI founder, while Khan's sister, Uzma, was allowed to meet the former premier.

Speaking to journalists outside the jail, Afridi said that he should be allowed to meet the PTI founder to receive "policy guidelines", emphasising that questions should be raised about why such a meeting is being obstructed.
