One amendment after another By the time this piece is published, Pakistan stands to lose a Supreme Court and any modicum of an independent judiciary.
Justice Yahya Afridi shall be the last chief justice of the Supreme Court of Pakistan as we once knew it.

A court that has withstood dictatorships, martial law and democratic breakdowns will be swept away by the same political parties that gave us the 18th Amendment, guaranteeing an independent judiciary.
Pakistan’s judiciary has not exactly crowned itself in glory over the past decades, with names synonymous with judicial overreach.
But as wrong as those actions were, the remedy now proposed is fatal: to render one court irrelevant and another compromised.
The judges in whose name this revenge is being exacted will feel no pain; it is the people of Pakistan who will bear the consequences for the foreseeable future.
A people deemed unnecessary, superfluous even, in the framing of this constitutional amendment.
Hardly surprising when a parliament of questionable legitimacy rushes to consolidate control over any form of judicial accountability.
That anxiety forms the backdrop to the 26th and 27th amendments.
The government’s stump speech insists these changes are needed to reduce case backlogs.
Yet, only about 2-3 per cent of Pakistan’s pending cases are before the Supreme Court.
The rest languish before the lower courts of whose reform we hear neither sight nor sound.
Only courts that ask difficult questions are prescribed constitutional amendments.
A constitutional court is an alien idea being shoehorned into our legal system from civil law jurisdictions.
Ours is a common law country, with the jurisdiction of the courts unified.

A constitutional question can be raised in any case, which means the 27th Amendment now asks us to parse through each case, figure out where jurisdiction lies and then ricochet between the two parallel courts, figuring out where litigation is supposed to occur.
Litigants will now enjoy a fractured judicial hierarchy that serves nobody but the current executive.
This is not speculation; the disastrous ‘constitutional bench’ experiment of the past year has already shown us this jurisdictional chaos.
Cases classification has caused innumerable migraines for litigants in the Supreme Court – now, expect the pain to endure.
The Federal Constitutional Court will begin its journey by purging another legacy of our common law system: the doctrine of precedent.
The 27th Amendment guarantees that it starts out unbound and unchecked by the prior precedent of this country built since its inception.
No precedent of the Supreme Court will be binding, especially not ones that say you can strike down constitutional amendments.
There is another constitutional Rubicon that is crossed: the first batch of constitutional court judges is to be appointed directly by the president and prime minister.
The Judicial Commission of Pakistan, or any other independent mechanism for that matter, is ignored to avoid any unnecessary surprises.
The separation of powers is deemed irrelevant.
From its inception, such a court would be a court whose legitimacy will remain under question in every decision it passes.
The thirst for control over the judiciary does not stop here.
It snowballs into the power to punish judges that have fallen out of favour with the current regime.
They can now be transferred without their consent via a JCP decision, a JCP where the executive currently enjoys a comfortable majority.
This new power should take care of any troublesome judges in the Islamabad High Court and beyond.
After all, how dare they call out executive interference in their affairs?
When the 26th Amendment was being passed, our concerns were brushed away as alarmist.
The judiciary would remain independent and fulfil its constitutional role.
Unless that constitutional role is rubber-stamping every executive misadventure, those assurances have fallen flat.

In its one-year term, the constitutional bench has validated military trials of civilians, distributed reserved seats to the ruling coalition, agreed to a radical restructuring of the Islamabad High Court and refused to hear challenges to the 26th Amendment itself.
And when there has been even a sliver of pushback, the government has seen fit to simply ignore it.
The constitutional bench had ordered that a law be passed allowing appeals from military trials.
The government has yet to implement this, much like how it chose to ignore the reserved seats case, or the decision to hold elections in Punjab within 90 days in 2023.
This regime is no friend of accountability.
The actions of the constitutional bench are a prelude to what we can expect from a constitutional court: a failure of judicial independence, separation of powers, and our dance with democracy.
The biggest loser in all of this is not just the Supreme Court, but also parliament.
Crippled at its core, it neither debates nor deliberates.
It is handed drafts that are approved in one-day marathon sessions, regardless of their impact on an entire nation.
Floor-crossing is seen as routine and senators appear from nowhere to vote against their parties only to then resign.
There is no need to mince words; this is the biggest attack on our constitutional system since Pakistan’s return to democracy.
The victims of the past have become the oppressors of today.
Gone are arguments of ‘balance’ and institutional harmony.
What remains is the slow, deliberate dismantling of the 18th Amendment’s vision, one amendment after another.
The writer is a lawyer based in Lahore.

A COP30 agenda for Pakistan Pakistan’s narrative at COP30 should begin with a simple premise that is both moral and practical: countries that contributed least to the crisis must not be asked to finance their survival with debt.
The monsoon that now swings between drought and deluge is no longer an anomaly.
It is the new operating condition of our society and economy.
When villages are inundated, when crops fail and when heat shuts schools and factories, the costs land first on families and local governments and then reverberate through national budgets.
That cycle is not a request for charity rather a bill for damages that have accumulated over decades and are now arriving with interest.
So, Pakistan should set out four clear asks that convert ambition into delivery on the ground and turn promises into protection for people in harm’s way.
These asks are framed to be implementable, measurable and aligned with equity and common but differentiated responsibilities.
One, climate finance for the most vulnerable must be provided primarily as grants or on highly concessional terms, and it must not be conditioned on debt accumulation or austerity.
This is the practical meaning of reparations in a climate context.
Public finance for adaptation, resilience and loss and damage should have a clear grant majority.
Any lending should be limited to projects with credible revenue streams that can repay without crowding out health, education or social protection.

A cap on the loan share of public climate finance, annual reporting in grant-equivalent terms and the wider use of climate-resilient debt clauses that pause repayments after disasters would align incentives with reality.
When the international system chooses loans over grants for floodplains and heat-exposed cities, it is not financing climate action but exporting climate risk into national balance sheets.
Two, the New Collective Quantified Goal must move from a headline to a timetable and from a number to a pathway that reaches subnational institutions.

At COP29, governments agreed a New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) to mobilise at least $300 billion per year by 2035 for developing countries, with a broader aim of catalysing $1.3 trillion annually from all sources by 2035.

At COP30, Pakistan should call for an agreed schedule that scales up annual flows with clear checkpoints, for a transparent ledger that distinguishes genuinely new resources from repackaged aid and for independent reconciliation of reported amounts and grant equivalence each year.

The test of this new goal should not be press releases but rather the rate at which funds reach provincial departments, city governments, water utilities, disaster management authorities and community organisations.

To make this real, parties should endorse rapid-access windows that can disburse directly to subnational entities, using standardised fiduciary templates and public dashboards that trace every rupee from approval to implementation.
Within this goal, at least half of public climate finance should be dedicated to adaptation.
Three, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage must operate with the speed and reliability of an emergency service rather than the pace of a ceremonial pledge.
Although during the first week at COP30 the Fund’s Board suggested operational readiness in principle, the details remain largely unresolved.

Pakistan should argue for a predictable replenishment schedule, a country window that supports locally led projects and pre-arranged triggers that release support when rainfall, river flow, heat, or cyclone thresholds are breached based on climate risk vulnerability assessments.

Parametric mechanisms can pay out within days for early recovery and social protection, while a parallel window supports medium-term reconstruction and risk reduction so that communities do not rebuild vulnerability.
The insurance and private capital can also complement this work, but they cannot replace the public responsibility of those with the greatest historical and current emissions.
Four, climate risk should be recognised as a traditional security threat that warrants rapid international assistance to protect critical systems and social stability.
At COP30, discussions in the first week also brought renewed attention to climate-related security risks, a theme that is particularly salient for Pakistan given its geography and regional dynamics.
Multiple interventions from global and regional actors emphasized that climate risks are beginning to destabilise food systems, migration patterns and cross-border relations worldwide.
Pakistan’s case is shaped by the hard geography of shared rivers, shared air and shared risk with its neighbouring country India.

The Indus Basin is governed by a long-standing treaty that reduced the risk of catastrophic miscalculation, yet disputes, data gaps and mistrust around seasonal flows and reservoir operations persist.
In heavy monsoon years, uncoordinated releases compounded downstream flooding in Pakistan which resulted in deluge and affected 4-5 million people.

Likewise, Punjab in Pakistan and India spans a single airshed When crop-residue burning, transport emissions and industrial pollution surge without adequate control measures on any side, smog intensifies on both sides and pushes hospitals to their limits.

Pakistan should therefore press for a climate-security assistance protocol that is cooperative by design: treaty-consistent, time-stamped and independently verifiable data sharing on reservoir levels and release schedules; joint stress-tests for flood corridors; and pre-cleared emergency channels for equipment, fuel and engineering support when thresholds are crossed.

In parallel, a clean-air diplomacy track should synchronise seasonal restrictions, accelerate residue-management technology and deploy compatible monitoring so each side’s actions are visible, comparable and accountable.
The objective is to prevent environmental indicators from becoming instruments of pressure or suspicion; the way to do that is verifiable cooperation.
To ensure these asks translate into results, Pakistan should table an accountability mechanism that binds pledges to delivery.

After the 2022 floods, the Geneva conference produced pledges of $10.98 billion for Pakistan, but only about 5.0 per cent took the form of grants, the remainder being loans, and by June 2025 just 27 per cent had actually been disbursed.
The gap between podium numbers and money on the ground cannot persist.
COP30 should therefore establish a pledge-to-impact regime with three pillars.
First, a legally anchored registry tracks every commitment in grant-equivalent terms, with quarterly milestones and automatic reclassification of undisbursed sums as ‘at risk’.

Second, a compliance and delivery review compares pledged timelines to actual transfers and project start dates; chronic under-delivery triggers make-good obligations, such as topping up the Loss and Damage window, buying down interest on existing climate loans to grant equivalence, or paying modest non-delivery fees into a pooled facility.
Third, all contributors and intermediaries publish machine-readable, recipient-level data so civil society, parliaments and auditors can verify flows.
A simple metric, the Pledge-to-Impact Ratio, should be reported annually for each contributor and for each fund: how much was pledged, how much arrived, how fast it arrived and what it achieved.
The new goal should include a distribution rule that prioritises high-vulnerability regions in South Asia, small island states and least developed countries.

The contributors and intermediaries should publish subnational distributions within recipient countries so funds do not cluster in capitals or in projects that are easy to finance but marginal to risk reduction.
In Pakistan, that means resources must reach delta districts at sea level, peri-urban settlements along hill torrents, and glacier-affected valleys where hazards are compounding.
Finance that arrives in Islamabad but not in Rajanpur, Dadu or Charsadda is climate finance in name more than in effect.
These international responsibilities do not absolve Pakistan of action at home.
Ultimately, the first week of COP30 reaffirmed that the real measure of climate finance is not the volume of pledges but the experience of people at the frontline.
The argument should return to people rather than process.
If the world can agree on those points and be held to them, climate justice will begin to feel like justice.
If it cannot, solidarity will be rehearsed while the most exposed face the next season alone.
The writer is an environmental scientist and leads the ecological sustainability and circular economy programme at the Sustainable Development Policy Institute (SDPI), Islamabad.
She is also a member of the Punjab Climate Change Committee.

Reclassification of 41 candidates on reserved seats goes beyond SC mandate: Justice Mandokhail No authority, including the court, can declare a candidate independent or alter their status: dissent note ISLAMABAD: Justice Jamal Khan Mandokhail has released a detailed dissent in the reserved seats case, stating that the ruling on 41 candidates overstepped constitutional powers and rested on factual inaccuracies.
"The judgment under review, to this extent, is in excess of the power granted to the Supreme Court by Article 187," he wrote in the dissenting note released a day ago.

Justice Mandokhail had served on the now-defunct Constitutional Bench, which ended after the 27th Constitutional Amendment, which overturned the top court's decision, by a majority of seven judges, granting Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) reserved seats.

The apex court stressed that all 41 candidates were independent when they joined the Sunni Ittehad Council (SIC) under constitutional provisions, and their status had never been a pending matter before the Court.
He observed that neither any authority nor the court has the power to change the status of any candidate.
"We have already held that no authority including the Court has the power to declare a candidate independent or change his status contrary to his declaration," he wrote.
The jurist declared that granting the candidates 15 days to join another party was both unconstitutional and unsupported by the record.
"This relief is an error of the Constitution and law, as well as an error of facts floating on the surface of the record," the dissent stated.
The judge also argued that Article 187 does not grant "unlimited powers", adding that complete justice applies only to matters actually under adjudication.
He warned that reclassifying the 41 members as independents amounted to judicial overreach.
Justice Mandokhail said no evidence existed to establish any PTI affiliation of the candidates before they joined SIC.
He further noted that the majority ignored Article 51(6)(d), which governs the allocation of reserved seats.
Once a returned candidate joins a political party, the dissent added, they cannot leave it without facing consequences under Article 63-A, including loss of the seat.
"No authority, including the Supreme Court, can alter the status of a vote," he wrote.
Pointing towards the flaws in the CB's ruling, Justice Mandokhail concluded that the judgment under review cannot be sustained.
Azad Kashmir is an administrative territory of the Pakistani-administered Kashmir.
It has 10 first-order administrative divisions called "districts," and each district is divided into tehsils.
Geographically, the northern districts of Azad Kashmir encompass the lower part of the Himalayas.
The southern districts of Azad Kashmir, which consist of the Bhimber, Kotli, and Mirpur districts have extremely hot weather in the summer and moderately cold weather in the winter.
Azad Kashmir receives rainfall in both the winter and summer seasons, with Muzaffarabad being among the wettest areas of Azad Kashmir.
The culture in the northern districts is similar to that of the people of Gilgit-Baltistan, where Balti, Gujari and other languages are spoken.
In the central districts like Poonch, etc., the Hindko and Gujari languages are spoken, and in the southern districts, the culture of the people is similar to that of the Potoharis.

List of districts History In 1985 Azad Kashmir consisted of 4 districts, Muzaffarabad, Poonch, Mirpur and Kotli Hattian was a subdivision of Muzaffarabad, Bhimber was a subdivision of Mirpur, Bagh and Haveli were subdivisions of Poonch.
In 1987 Bagh became a separate district from Poonch with Haveli as a subdivion - the other districts remained unchanged.
In 1996, Azad Kashmir consisted of 7 districts, Muzaffarabad, Bagh, Poonch, Pallandri, Mirpur, Kotli and Bhimber.
In 2006, Azad Kashmir consisted of 8 districts, Muzaffarabad, Neelum, Mirpur, Bhimber, Kotli, Poonch, Bagh and Sudhnuti (formerly Pallandri).
The current set-up of 10 districts was established in 2009.

Oman’s labor law explains annual leave for expats - By Web Desk - - Oct 20, 2026 The Bureau of Emigration and Overseas Employment of Pakistan has issued labor rights guidelines for Pakistani workers employed in Oman, highlighting annual leave entitlements, leave arrangements, travel benefits and end-of-service payments.
The guidelines explain the provisions of Oman’s Labour Law, promulgated under Royal Decree No.
53/2023, which guarantees employees at least 30 days of annual leave with full pay under Article 78.
Employees can take annual leave after completing at least six months of service with their employer.
They may carry forward up to 30 days of unused leave, although this limit may be exceeded if work requirements prevent them from taking their leave.
Annual leave periods may also be combined by mutual agreement.

The law provides an additional benefit for non-Omani workers, entitling them to return air tickets during annual leave to travel to their home country and back to their workplace after the leave period.
It also states that employees cannot waive their right to annual leave.
However, an alternative leave arrangement may be introduced in sectors specified by the Minister of Labour, provided it offers greater benefits to workers.
Article 81 sets out further rules governing annual leave.
Employers may divide annual leave into separate periods according to operational requirements, although this provision does not apply to young workers.
Where work demands require it, employers may postpone an employee’s annual leave for up to six months.
The law also seeks to ensure that workers receive adequate rest, requiring every employee to take at least 30 days of annual leave once every two years.
In certain circumstances, employers may compensate workers financially for unused annual leave, calculated based on their basic wage, provided the employee gives written consent.
If employment ends before a worker has used their accumulated annual leave, the employer must pay compensation equivalent to the employee’s full wage for the outstanding leave days.
Defending the amendment The planned 27th Amendment to the constitution of Pakistan was unanimously passed by the Senate of Pakistan on November 10, by a vote of 64-0.
The proposed changes to the constitution rest mainly on two fronts, the armed forces and the country’s judicature.
The proposals for both, the federal government argues, are meant to make the functioning of both institutions more efficient and streamlined.
As for the armed forces, the proposed changes contained in the 27th Amendment to Article 243 are being pushed to modernise and streamline the operation and command of the armed forces.

The argument is made that even India has created the post of chief of defence staff, whose task would be to act as a strategic adviser to the government of the day, led by the prime minister, on all matters related to the three services.
The three services – army, navy and air force – will, of course, continue to be led by their respective service chiefs who will have complete operational control and command as before.
That said, the proposed changes raise many questions, not least about the checks and balances contained in the constitution and also regarding democratic governance in the country.
For instance, the creation of a Federal Constitutional Court may be seen as an attempt to dilute the powers of the Supreme Court.
Now, moving on to the proposed changes relating to Article 243 of the constitution.
The federal government is well within its rights to legislate that armed forces officers may be elevated to the rank of field marshal, marshal of the air force or admiral of the fleet.
However, a contentious debate has followed other proposals, especially those that say that all such officers will retain their title, privileges and rank for life.
Furthermore, holders of these offices will enjoy the same constitutional protection afforded to the president of Pakistan by Article 248 – related to immunity.
While having such immunity may make sense while the official is holding the said office, anything beyond that would have been a stretch – something the final draft seems to have taken care of.
The prime minister was also absolutely right in refusing to include any such constitutional immunity for his post after some of his supporters advocated such inclusion.

Any holder of public office or an appointed office, such as that of a service chief or a service chief who has been promoted etc, should be accountable and answerable for his/her actions to the constitution, given that he or she is appointed under the constitution to serve and protect the citizens and state of Pakistan.
This is why lifetime immunity without any conditions would not have made sense.

The advantages of the proposals relating to Article 243, it has been argued, are that they create a clearer chain of command of the three services of the armed forces, and this would give the system greater clarity.
However, it is difficult to justify and defend the grant of immunity for life, which in any case is not what Article 248 bestows on the office of the president.
The proposals may also dilute civilian supremacy and remove constitutional checks and balances on a very important state institution.
Of course, it may be argued that this was already the case in Pakistan – but to that a counter-question can easily be asked: So should that influence be accepted and in fact further expanded?

As for the proposals that relate to the judiciary, it has been argued that shifting the power to transfer superior court judges to a judicial commission while also increasing parliamentary oversight of the process of appointment and transfer of judges should strengthen democracy, since parliament is elected by the people.
Of course, at the same time, it would be accurate to say that the passing of the 27th Amendment will mean that the Supreme Court of Pakistan will no longer be supreme.

At the very least, the draft of the proposed 27th Amendment should have been posted on the website of the National Assembly so that the general public could debate it, and so that they could at least be informed about the significant changes that have been proposed in the country’s polity.
The aim and objective of any amendment to the constitution should unequivocally be to further the public good and make life better for citizens of Pakistan.
They should not be seen as benefiting a single individual or institution at the expense of others.
The writer is a journalist based in Karachi.

Federal Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Dr Tariq Fazal Chaudhary on Tuesday said the imposition of emergency and Governor’s Rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa followed the provincial government’s lack of cooperation with the federal government and state institutions in the fight against terrorism.

KP emergency, governor’s rule aimed at restoring peace: Dr.Tariq ISLAMABAD, Oct 20 (APP):Federal Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Dr Tariq Fazal Chaudhary on Tuesday said the imposition of emergency and Governor’s Rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa followed the provincial government’s lack of cooperation with the federal government and state institutions in the fight against terrorism.
Addressing a press conference, he said emergency and Governor’s Rule were imposed through a presidential order on October 11 under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution, respectively.
Both measures were subsequently endorsed by Parliament and a joint sitting, completing the constitutional requirements, he added.

He said Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi had assumed the powers of the provincial government, while an 11-member advisory council comprising highly qualified professionals with distinguished records in their respective fields had been constituted to assist him.
Local tribal elders had also been included in councils formed for 12 terrorism-affected districts to ensure community participation in consultations and intelligence-based operations.

Dr Tariq Fazal said the imposition of emergency might have been avoided had the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI)-led provincial government cooperated with the federal government, state institutions, law enforcement agencies and security forces in counterterrorism efforts.

He recalled that during negotiations held in Islamabad on the prime minister’s direction, the federal government had sought the provincial government’s cooperation and assurances regarding counterterrorism measures.

The minister said terrorism had affected the entire country and could not be controlled without full cooperation between the provincial government, federal institutions, the armed forces and security agencies.

He added that terrorist incidents had increased significantly, particularly over the past two years, while personnel and officers of the armed forces, police and Frontier Corps continued to sacrifice their lives in counterterrorism operations.

He said Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had contacted the provincial leadership several times through back-channel communications to seek cooperation, with some contacts reported in the media and others remaining unreported.
However, he said that the provincial government’s non-cooperation had continued, leaving the federal government with no option but to take the decision.

Dr Tariq Fazal also identified cross-border infiltration from Afghanistan as a major security challenge and alleged that the provincial government had refused to cooperate with the federal government’s policy to address the issue.

He said the federal government possessed information about the situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa beyond what had been reported in the media and was committed, alongside the security forces, to controlling infiltration and eliminating terrorism.

The minister urged all opposition parties to develop a political consensus against terrorism, saying national security, peace and the future of Pakistan’s children must remain above political differences.

Criticising PTI, Dr Tariq Fazal said the party had remained in power in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa for 12 to 13 years but had been unable to establish the desired level of peace, particularly over the past two to two-and-a-half years.
He questioned the party’s approach to counterterrorism, saying security personnel were sacrificing their lives while political activities and protests continued on the streets.
He urged the PTI leadership to reconsider its position, engage with the federal government and develop consensus on counterterrorism efforts.
He said intelligence-based operations were already under way in the province and called on opposition parties to participate in these efforts rather than oppose them.

Referring to previous negotiations between the government and opposition, Dr Tariq Fazal said Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had invited the opposition for talks and the government had participated in the process sincerely.
He said representatives of both sides had held extensive discussions over two days, working on several drafts until around 2:30am.
According to him, the government had incorporated the opposition’s proposals into the draft agreement, but the opposition leadership ultimately rejected it.
He clarified that his criticism was not directed at the six opposition representatives who participated in the negotiations.
Instead, he questioned the role of the broader opposition leadership in rejecting the proposed agreement.

The minister said the negotiations had initially proposed imposing emergency measures in 12 terrorism-affected districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to facilitate cooperation between the provincial and federal governments in restoring peace.
The proposal was subsequently narrowed to five districts, where the opposition was asked to cooperate with law enforcement agencies and support operations against terrorists.
However, he said, the opposition had not accepted even the revised proposal.
Questioning the provincial government’s approach, he asked whether restoring peace in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was solely the federal government’s responsibility.

He said provincial governments facing terrorism generally sought additional federal security personnel, resources and intelligence-based operations, whereas the federal government had repeatedly urged the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government to cooperate with law enforcement agencies.
Dr Tariq Fazal reiterated that the government remained ready to resume negotiations.
He said the prime minister had again extended an invitation to the opposition from the floor of the House, making it clear that talks could take place if the opposition was willing.

Comparing the situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa with Balochistan, the minister said terrorism was also a serious challenge in the latter province, but its provincial administration and chief minister were cooperating with federal institutions and law enforcement agencies in the fight against militants.
He said the Balochistan chief minister was confronting terrorists on the front line and cooperating with security agencies rather than refusing to participate in counterterrorism operations.
He described this difference between the approaches of the two provincial administrations as significant in addressing the country’s security challenges.
He expressed regret that some people were linking the imposition of emergency and Governor’s Rule to other issues, including mineral resources.
The minister said the people of a province had the first right to benefit from its natural resources.

International companies involved in joint exploration projects, he added, were expected to follow international standards and ensure that exploration activities did not create difficulties for local communities.

He said all four provinces needed further investment in education and healthcare, adding that revenues generated from natural resources, including minerals, oil and gas, could help finance development and improve public services.
However, he stressed that political consensus and a conducive environment were essential for effectively utilising these resources.
He also said Pakistan was being recognised internationally as a regional stabilising force, referring to the efforts of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir.
He urged political parties not to undermine the country’s progress through political confrontation.

He expressed confidence that lasting peace would eventually be established in the province, paving the way for development and prosperity. “We can sacrifice politics, but we cannot sacrifice the state, national interests or state institutions,” he said, reaffirming the government’s commitment to national security, stability and development.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) categorizes coral reefs as essential habitats, acting as nurseries and spawning grounds for countless fish species, crustaceans, mollusks, and marine food webs.

According to the MIT Science Policy Review, coral reefs deliver substantial economic and cultural benefits – through fisheries, tourism, recreation, and even pharmaceutical discoveries – worth trillions of dollars globally.

The initial swell in ocean-centric marketing followed Hawaii’s 2018 ban on sunscreens containing oxybenzone and octinoxate – chemicals that filter ultraviolet (UV) radiation, which are harmful to ocean ecosystems.

The bill was informed by a 2015 study published in the Archives of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology, which examined how chemical sunscreens can damage coral larvae and cells, causing coral bleaching, making them vulnerable to infection, and preventing them from getting the nutrients needed for survival.

The study found that “the chemicals cause bleaching, deformities, DNA damage, and ultimately death in coral when they’re washed off beachgoers or discharged into wastewater treatment plants and deposited into bodies of water,” states a CNN article.

The Hawaii legislation represented a watershed moment in environmental regulation, drawing global attention to the hidden ecological costs of UV chemical filters and inspiring other nations, such as the US Virgin Islands, Palau, Aruba, and Thailand, to adopt similar restrictions to protect ocean life.

While the chemical impact of sunscreens on marine environments is well-documented, critics argue that the personal care product (PCP) industry doesn’t always honor the principles of the 2018 legislation passed by Hawaii.

How the Chemicals in Sunscreen Are Harming Ocean Life: According to a 2023 National Geographic article, “14,000 tons of sunscreen are thought to wash into the oceans each year,” and 82,000 chemicals from PCPs are found in the seas.
The Basic Principles Committee (BPC) was a specialized committee set up in March 1949 by Khawaja Nazimuddin on the advice of prime minister Liaquat Ali Khan.
The committee's sole purpose was to determine the basic underlying principles that would determine future constitutions and legislature in Pakistan.
Initial recommendations and proposals suggested by the BPC were strongly criticized in the local media and the public.

Much of the criticism came from East Pakistan where the committee proposals were said to be subversive of the ideology of Pakistan, under-representing the majority province and neglecting the Bengali language thoroughly in the constitutional and legislative process.
The suggestion of the formation of a religious oversight board was also seen as "undemocratic [and] an insult to Islam".

Formation Before the first constituent assembly of Pakistan could formulate any constitution or legislature, it was necessary to put in order the basic principles that would determine how the constitution should be framed.
On 7 March 1949, the Objectives Resolution was presented, which serves to this day as the grundnorm for constitutional process in Pakistan.
The resolution was adopted by the constituent assembly on 12 March 1949, when 21 members voted for it.
The Basic Principles Committee (BPC) was formed on the same day by the constituent assembly.
The committee was set up by governor-general Khawaja Nazimuddin upon advice from Prime Minister Liaquat Ali Khan.
It was presided over by Maulvi Tamizuddin Khan with Liaquat Ali Khan serving also as its vice-president.
The committee had 24 other members, though not all were members of the constituent assembly as well.
The purpose of the BPC was to formulate the basic principles based on the Objectives Resolution using which the future constitutions of Pakistan would be framed.
The committee was asked to propose basic principles and concerned recommendations that would help the constituent assembly with their constitutional and legislative tasks.

In order to do so, the committee had its initial two meetings in April 1949 where three distinct sub-committees were formed to deal with specialized tasks: A subcommittee to deal with matters of federal and provincial constitution and distribution of powers; A subcommittee to deal with matters of adult franchise; and, A subcommittee to deal with matters of the judiciary.
First proposal The BPC presented its initial report to the constituent assembly on 28 September 1950.

The main features presented in the report were also simultaneously published in an article in the Dawn newspaper a day later, ushering strong criticism from the public, particularly from critics in East Pakistan.
Salient features The report called for the state of Pakistan to be a federation where Urdu was to be the state language.

It also formally recognized the Objectives Resolution as an integral part of the constitution of Pakistan and the legislative process, suggesting that the resolution should be incorporated into the constitution as "a directive principle of [state] policy".
The report also presented a suggestion for the central legislature was to be a bicameral with an upper house consisting of 100 members, and a lower house consisting of 400 members.

The upper house was to be elected by the provincial legislature serving as the representative institution of the provinces, while the lower house was to be elected by the people on the basis of adult franchise.
The tenure of both houses was to be five years with both enjoying equal power.
The decisions regarding budget or monetary bills were to be decided in joint sessions of the two houses.
The head of state was to be elected by a joint session of the two houses for a term of five years working on the advice of the prime minister.
The federal legislature would have the authority to remove the head of state.
The head of state was given added powers like the authority to abrogate the constitution and issue ordinances.
Each province would have its own legislature elected on the basis of adult franchise for a term of five years.
The head of the provincial legislature was to be elected by the head of state for a term of five years working on the advice of the chief minister.
The Supreme Court was to be the head of judiciary consisting of a chief justice and 2 to 6 judges.
It was suggested to establish High Courts for each province.
It was also the first time that the establishment of a religious oversight board was suggested.

A board of ulema (religious scholars) was suggested to be appointed by the head of state and provincial governors to examine the processes of law-making ensuring those laws to be in accordance with the Quran and the Sunnah.

Legislative power was to be divided into three lists: Federal list, comprising 67 subjects on which the central legislature would legislate; Provincial list, comprising 35 items on which the provincial legislature would legislate; and, Concurrent list, comprising 37 items on which both the central and provincial legislatures had the authority to legislate.
The residuary powers were vested in the centre.
The procedure to amend the constitution was made very rigid.
It required majority approval from the central and provincial legislatures.
In case of any dispute, the Supreme Court would have the authority to interpret the constitution.
Reaction and criticism These initial recommendations raised a firestorm of protest.
It was called reactionary, undemocratic, an insult to Islam, smacking of fascist approach, subversive of the ideology of Pakistan and a gross betrayal of the solemn pledges made to the people.

In particular, the report was highly criticized by Sris Chandra Chattopadhyay who observed that East Pakistan, being more populous than West Pakistan, would be under-represented if both were given an equal number of seats in the upper house.
This would have effectively rendered the eastern province a minority.
Bengali critics also voiced concern over making Urdu the national language while thoroughly neglecting the Bengali language from the constitutional arena.
There was also criticism of the proposals for a strong centre with vast powers on financial matters.
On 4 October 1950, in an editorial published in the Nawa-i-Waqt, the report was called a "charter of people's slavery".
Amidst furious criticisms, Liaquat Ali Khan refrained from considering the report and invited the committee to present revised proposals and suggestions.
He also called for general suggestions and comments from the public in order to incorporate public opinion.
Another special sub-committee was formed therein to facilitate such measures.
This sub-committee was headed by Sardar Abdur Rab Nishtar and later presented a revised report in the constituent assembly in July 1952.

Second proposal In light of the criticism received for the first proposal, the committee moved towards including greater participation of public opinion into their successive report to the constituent assembly.
An interim draft for a second report of the BPC had been finalized by the third week of November and was to be presented to the Constituent Assembly on 23 November 1952.
Its presentation was however postponed at the very last minute due to reservations held by some members of the committee.
The BPC held a meeting on 19 December 1952 where the final draft for the second proposal was signed.
But, in the conspicuous absence of Mumtaz Daultana, Nurul Amin, Begum Jahanara Shahnawaz, A.H.
Gardezi, Justice Abdul Rashid and Mohammad Akram Khan, the report was signed by Malik Shaukat Ali signed it conditionally.
The report was presented to the assembly on 22 December 1952.
Salient features The main features of the committee's second report focused prominently on the place of Islam in the future constitution of Pakistan.
The Objective Resolution was adopted as a preamble to the proposed constitution and the principles defined therein were to guide the state.
With Sardar Abdur Rab Nishtar at the helm of the committee, the second proposal adopted a more Islamic stance.
Some suggest it merely contained "religious rhetoric".
A specific clause was added to the proposal which laid down procedures to prevent any legislation that is made outside the limits prescribed in the Quran and the Sunnah.
It was suggested that existing laws be also brought in conformity with the Islamic principles.
The report emphasized the importance of a board of ulema that would vet legislation to make sure that it was in keeping with the teachings of Islam.
The committee also recommended that the head of state be a Muslim and that separate electorates be maintained for Muslims and non-Muslims.
During the debate concerning the proposition of the head of state being a Muslim, Sardar Shaukat Hayat Khan observed that the provision was undeniably against fundamental rights.

There was even more criticism surrounding the inclusion of religious rhetoric in the committee's proposals especially in the formation of the board of ulema; critics called such initiatives "undemocratic [and] an insult to Islam".
Nawa-i-Waqt defended the suggestion of creating the board as being "utterly democratic".
On 31 December 1952, Dawn newspaper expressed concern that the committee may have exceeded the limits prescribed in the Objectives Resolution.

During a recent visit to Borneo island in the Malay archipelago, I came across a shrimp farm on the coast of the rainforest-covered island, run by a Chinese woman entrepreneur.
Using a seawater reservoir behind a mangrove forest, she had built a business exporting shrimp around the world.
My mind drifted home to Pakistan’s 1,058-kilometre coastline, along Sindh and Balochistan.
Why, I wondered, do we see so little aquaculture of this kind?
I was reminded of a conversation I had with the owner of a hatchery recently established in Gharo in Sindh.
He told me that one of his biggest worries was transporting the hatchlings quickly and safely to fish and shrimp farms in Muzaffargarh, Punjab.
The hatchery is in coastal Sindh, close to the sea and the Indus delta, yet its young fish and shrimp have to travel hundreds of kilometres inland to find farms.
I asked him why people were not investing in fish and shrimp farming in Sindh?
He did not have a clear answer, except to say that there were not enough investors and the business climate is also not supportive.
But the lack of investors is not really an explanation.

The problem in rural Sindh may not be a lack of capital, but its concentration — and the failure to create the conditions in which small businesses can grow into industries Sindh has fertile land, a long coastline and a river, alongside abundant agricultural produce, livestock, fisheries and traditional crafts.
Yet much of this potential has not translated into local processing, packaging and cold-chain businesses that could create jobs beyond agriculture.
THE AGRARIAN DIVIDE Economic historian Imran Ali has documented how British canal colonies transformed western Punjab from the late 19th century.
Irrigation brought semi-arid land under cultivation, encouraging commercial agriculture and the growth of new settlements and market towns.
The colonial project also served revenue, political and military objectives.
Regardless of their motives, the economic landscape was transformed.
Sindh too underwent an irrigation revolution, particularly after the Sukkur Barrage opened in 1932.
But perhaps the social structure on to which this new agricultural wealth was grafted was different.
Economist Mahmood Hasan Khan points out the growth of small owner-cultivators and market relations in parts of Punjab, while the older landlord-sharecropper structure remained much stronger in Sindh.
Economist Akmal Hussain argues that owner-cultivators have greater incentives to invest, potentially generating the savings and demand needed for industrialisation.
Where agricultural income is concentrated in fewer hands, the pattern of investment may be different.

THE CONCENTRATION OF CAPITAL It would, however, be too easy to explain Sindh’s predicament simply by invoking “feudalism.” Political economist Akbar Zaidi argues that agriculture in Pakistan has undergone a substantial capitalist transformation.
Commercialisation and the ‘Green Revolution’ brought capitalist farmers, machinery and wage labour and, in some areas, small manufacturers, skilled workers and service businesses.
Sindh’s sugar mills, cotton ginning and rice milling show that agricultural wealth did become industrial capital.
But large enterprises owned by wealthy families are not the same as a broad base of independent businesses.
Both represent investment and capitalism, but the latter creates a much wider entrepreneurial class.
A farmer investing in transport, a workshop repairing agricultural machinery or a manufacturer producing spare parts can generate further demand for suppliers, traders and services.
Why has this chain remained so weak across much of rural Sindh?
THE CITY AND THE HINTERLAND Perhaps the problem was never simply the absence of capital.
It may have been the concentration of capital and the failure to spread entrepreneurial investment widely enough through its towns and communities.
Economist Kaiser Bengali has described Sindh as having a “dual identity”: Karachi on one side and the rest of the province on the other.

Much of Sindh’s Hindu mercantile and entrepreneurial class migrated to India, while Muslim migrants from different parts of the Subcontinent brought new commercial skills, networks and capital to Karachi.
Over the following decades, Karachi became Pakistan’s great port, financial centre and industrial metropolis.
For someone from rural Sindh with money to invest, a good education or entrepreneurial ability, Karachi offered far greater opportunities than his own town.
Sindh generated considerable wealth at both ends of its economy: agricultural wealth in the countryside and commercial and industrial wealth in Karachi.
Yet the economic centres in between remained relatively weak.
BEYOND INDUSTRIAL ESTATES History, however, can only explain so much.
Nearly eight decades have passed since Independence, and we also have to ask what we have done since then.
Why have Sukkur, Larkana, Nawabshah, Mirpurkhas, Khairpur, Thatta and Badin not developed stronger clusters of small industry?
Industrial estates and special economic zones have been established or proposed outside Karachi, but infrastructure alone does not create an industrial ecosystem.
Regional businesses also need technical training, accessible finance, shared processing and testing facilities, and reliable market connections.
Perhaps the more fundamental question is why we wait for investors instead of creating the conditions that produce investors.
THE MISSING STEP A recent article by journalist Owais Tohid about thousands of women establishing tiny businesses across rural Sindh provides an interesting clue.
These women are raising livestock, stitching clothes, producing handicrafts and running other small businesses with relatively modest amounts of capital.
The problem is what happens next.
How does a woman employing herself begin employing five or ten other women?
How does a workshop become a factory?
How does one successful shrimp farm become twenty, surrounded by hatcheries, feed suppliers, cold storage, processors, transporters and exporters?
This brings me back to that hatchery in Gharo.
The coastline is there, as are the seawater, the hatchery, the technical knowledge and the market.
And yet the hatchlings travel hundreds of kilometres to find the entrepreneurs willing and able to farm them.
Successive governments in Sindh must also bear part of the responsibility.
A political economy historically dominated by large landowners may not have had sufficient incentive to create a broad class of independent entrepreneurs.

Industrial estates have been established, but we have rarely pursued industrial development around the natural strengths of individual regions with the persistence it requires: dates in Khairpur, fisheries and aquaculture along the coast, rice in upper Sindh, fruit processing around Mirpurkhas, and livestock and dairy across much of the province.
Nor can poverty alleviation alone be an economic policy.
There is an obvious need for social protection in a province where millions remain poor.
But cash support, however necessary, cannot by itself create economic mobility.
The larger challenge is to create the conditions in which people can move beyond poverty.

A tenant becoming an owner, a woman running a tiny business beginning to employ others, a workshop growing into a factory, or a farmer’s produce being processed and packaged before it leaves the district rather than being sent elsewhere for someone else to add value to it — these are perhaps better measures of economic development.
The challenge for rural Sindh, therefore, may not simply be to find more investors.

It is to understand why enterprise has failed to spread despite the province’s considerable natural resources and agricultural wealth, and then to create the conditions in which capital, skills and entrepreneurship can come together.
Ultimately, the measure of development should not merely be how many poor people the state is able to support, but how many people are able to reach a point where they no longer need that support.

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Tuesday encouraged members of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) to use national currencies for “mutual settlement” and establish other financial mechanisms to “offset international financial shocks”.
He made the remarks while addressing the SCO Council of Heads of Government (CHG) meeting in Tajikistan’s capital Dushanbe, where he arrived a day earlier.
The SCO comprises 10 member states, namely Pakistan, China, India, Iran, Russia, Kyrgyzstan, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.
The two observer states are Afghanistan and Mongolia.

The CHG is the SCO’s second-highest decision-making body and provides guidance on economic, financial, trade, connectivity and socio-economic cooperation, as well as the organisation’s budgetary matters.
Dar reiterated his call to accelerate local currency settlements in a later address to an expanded-format session of the meeting.
Two members of the SCO, Russia and Iran, face Western sanctions restricting their access to international markets and stifling their economic growth.

In the joint communiqué for the Pakistan-chaired 2024 CHG meeting, SCO member states had reaffirmed the need for consistent implementation of a roadmap on gradual increase in the share of national currencies in mutual settlements.

It underlined the need to protect and promote the World Trade Organisation’s multilateral trade system for inclusive global growth and reduce reliance on the American currency for international trade transactions.

At that summit, PM Shehbaz Sharif had noted “growing consensus among the member states on the use of mutual currencies for settlements” and said such a transition would “shield us from global financial disruptions”.

Speaking in Dushanbe, Dar highlighted that the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) offered “every SCO partner a compelling opportunity to participate in and accelerate our shared journey towards comprehensive economic integration”. “For our region to achieve seamless economic integration, targeted investment in core sectors, most notably in energy and transport, is vital,” he stressed.

The foreign minister criticised “protectionist policies and unilateral coercive measures”, saying they contradicted the principles of international law, “suppress economic growth, block technological progress and increase inequality”. “Therefore, reform of the global financial architecture and trade regimes is essential for achieving equitable global development,” the deputy PM declared.

He said Pakistan strongly advocated for “expanding investments into high-potential industries, including agriculture, mining and minerals, and information technology, to build a resilient and interconnected economic future”.

He expressed Pakistan’s “belief that artificial intelligence, digital transformation, innovation, energy cooperation and international information security should become important pillars of future cooperation within the SCO”.
Dar then recalled the priority areas identified by PM Shehbaz for the SCO Council of Heads of State (CHS) summit that Islamabad is set to host in 2027.

These comprised peace, security and mutual trust; regional connectivity and trade; innovation, AI and digital transformation; climate resilience and sustainable energy; and people-to-people exchanges.
He emphasised that strategic investment in transport and energy infrastructure was not merely beneficial but “absolutely imperative for true regional economic integration”.

At the outset of his speech, Dar extended his appreciation to the Tajik government and people for their “very warm and generous hospitality”. “For the past 25 years, the SCO has remained anchored in the Shanghai spirit of mutual trust and respect for diversity and expanded its mandate to encompass trade, infrastructure, culture and innovation,” he noted.

Dar went on to state that Pakistan’s journey within the SCO highlighted its commitment to the Shanghai spirit, recalling that the country’s chairmanship of SCO’s Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (SCO-RATS) and the SCO Working Group on Poverty Alleviation.

He said Pakistan intended to highlight the role of small and medium enterprises in reducing poverty. ‘Pakistan wants peaceful, regionally integrated Afghanistan’ During his speech at the CHG summit, DPM Dar also raised the issue of cross-border terrorism emanating from Afghanistan.
He reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to a peaceful and stable neighbourhood as an essential foundation for regional development and prosperity.

Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan, that are used for attacks in Pakistan.
Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded.
Concluding his address, Dar congratulated Tajikistan and the heads of SCO’s permanent bodies on the successful completion of the CHG meeting, and congratulated Uzbekistan for taking over the chair.
He also commended the SCO national coordinators for their help in finalising documents.

Dar further highlighted that the intra-SCO trade had expanded significantly, proving that cooperative multilateralism can effectively drive stability and sustainable development across our shared continent. “The future prospects of the SCO remain bright,” the deputy premier remarked, noting that the region was situated at the crossroads of major international trade corridors.

By leveraging our vast natural resources, technological advancements, and vibrant human capital, the SCO could lead digital transformation, industrial growth, and sustainable economic development across Eurasia, he emphasised.
To realise this vision, the foreign minister also proposed recommendations to deepen economic cooperation among SCO countries and expand international partnerships.
Firstly, Dar called for empowering the SCO Chambers of Commerce and Business Council by establishing direct business-to-business links and organising joint trade expos.
He also urged member states to streamline customs procedures to support SMEs.

Secondly, he proposed the strengthening of the SCO Interbank Consortium (IBC). “We must accelerate local currency settlements and enhance the SCO Interbank Consortium framework to mitigate external financial risks, harmonise cross-border payment systems, and facilitate seamless trade financing,” he said.
Pending the establishment of the SCO Development Bank, the IBC can play a more active role in financing infrastructure upgrades, Dar added.
He underlined that Habib Bank Limited (HBL), the current chair of the IBC, can help advance this agenda through close coordination with fellow members.

At last, the foreign minister recommended expanding international partnerships. “The SCO should actively expand structured partnerships with international organisations including the United Nations, Asean, the Economic Cooperation Organisation (ECO), and other international and regional financial institutions, to reinforce an open, rules-based, and inclusive regional order,” Dar underscored.
Together, let us forge a shared future of enduring prosperity for all our people,” he resolved.

Dar meets Tajik top leadership Ahead of the SCO meeting, DPM Dar called on Tajik President Emomali Rahmon, along with other heads of delegations. “President Rahmon welcomed the leaders and emphasised the importance of strengthening regional economic cooperation under the SCO to promote connectivity, stability and shared prosperity,” the Foreign Office (FO) said.
He, along with other delegates, was then welcomed by PM Qohir Rasulzoda.
Later in the day, Dar met with Tajikistan’s FM Sirojiddin Muhriddin on the sidelines of the meeting.
The two ministers “reaffirmed the longstanding brotherly ties between Pakistan and Tajikistan, rooted in shared history, culture and faith”, FO said.
They underscored the need to further expand trade and economic cooperation, enhance regional connectivity and strengthen cooperation in energy, security and people-to-people exchanges.

The foreign ministers also exchanged views on regional and global developments and underscored the importance of continued coordination at regional and multilateral forums to advance shared goals of peace and prosperity, FO added.
The deputy premier then returned to Islamabad in the evening after concluding his “productive visit”, FO said.
During his visit, Dar also held bilateral meetings with his counterparts from SCO member states on the sidelines of the SCO moot, according to FO.
On Monday, Dar held a meeting with the Tajik premier.
He also met with China’s PM Li Qiang and Mongolia’s First DPM Jadambyn Enkhbayar on the sidelines of a banquet dinner hosted for the delegates.
Pakistan, which hosted a CHG meeting in October 2024, is now scheduled to host the CHS summit in 2027 after it assumed the chairmanship last month.
On Sept 30, Dar reviewed preparations for the CHS summit as SCO national coordinators, who were in Islamabad for a meeting, called on him.
In July, Pakistan hosted the 12th meeting of the Heads of Border Services of the Competent Authorities of the SCO.

Emvistegrast pill succeeds in mid-stage bowel disease trial - By Reuters - - Oct 19, 2026 Gilead Sciences said on Monday its experimental once-daily pill emvistegrast reduced symptoms of a chronic bowel illness in more patients than placebo in a mid-stage trial.
Emvistegrast met its main goal in a mid-stage study of adults with moderate to severe ulcerative colitis, a chronic condition that causes inflammation and ulcers in the digestive tract.
The oral drug is designed to block the α4β7 integrin pathway, a target already validated in inflammatory bowel disease.
After 12 weeks, 66% of patients on the 200 mg dose saw their disease symptoms improve, compared with 37% on placebo.
Clinical remission rates were also higher, with 31% of patients on treatment achieving remission versus 8% in the placebo group.
The drug was generally well tolerated, with overall side-effect rates comparable between the treatment and placebo arms and no serious side effects linked to the study medication.

BMO Capital Markets analysts called the data “an incremental positive for Gilead’s inflammatory strategy that establishes emvistegrast as a credible oral α4β7 option.” Based on the results, Gilead said it plans to start a late-stage monotherapy study of the pill in 2027.
About Emvistegrast Emvistegrast (GS-1427) is an investigational oral α4β7 integrin inhibitor being developed for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).
The α4β7 pathway is a clinically validated target in IBD, and emvistegrast is part of Gilead’s broader effort to advance differentiated therapies for inflammatory diseases.
Emvistegrast is not approved anywhere globally, and its safety and efficacy have not been established.

About the SWIFT Study SWIFT is a Phase 2 randomized, placebo-controlled study evaluating the efficacy, safety and tolerability of emvistegrast in adults with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis.

The study was designed to assess the potential of emvistegrast to improve disease activity and clinically meaningful outcomes for people living with ulcerative colitis, while further characterizing its safety profile.
