Fakhar-e-Alam Peshawar , Oct 18 (APP)::Every morning, mothers send their children to school with a kiss, a prayer and the hope of seeing them return with stories of lessons learned and dreams taking shape.
But for the families of 34 children killed in the collapse of Alkhair School in Peshawar’s Dir Colony, one ordinary Thursday morning shattered that promise forever.

Among those who never returned home was 11-year-old Sanan Asad, … Peshawar school tragedy: When a mother’s morning kiss became a final goodbye Fakhar-e-Alam Peshawar , Oct 18 (APP)::Every morning, mothers send their children to school with a kiss, a prayer and the hope of seeing them return with stories of lessons learned and dreams taking shape.
Among those who never returned home was 11-year-old Sanan Asad, whose dream of becoming a police officer ended beneath the rubble of a three-storey building that collapsed at around 8:45 a.m.

His schoolbag, books and uniform remain painful reminders of a future that will never unfold, while his mother struggles to comprehend the loss of a son she expected to see again within hours. “Sanan was a very obedient son.
Their uncle, Tauseef Ahmad, rushed to the school after receiving news of the collapse.
As he approached the building, he heard children crying beneath the rubble. “I suddenly saw Sanan’s body being recovered by the rescue officials from the debris,” he recalled.
At the family hujra, relatives and neighbors now gather to offer condolences following the funeral prayers and Qul for the five children.
For Sanan’ s mother, ordinary household moments have become unbearable reminders of her loss.
Beyond the grief, the collapse has raised urgent questions about the safety of educational institutions across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
An initial police investigation identified the building’s age and poor construction quality as major factors.
The preliminary report submitted by SSP Operations to the Capital City Police Officer, Peshawar, intensified concerns about structural inspections and enforcement of building standards.
Professor Dr Ibrahim Khan, former director of education, said the children had barely begun their lives. “They had dreams in their eyes.
Their parents sent them to school in the hope that education would give them a better future.
Sadly, they went to school to receive education, not to lose their lives,” he told APP.
Questioning whether repeated incidents could continue to be treated as isolated accidents, he cited figures suggesting nearly 300 children had died in similar incidents over three years.

He questioned whether education officials were fulfilling their responsibilities to inspect school buildings, ensure children’ s safety and enforce the law, stressing that negligence and abuse of authority must have consequences where established.

Following the tragedy, the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Elementary and Secondary Education Department ordered immediate safety assessments, prioritizing schools identified as potentially dangerous through complaints, media reports and other credible sources.
Authorities have been directed to suspend classes immediately in buildings declared unsafe and relocate students to nearby schools or other secure locations.
Classes may resume only after necessary repairs and certification by the relevant technical authority.
Districts have also been instructed to submit reports covering inspections, unsafe buildings, relocation arrangements and corrective measures by noon on October 21.
Education Adviser Dr Syed Amir Abdullah said a province-wide review had been launched.
Private schools are to be assessed through district authorities, while unsafe public-school buildings will be repaired, vacated or closed as necessary.
The government has also announced financial assistance for bereaved families.

Deputy Commissioner Peshawar Afaq Wazir distributed compensation cheques worth Rs21 million among families of the deceased children on the directives of Governor Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Faisal Karim Kundi.
Families who traveled to their native districts for the burials will receive assistance upon their return, officials said.
The deputy commissioner also confirmed that the school owner had been arrested and an FIR registered.
For families like Sanan’ s, however, no compensation can measure the value of a child.
No cheque can restore a son who dreamed of wearing a police uniform and no official statement can bring back the laughter that once filled their home.
Pakistan has witnessed too many tragedies in which children have paid the ultimate price for negligence and failures of oversight.
Condolences are offered, inquiries ordered and promises made, but grieving parents must live with their loss long after public attention fades.
The Dir Colony tragedy must therefore become a turning point.
Every public and private school in the province needs a credible structural safety assessment, verifiable safety certification and regular inspections.
Where negligence or criminal misconduct is established, accountability must follow without political or administrative pressure.
Sanan, Mubasshir, Amir, Haleema and Romaisa will never return to their classrooms.
Their deaths must not become another statistic forgotten with time.
Behind every inspection report is a child’s life, and behind every school gate is a parent’s trust.
The nation must turn its grief into action so that no mother ever again sends her child to school with a loving kiss in the morning, only to receive a lifeless body in return.

Tesla renames 'full self-driving' to 'assisted driving' in Europe: What to know European regulators flagged Tesla's old name as misleading because the system demands constant supervision, keeping drivers fully responsible.

Tesla has quietly rebranded its controversial "Full Self-Driving" (FSD) software package to "Assisted Driving" across several European markets as the automaker ramps up efforts to secure regulatory approval from European safety authorities.

EAs reported, EV-maker Tesla has started calling its "Full Self-Driving" feature "Tesla Assisted Driving" on its European websites, dropping a name regulators have said was misleading, as CEO Elon Musk pushes for EU-wide approval for the software.
The rebrand comes after Germany said on Tuesday Tesla had offered to switch to the new name.
Musk has described the self-driving technology as key to the company's future growth.
Tesla's FSD page for Slovakia now redirects to a "Tesla Assisted Driving" page, as do pages in other European countries such as Germany, Spain and the Netherlands.

The US site still refers to it as "Full Self-Driving (Supervised)." A Reuters report published this week detailed how Tesla mounted a campaign to win approval for FSD in Europe, including encouraging owners and supporters to lobby national regulators for faster approvals.
Several regulators have said the old name is misleading because the system requires constant supervision and drivers remain legally responsible.
According to documents, a Norwegian Tesla owner in November also asked the Norwegian Public Roads Administration whether Tesla's changes to how it described FSD addressed concerns about the name.
Eight EU countries already allow the system, with Slovakia expecting to become the ninth within days.
An EU-wide vote has been pushed from October to at least December, with countries like France conducting additional testing.

By shifting the nomenclature to "Assisted Driving", aligning more closely with standard Level 2 driver-assistance classifications, Tesla aims to clear the compliance hurdles needed to legally roll out its advanced driver-assistance features on European roads.

For Pakistan, Turkey is one of its closest countries: an ally, a partner, a country whose history is better known here than that of many others.
But even a close country may not be known in its entirety.
Turkey’s secularism is neither a borrowing nor a compromise, but the principle on which Mustafa Kemal Atatürk founded the republic and which was incorporated into its constitution in 1937.
For seventy years, it determined what Turkish schools, universities and the civil service looked like.
For the past two decades, Turkey has been governed by a different tradition, a religious-conservative one, and beyond its borders the first tradition is not always remembered.
In autumn 2026, it was brought back into focus by a dispute sparked by Azerbaijan, which approved uniform requirements for school dress in September.

The decision concerned only public schools, but it was discussed far beyond them — most loudly in Turkey, where a presidential adviser, lawmakers from the ruling party and protesters outside the Azerbaijani consulate in Istanbul called on Baku to reconsider it.
For Pakistan, where the hijab is an everyday feature of school life, this reaction is understandable.
But it reflects only one of the two traditions that coexist in Turkey.
The other deserves no less attention.
In substance, the decision was narrower than the reaction to it might suggest.

The headscarf was not included among the elements of the school uniform; the regulation concerns only public schools and only uniforms: universities, workplaces, streets and mosques remain unaffected.
The same document permits national dress at school events.

The country’s highest religious authority, the Caucasus Muslims Office, called the hijab an important religious obligation — and stated in the same declaration that citizens have no right to oppose decisions of the state.
Azerbaijan is a secular state under its Constitution and a Muslim country in terms of its population, and these two characteristics have never been considered contradictory there.

The Turkish Republic was founded on the same principle — and although restrictions on headscarves in universities and government institutions have been lifted under the current government, the tradition on which the republic was built has not disappeared.

It is represented by the Kemalist opposition, a significant part of academia, the judiciary and the military — and by a substantial part of society for whom the secular state remains part of national identity, rather than a rejection of faith.
It was from this Turkey that different assessments of Azerbaijan’s decision emerged.
Theologian and columnist Cemil Kılıç urged Azerbaijan to ‘carefully preserve its secular identity’.

Our brotherhood stands above current political events, disagreements and debates.’ Just how alive this tradition remains was demonstrated by Northern Cyprus, where, six months before the events in Azerbaijan, the same dispute unfolded in the opposite direction.
In April 2025, the government of the Turkish Cypriot administration, which is close to Ankara, allowed female students in upper secondary school to wear headscarves in public schools.

The response was the largest protests in Turkish Cypriot history: on 8 April, around thirteen thousand people marched through northern Nicosia under the slogan ‘Cyprus is secular and will remain secular’; in May, a general strike brought the north of the island to a standstill.
President Erdoğan sharply condemned the protesters and promised to visit.

In September, the Constitutional Court of the Turkish Cypriot administration overturned the permission following a lawsuit by the teachers’ union, on the grounds that only parliament had the authority to make such a decision.
In October, Turkish Cypriots elected the leader of the secular opposition, Tufan Erhürman, as president.
In other words, Turkish Cypriots — a Turkic people, Muslims living under Turkey’s protection and with its financial support — defended secular schooling in defiance of Ankara.
Six months later, Azerbaijan made the same decision and faced the same criticism from the same circles.
In both cases, the dispute took place within the Turkish world itself — over what public schools should be like and who has the right to decide.
Baku’s response, delivered on 13 October by the ruling New Azerbaijan Party, addressed precisely this dispute.

The secular tradition in Turkey is neither a thing of the past nor merely an opposition position, but part of what Turkey remains: its Constitution, its universities, its military, millions of its citizens.
Azerbaijan arrived at the secular state by its own path and reached the same conclusion: faith belongs to the individual, school belongs to everyone.
In this sense, the autumn controversy is not a confrontation between Ankara and Baku.
It continues a debate Turkey has been having with itself for a century: about the place of religion in the state, about who schools belong to, about Atatürk’s legacy.
Azerbaijan’s decision merely carried that debate beyond Turkey’s borders — and Baku found both its own position and supporters among Turks themselves.
For readers in Pakistan, the debate offers another perspective on the different traditions that coexist within a close partner, Turkey.

China orders development of national blockchain network in economic blueprint: Here’s why China is planning a national blockchain network as part of its significant new economic plan Beijing is reportedly moving to centralize blockchain infrastructure under state control as an integral component of a broader digital economy strategy.

This system would stand in stark contrast to public and permissionless blockchains used for Bitcoin and Ethereum.

Blockchain infrastructure projects are primarily discussed by Chinese officials though the digital yuan itself does not rely on an open blockchain in the way decentralized cryptocurrencies do.

Cryptocurrency markets have historically had a muted reaction to Chinese blockchain infrastructure announcements since such projects are typically insulated from public crypto trading and token markets.
Nonetheless, investors particularly operating in the Chinese market may watch for further crucial details on strategic network development.

SVI hosts two-day Non-Proliferation Conference – 2026 ISLAMABAD, Oct 20 (APP):The Strategic Vision Institute (SVI), Islamabad, hosts the second iteration of Islamabad Non-Proliferation Conference 2026, a two-day international event bringing together a distinguished group of scholars and experts from around the world.
The conference aims at fostering constructive dialogue on global strategic issues and sharing Pakistan’s policy perspectives.
Dr Naeem Salik, Executive Director (ED), SVI, welcomed the distinguished guests to the International Nonproliferation Conference (INC) 2026.
Dr Nasir Hafeez, Director, SVI, subsequently introduced the conference to the esteemed audience.
The inaugural address was delivered by Lt.
Sarfraz Sattar, HI (M), (Retd.), Advisor, NCA.

He mentioned that the disruptive technologies sit at the heart of the push towards bigger and better Nuclear Weapons, against the efforts of restraint or stability on the road to disarmament and sustained economic development.

He said, that there has been a shift in the nuclear age marked by the change of threat perception from rouge or non-state actors getting access to nuclear weapons towards the challenge of Great Power Competition and the possibility of interstate conflict in a more contested international system.
He mentioned South Asia as a nuclear flashpoint, owing to India’s ultranationalist tendencies.
We face Hindutva ideology which is in pursuit of Akhand Bharat.
He further mentioned that the nuclear non-use taboo seems to be weakening as we see the likelihood of interstate wars increasing both in lethality and expense.
The sole function of global nuclear order is also under extreme stress.
Khalid Ahmed Kidwai, (Retd.), Advisor Development, National Command Authority (NCA), delivered the keynote address.

He examined Pakistan’s perspective on credible deterrence, strategic balance, and strategic stability in South Asia, tracing their evolution in the pre-May 2025 conflict period and assessing their implications in the post-conflict strategic environment.

Kidwai (Retd.) emphasized that Pakistan’s Full Spectrum Deterrence (FSD) is fundamentally defensive, aimed at preventing aggression across the entire spectrum of conflict and preserving strategic stability in South Asia.

Pakistan’s Full Spectrum Deterrence generated strategic effects in both regional and international arenas in the May 2025 India-Pakistan conflict, as the role of conventional and nuclear deterrence in limiting escalation was demonstrated.

He highlighted SIPRI Yearbook 2026 findings on India’s deployment of approximately 12 nuclear warheads aboard a nuclear submarine for deterrence patrols, expressing concern that the absence of pre-notification of Indian SLBM tests could undermine South Asian strategic stability, raise questions about India’s NFU policy, and increase the risks of miscalculation and nuclear escalation.
He reaffirmed Pakistan’s right to take appropriate measures to safeguard its national security and preserve the regional strategic balance.
Furthermore, he stressed the importance of preventing technological imbalances from undermining strategic stability in South Asia.

To comprehensively address the spectrum of challenges, the conference hosts seven working sessions on critical topics such as deterrence dynamics and escalation risks in South Asia, the evolving deterrence landscape in a transforming global nuclear order, and the collapse of the arms control architecture and challenges to the non-proliferation regime.

Italy to send 500 troops to Milan after clashes - By AFP - - Oct 20, 2026 ROME: Italy is preparing to send 500 troops to Milan after looting and clashes between police and mostly young protesters, with some luxury brands shutting their shops in the city.

The government is also considering a wider crackdown, including restrictions on public gatherings, easing rules on detention for minors and harsher sanctions for their parents.
Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini called the clashes “shameful” and said on RTL 102.5 radio that the cabinet meeting would announce a series of “immediate measures” including the troop deployment.
Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said on Monday hoped the cabinet meeting would approve provisions for the army “to allow them to act like law enforcement”.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Saturday said the violent perpetrators were “thugs who exploit demonstrations to spread chaos, attack those who guarantee security, and hold entire cities hostage.” “To demonstrate is a right.
To lay our cities to waste is not,” she wrote on X.
High school and university students, farmers and truck drivers are leading nationwide protests in Italy, mainly against the rising cost of living.
Hard-right leader Meloni faces elections next year in which the state of the economy, security and immigration are likely to be the key issues.

Keeping hope at 1.5 As delegates meet in Belem, Brazil, for the COP30 climate summit, the world stands at a perilous moment in its fight against global warming.

About a decade after the signing of the Paris Climate Agreement, the global community’s commitment to keeping temperature rise below 1.5 C above the pre-industrial levels, which is described as the line between disruption and devastation, is waning.
For countries like Pakistan, already bearing the brunt of a warming planet, the erosion of that goal could only mean the difference between survival and collapse.

The UN’s latest Emission Gap Report 2025 launched on November 4 paints a sobering picture: even if every existing climate pledge is fully carried out, the world is still heading towards a 2.3 C to 2.5 C rise by the century’s end.
That would push millions in vulnerable regions of Asia, Africa and the Pacific beyond the limits of adaptation.
Only 64 nations, which represent just 30 per cent of global emissions, have submitted new or updated Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) ahead of COP30.
The gap between commitments and actual emissions cuts continues to widen.

For Pakistan, which produces less than one percent of global greenhouse gases but ranks among the ten most climate-affected countries, this indifference by the world’s biggest polluters is an existential threat.
Pakistan’s updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0), unveiled in 2024, stands out for its scope and seriousness.
It pledges a 50 per cent reduction in projected emissions by 2035 – 17 per cent through domestic efforts and another 33 per cent conditional on international support in finance and technology.
Achieving this target will require an estimated $565 billion in investment.

The plan reflects a clear roadmap aligned with the Paris vision: scaling up renewable energy, restoring degraded ecosystems, promoting electric mobility and transforming agriculture through climate-smart practices.

Pakistan aims to generate 62–69 per cent of its power from renewables, convert 30 per cent of transport to electric vehicles and expand reforestation under the Upscale Green Pakistan Programme – all crucial for cutting emissions and building resilience.
But ambition alone is not enough.

The country’s recent experience of devastating floods in 2022 and more recently in 2025 as well as recurring and growing incidents of glacial lake outburst floods in Gilgit-Baltistan and Chitral shows how climate change is already redrawing Pakistan’s geography.
Without sustained international finance and technology transfer, the country’s climate vision risks being outpaced by intensifying disasters.
The stakes at COP30 could not be higher.
This year’s conference marks the first comprehensive stocktake of global progress since Paris, and the findings are grim.
Global greenhouse gas emissions reached record highs in 2024, climbing 2.3 per cent in just one year.
Scientists now warn that even a brief overshoot beyond 1.5 C could trigger irreversible climate tipping points from melting polar ice to collapsing rainforest ecosystems.
The responsibility for reversing course lies largely with the G20 nations, which emit 77 per cent of the world’s greenhouse gases.
Yet most have failed to deliver on their pledges.
As the UNEP notes, the latest round of promises has “barely moved the needle”.
Even the most optimistic outlook still leaves a 40 per cent shortfall in the emission cuts needed to keep 1.5 C alive.
Pakistan’s stance at COP30 carries both urgency and moral authority.
Having previously chaired the G77 plus China group and played a key role in advancing the global Loss and Damage Fund, Islamabad remains a strong voice for climate justice.
The memory of 2022’s catastrophic floods still fuels its moral argument: those least responsible for warming should not bear its heaviest burdens.
Pakistan’s approach blends domestic policy with international diplomacy.

It has integrated climate adaptation into national development plans, advanced carbon market mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, and is using its platform to demand fairer access to global green finance.
Some experts now warn that surpassing 1.5 C may be inevitable.
But accepting that outcome would be a moral failure.
Every fraction of a degree avoided means fewer deaths, fewer destroyed homes, fewer families uprooted.
For Pakistan, the difference between 1.5 C and 2 C could decide the future of its glaciers, coastlines and food security.
Keeping the Paris goal alive is now an ethical obligation and a global survival strategy.
COP30 must move beyond rhetoric to real results, restoring trust in multilateral climate cooperation and reaffirming that equity and urgency must go hand in hand.
The last decade was marked by hesitation.
The next must be defined by transformation.
Pakistan’s NDC 3.0 shows what determined climate leadership can look like, but it cannot succeed in isolation.
Without solidarity, climate justice will remain an empty slogan.
As the world gathers in Belem, the choice is stark and simple: act decisively now to preserve a livable planet, or explain to future generations why we failed to defend it.
The writer is a climate public policy analyst, research scholar and former UNFCCC fellow.

In this atmosphere of sadness, it is heartwarming to come across the life story of a son of the soil who grew up in that enchanting valley just after Pakistan emerged as a new country on the world’s map.
The toddler born into a traditional Pashtun family had to leave the village with his parents, Mohammad Ayub and Feroza, as the former was appointed as Pakistan’s consul general in Mashad, Iran.
Young Mahmood Ali Ayub was thus exposed to the outside world that would later become his natural abode.
He would comfortably grow in cosmopolitan surroundings as a student and later as a professional.
There was something else rather special about Mahmood as he grew from adolescence to adulthood.
He always wanted to excel, a trait that left his peers envious and his mentors in awe during his college and university days.
Mahmood’s academic journey took him to Burn Hall School in Abbottabad, Aitchison College in Lahore and finally to Edwardes College in Peshawar, where he graduated.
No surprise that he moved on to the historical St Andrews University in Scotland.
The author recalls that he joined St Andrews on the recommendation of Lt-Gen Wajid Ali Burki, a renowned ophthalmologist, an alumnus of the university, who happened to be his father’s friend.
Mahmood Ayub recounts that he was fascinated by Marxism in his university days, diametrically opposed to his economics professor, James Nisbet.
Mahmood and a group of like-minded students formed a left-wing student group which was “something of a rebellious thorn” in a predominantly right-wing institution.
While at St Andrews, Mahmood joined a protest march in Aberdeen against a South Africa vs Scotland rugby game.
"The South African team was composed entirely of white players, a clear reflection of the racial segregation under the apartheid regime".
The demonstrators, numbering two hundred, were arrested only to realise that none of them could afford bail money.
However, one of the students managed to reach out to John Lennon, the iconic singer and a vocal supporter of civil rights.
Lennon paid bail money for all of them, earning their life-long respect and admiration.
Young Mahmood’s activism was not confined to Scotland. “On a couple of occasions, I travelled to Paris to participate in anti-Vietnam War demonstrations.
Paris, at the time, was a hotbed of student activism, and I relished the opportunity to engage with leaders from various movements”.
Mahmood’s leftist activism did not detract him from the life goals he had set for himself.
As often happens in our society, he sat in the CSS examination out of respect for his family and stood second in the highly competitive concourse.
What he observed in two months of training for a lifelong career helped him make up his mind to return to Yale to pursue higher studies in economics.

As luck would have it, that short period in Lahore was enough to make up his mind to marry Mansoora Hasan, an upcoming artist known for her appearance in PTV comedy serial ‘Such Gup’ under the supervision of Shoaib and Salima Hashmi.
Mansoora would later grow into an accomplished painter with exclusive exhibitions of her works in several countries.
Once back in the US, Mahmood would join the World Bank’s Young Professionals Programme, leading to a long career at the global development institution.
Looking back, I can say that his departure from the Pakistan Foreign Service deprived the country of a potentially outstanding diplomat who would have done us proud.
In a pleasant coincidence, we met 25 years later while I was posted as ambassador to Senegal and neighbouring countries, and Mahmood Ayub was heading the World Bank’s operations for the area.
Writing has been another passion of Mahmood Ayub.
His work in the Caribbean and Bolivia in his early years at the World Bank led to a publication, ‘Determinants of Performance of Public Industrial Enterprises’, coauthored with Sven Hegstad.
The book examined the factors that influence the performance of public industrial enterprises and was well received within the World Bank and in academic circles.

Mahmood’s next assignment was as chief of the Information and Technology Division to bridge the gap between the operational divisions and the technical teams, facilitating the adoption of technological solutions to improve their efficiency.

Recounting his experience in the Maghreb, Mahmood writes, “I travelled frequently to Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia, and apart from learning about each country’s economic and social challenges, I also imbibed their rich cultural heritage”.
Mahmood Ayub’s exposure to the Maghreb countries served as a stepping stone to his subsequent assignment as director for Egypt, Yemen and Djibouti, with a base in Cairo, from 2000 to 2005.
Following his return from Cairo to Washington, Mahmood Ayub took early retirement from the World Bank to join the UNDP where his former boss Kemal Dervis had taken over as the new administrator.
This transition “marked a new chapter in my career, offering fresh challenges and opportunities to contribute to international development efforts in a different capacity".
Mahmood Ayub describes his assignment as UNDP representative to Turkey (now Turkiye) as nothing less than a dream posting.
The writer also admires Hafez Shirazi, the 14th-century Persian Sufi poet whose work is regarded as the pinnacle of Farsi literature.
Mahmood found his poetry an inspirational “treasure trove of wisdom and beauty filled with insights that resonate deeply with the human experience".

The author was deeply drawn to the work of Hafez during the most challenging phase of his life marked first with the loss of his son at a young age and a few years later by the death of his cherished life partner, Mansoora Hasan.
Full credit to Mahmood Ayub for dedicating his life after tragedy to sharing his knowledge with society by writing a masterpiece on three 20th-century women poets.
The book, titled ‘Tragedy and Defiance’, explores the lives and poetry of Sylvia Plath from America, Forugh Farrokhzad from Iran and Perveen Shakir from Pakistan.
He writes that “each of these poets faced their own challenges and misfortunes, yet their voices resonate powerfully through their art".

Mahmood Ayub did not stop there and went on to pen his own life story, published this year, which has enabled me to share some remarkable high points of his personal and professional life with the readers.

Texas Democrats eye breakthrough as Republicans face voter anger - By AFP - - Oct 19, 2026 SAN ANTONIO, United States: After more than three decades of Republican dominance, Democrats in Texas see a rare chance to break through in November’s midterm elections, as voter anger over immigration raids and the cost-of-living tests US President Donald Trump’s support.
No Democrat has won statewide office in the conservative southern state since 1994, and Trump carried Texas by nearly 14 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election.
But with a US Senate seat and the governorship at stake on November 3, recent polls suggest Republicans face an unusually competitive challenge.

At the forefront is James Talarico, a 37-year-old former teacher and state lawmaker whose blend of Christian faith, economic populism and appeals for political unity has helped make the Senate race one of the country’s most closely watched.

A University of Texas poll released this week put Talarico ahead of Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general and a staunch Trump ally, by 50 percent to 47 percent — a lead within the survey’s margin of error.
A separate UMass Lowell poll found the two candidates tied.

A Presbyterian seminarian, Talarico has sought to attract independents and Republicans disillusioned with Trump, arguing that Texans have more in common than the country’s increasingly bitter political divisions suggest. “I’ll always put Texas before any political party,” he has said.

Trump, however, has campaigned aggressively for Paxton, warning at a recent rally in San Antonio that losing the seat could jeopardize the Republicans’ narrow Senate majority. “It’s a killer in Congress because we have a very close majority.
We can’t let that happen,” Trump said, mocking Talarico with the nickname “Talafreako” and accusing Democrats of wanting to reopen the country’s borders.

Paxton’s baggage Trump backed Paxton over incumbent Senator John Cornyn in a bitter Republican primary battle, despite warnings that the attorney general’s history of controversy could imperil the party’s hold on the seat.
Paxton was impeached by the Republican-controlled Texas House in 2023 over allegations of corruption and abuse of power, although the state Senate subsequently acquitted him.
In an extraordinary twist, Dan Cogdell, one of the lawyers who defended Paxton during the proceedings, has since endorsed Talarico.
More recently, The Wall Street Journal reported that Paxton spent New Year’s Eve in Dubai with two American businessmen indicted over alleged healthcare fraud.
Yet Paxton retains support among Trump-aligned conservatives, including some who acknowledge misgivings about their candidate.
Cracks in Trump’s coalition Beyond Paxton’s personal controversies, Democrats are looking to exploit growing discontent over immigration enforcement and the economy.
Trump’s commanding victory in Texas in 2024 owed partly to substantial gains among Latino voters, particularly along the state’s southern border with Mexico.
But some of those voters are now reconsidering their support.

Cattle industry groups in Texas, Kansas and Oklahoma have also warned that immigration raids are disrupting agricultural businesses, deterring legally employed workers and threatening to drive up beef prices.
A May survey by the Latino civil rights group UnidosUS found that one in five Texas Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 would not do so again if given another chance.

The broader discontent has also given Democrats hope in the race for governor, where three-term Republican incumbent Greg Abbott faces an unexpectedly close contest against state lawmaker Gina Hinojosa.
Hinojosa has focused her campaign on the cost of living, seeking to appeal to voters beyond the traditional Democratic base.
For Melendez, disillusionment with Trump has become reason enough to switch sides. “I didn’t vote for Trump because I liked him,” he told AFP. “I voted for Trump to punish Biden.

CCP greenlights Lotte Chemical Pakistan’s stake acquisition in Engro Polymer & Chemicals - The assessment found that LCPL does not operate in any of the identified relevant markets The Competition Commission of Pakistan approved Lotte Chemical's acquisition of shares in Engro Polymer.

The assessment found no significant impact on market competition due to no operational overlap. - CCP's approval of the share acquisition. - Products manufactured by Lotte Chemical and Engro Polymer. - Market assessment for PVC, caustic soda, and hydrogen peroxide.

The Competition Commission of Pakistan (CCP) has approved the proposed acquisition of a shareholding in Engro Polymer & Chemicals Limited (EPCL) by Lotte Chemical Pakistan Limited (LCPL) from Engro Corporation Limited, following a Phase-I competition assessment under the Competition Act, 2010, read a statement on Tuesday.
LCPL is a public limited company engaged in the manufacture and supply of Purified Terephthalic Acid (PTA) in Pakistan.
PTA is primarily used as a raw material in the production of polyester and polyethylene terephthalate (PET).
EPCL, the target company, manufactures and supplies Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC), caustic soda, hydrogen peroxide and other chlor-alkali products.
Back in March, Lotte Chemical Pakistan Limited announced its intention to acquire shares and control of EPCL.
For its competition assessment, CCP identified PVC, caustic soda and hydrogen peroxide as the relevant product markets, with Pakistan constituting the relevant geographic market.
The assessment found that LCPL does not operate in any of the identified relevant markets.
Furthermore, neither LCPL nor any of its associated, affiliated or group companies purchases products from EPCL, read the statement.
The proposed transaction therefore gives rise to neither a horizontal nor a vertical overlap between the merging parties.
In the PVC market, EPCL is the sole domestic manufacturer, while imports provide an important competitive constraint.
In the markets for caustic soda and hydrogen peroxide, EPCL holds comparatively lower market shares and competes with other market participants.
CCP further observed that the proposed acquisition entails a change in the ownership and control of EPCL without, in itself, increasing the target company’s production capacity, sales or output.
The transaction is therefore not expected to increase market concentration, create barriers to entry or materially enhance the market power of either party.

Based on its Phase-I assessment, the regulator concluded that the proposed transaction is unlikely to substantially lessen competition or create or strengthen a dominant position in any of the relevant markets.
The transaction has accordingly been authorised under Section 31(1)(d)(i) of the Competition Act, 2010.

Every morning, private school vans move through Islamabad and Rawalpindi carrying children to their educational institutions.
For parents, the journey is part of the daily routine, but for some children, the short trip to school can bring risks that often go unnoticed.

Before the classroom door: Lost schoolbags, packed private vans and children at risk Moniba Iftikhar ISLAMABAD, Oct 11 (APP):Every morning, private school vans move through Islamabad and Rawalpindi carrying children to their educational institutions.

Behind the doors of some vans, children are packed into limited space, schoolbags are placed between seats or hung outside the vehicle and drivers hurry through busy roads to complete their routes on time.
For Class 6 student Yumna, the concern became clear when she reached school one morning without her schoolbag.
The bag had reportedly fallen from the private van somewhere along the route.
Her books, notebooks and homework were gone, while neither the driver nor other passengers noticed the incident.
Teacher Fouzia of F-10/2 Model Girls College noticed Yumna Amin without her schoolbag and immediately contacted her mother, asking her to speak to the driver and find out where the bag had been lost.

The belongings could be replaced, but the incident raised a more serious question: if a schoolbag could fall from a moving vehicle without anyone noticing, how closely were the children being watched?
Yumna also complained about the limited space inside school vans, saying children often have to share insufficient room with their schoolbags.
She also raised concerns about drivers rushing through traffic, leaving young passengers exposed to risks beyond their control.
For many families, however, private school transport is not a choice but a necessity.
Parents leave for work early, while professional and household responsibilities make it difficult to manage school timings themselves.
Vans, buses and rickshaws therefore remain an important means of transport for schoolchildren.
Mrs Nayab Ali said repeated encounters with what she described as irresponsible behaviour by school-van drivers eventually led her to arrange the pick-and-drop of her own children.
She said many parents could not make the same arrangement because of work and family commitments and therefore had to depend on school transport.
She stressed that such dependence should not become blind trust and that people entrusted with children must be properly verified and held accountable.

Another parent Arsalan Rao said he had repeatedly seen school pick-and-drop drivers violating traffic rules. “Countless times, I have seen van drivers flout traffic rules, yet traffic police often appear to do little to check such deplorable behaviour,” he said.
He said reckless driving was particularly serious when children were travelling inside the vehicle, as a speeding driver was putting the lives of all passengers at risk.

Speaking to APP, Rawalpindi traffic official Lehar Mirza said strict measures were being taken against school-van operators violating traffic and safety regulations, particularly those carrying children beyond the designated seating capacity.
Lehar Mirza said the issue was not simply about traffic violations but directly concerned the safety and lives of schoolchildren.
A school van, she stressed, was carrying children whose safety could not be compromised merely to accommodate additional passengers.

She said vehicles designed for a limited number of children must not be overloaded, as overcrowding leaves children without proper seating and makes it difficult for them to move or protect themselves during sudden braking, collisions or other emergencies.
She also warned against hanging schoolbags outside vans, saying bags could fall onto roads, create hazards for other motorists and pedestrians, or become lost without the children or driver noticing.

Lehar Mirza said traffic officials in Rawalpindi with the directives of Senior Chief Traffic officer Farhan were carrying out checks and would continue enforcement against violators, with warnings and fines being issued where necessary.
She said the special drive was expected to produce better results in the coming days as monitoring was being strengthened.
Alongside enforcement, she said awareness sessions were being conducted in schools to educate students, parents, drivers and school administrations about road safety and responsible school transport.
She urged parents to cooperate with authorities and avoid sending their children in overcrowded or unsafe vans. “Parents also have a responsibility.
If a van is overcrowded, unsafe or the driver repeatedly violates traffic rules, the matter should be reported rather than accepted as part of the daily routine,” she said.

Speaking to APP, Inspector Traffic Rana Ishtiaq Ahmed of the Education Wing of Islamabad Traffic Police said the department had intensified its road-safety campaign around government and private schools in and around the Capital.
He said police personnel had been deployed near various private schools, while awareness activities were being conducted for students, teachers, parents, drivers and school administrations.
Rana Ishtiaq Ahmed said traffic discipline was not limited to avoiding fines.
Pedestrians, particularly children, should be given the right of way at zebra crossings.
He said traffic police encounter around 60 to 80 violators daily, including school-van drivers involved in pick-and-drop services.
Depending on the offense, fines ranging from Rs500 to Rs1,500 are imposed, while vehicles failing to meet safety requirements may also face action.
He identified overcrowding as one of the major concerns, saying vehicles designed to carry around 10 children were sometimes found carrying 18 to 20.

Ishtiaq Ahmad also said a strict crackdown was being launched against private pick-ups and vans fitted with rear grills or metal frames used for hanging schoolbags, as such modifications could pose safety risks to children.
He urged parents not to compromise their children’ s safety merely to save money and stressed that drivers must be properly trained and licensed.

Taqi Jawad, Public Relations Officer and official spokesperson for Islamabad Capital Territory Police, said traffic personnel were also warning school-van drivers against over speeding, dangerous manoeuvring, illegal parking, overloading and other violations.

An official of an authorised online school transport service operating in Islamabad and Rawalpindi said safer school transport could be provided through CNIC verification, background checks and police verification of drivers.
The service provides parents with real-time journey updates, fixed pick-up and drop-off schedules, controlled passenger numbers and emergency communication.
These measures provide a useful standard for responsible school transport: verified drivers, roadworthy vehicles, proper seating, controlled passenger numbers and communication with parents.
Parents, meanwhile, can ask basic questions before entrusting their children to any vehicle: Who is driving?
Is the driver properly licensed and verified?
Does every child have a seat?
Yumna’ s schoolbag can be replaced.
Her books can be bought again and her homework rewritten.
But the incident offers a simple reminder that the journey to school deserves the same attention to safety as the classroom itself.
The school run is a daily responsibility shared by parents, drivers, schools, transport providers and authorities.
Each has a role in ensuring that children reach school and return home safely.
Education begins with reaching the classroom safely.
For every child travelling to school each morning, that journey should be secure, orderly and worthy of the trust placed in the adults responsible for it.
A bag may be lost and replaced, but a child can never be replaced.

Alberta rejects plan for referendum on leaving Canada: media - By AFP - - Oct 20, 2026 EDMONTON, Canada: Canada’s province of Alberta overwhelmingly rejected a plan to hold a binding independence referendum, media projected Tuesday, in a decisive defeat for separatists that drew support from allies of US President Donald Trump.

Public broadcaster CBC projected a clear win for the federalist side, with official results showing more than 76 percent support for national unity, with roughly at least a third of the votes counted.
Canada was waiting Monday for the results of a vote on whether the oil-rich province of Alberta wants a binding independence referendum, following a divisive campaign that tested national unity.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has argued the vote has been held “at the worst possible time,” citing the need for national stability as US President Donald Trump wages a trade war and levels annexation threats.
Polls indicated less than a quarter of people in the western province want independence, but separatist leader Mitch Sylvestre told AFP on Monday he remained optimistic.

Alberta’s elections authority said all polls had closed by 10:10 pm (0410 GMT Tuesday), but vote counting had been underway for several hours, including tallies of the 1.4 million advance ballots cast.
There are 3.1 million eligible voters in the province.

At the federalist election night party in Edmonton, a band warmed up ahead of an anticipated positive result. “It was amazing to see the enthusiasm and resolve among Canadians,” said Thomas Lukaszuk, who heads Forever Canadian, the group that campaigned across the province for national unity.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, a conservative, said she voted against independence but called the referendum to settle an issue that has divided the province.
If a majority wants to separate, she has pledged to hold a binding referendum.
If the federalists win, Smith said the secession question should be considered closed.
Alberta has the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, and much of the separatist momentum has been driven by anger over oil industry management.
Smith has blamed Carney’s predecessor Justin Trudeau for igniting the separatist fire, accusing him of trying to crush oil production to advance his pro-climate agenda.
Alberta’s independence push has also drawn sustained interest from Trump allies.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called Alberta a “natural partner” for the United States.

Elon Musk, the world’s richest person and a top Trump supporter, posted on X this month that Alberta “should separate.” Separatist leaders have also held meetings at the US State Department and with Republican political operatives. ‘Huge uncertainty’ Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has worked to improve relations between the province and Ottawa since taking office last year.
He has partnered with Smith on advancing a new pipeline to export more Alberta bitumen overseas, a project considered a nonstarter during Trudeau’s tenure.
But he has also warned Albertans that even a nonbinding vote on independence would be a “dangerous bluff,” drawing on his experience during Brexit, when he was the Bank of England’s governor.
He said the “huge uncertainty” that followed the Brexit vote hurt the British economy, cautioning Alberta over unintended economic consequences.

PM asks FBR to plug tax gap amid pruning plans Govt scraps plan for new tax agency ISLAMABAD: The federal government on Monday dropped the idea of setting up a new tax agency but decided to compulsorily retire non-performing officers by amending the Civil Servants Act, which would allow it to retrench bureaucrats as part of any restructuring.

Chairing a high-level review meeting, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif directed that the pace of reforms within the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) be accelerated, noting that the initial results of the ongoing reforms were encouraging.
The prime minister emphasised that the FBR must continuously enhance its institutional capacity to effectively bridge the tax gap.
He stressed that technology, effective professional training, transparency and accountability must remain central to ensuring that the ongoing reforms yield concrete results.
"It is the responsibility of FBR officers to improve their performance in line with the expectations of the nation," a statement from the Prime Minister's Office quoted Shehbaz as saying.
"The ongoing reforms were in the broader interest of the state, and the process would continue in any case," the prime minister added.
The prime minister called for zero-tolerance and indiscriminate action against corrupt elements within the department.
Staff showing genuine improvement in conduct and performance should be given an opportunity to reform, while there should be no room for corruption or underperformance, he emphasised.
Officials briefed the meeting on the use of technology, procedural workflows and human resource management.
They said the FBR reforms had narrowed the estimated tax gap from 6% to 5% of GDP, while the effective use of technology had substantially reduced the discretionary powers of FBR officials.

According to officials who attended the meeting, it was decided to overhaul the FBR's human resources to make the organisation more efficient, less top-heavy and more taxpayer-friendly by removing officers who were either underperforming or falling short of professional benchmarks.
The prime minister directed that action be taken against corrupt elements without discrimination.
The FBR was instructed to submit a report on human resource restructuring and reorganisation to the prime minister within this week.
Earlier this month, debate was triggered after the idea of setting up an entirely new organisation was floated at a high-level meeting.

Some participants were of the view that setting up a new organisation would take years and that, by the time it became fully operational, it could develop problems similar to those faced by the existing FBR.
After The Express Tribune published a story about the proposed new organisation, the Inland Revenue Service Officers Association (IRSOA) threatened to observe a pen-down strike.
The IRSOA later withdrew the threat after seeking assurances from senior officials.
Officials told The Express Tribune that Shehbaz expressed displeasure over the officers' conduct, saying there was no room for an association that could blackmail the government.
The FBR's senior management said action could be taken against officers for illegally establishing a collective bargaining body.
The government, however, decided to restructure the FBR's human resources both vertically and horizontally.
Surplus and non-performing officers would be sent packing.
The meeting was told that amendments to the Civil Servants Act had been pending before the National Assembly since 2024.

The government also decided to fast-track the parliamentary approval of these amendments to secure the legal authority to compulsorily retire tax officials, a senior government official confirmed to The Express Tribune.

According to a proposed new clause 22 A and 22 B, which will be applicable on all service groups, the government will have powers to declare any officer redundant as a result of any restructuring and reorganisation, give him or her a severance package and to compulsory retire the person.

The clause 22B states, the federal government may at any time decide full or partial abolition, restructuring or reorganisation of a division, department or office and in respect of civil servants liable to be affected thereby declare the posts, cadres, or nomenclatures of civil servants to be abolished and incumbent civil servants thereof rendered surplus or redundant.

The sub clause 2 of clause 22B states, on receipt of decision of the federal government, the appointing authority shall offer a severance package to the civil servant declared redundant who shall be obliged to accept it, but can file an appeal only against the monetary value.
According to sub-clause 3 of the clause 22B, the service of a civil servant who stands redundant shall be liable to termination by the appointing authority.

Meanwhile, an FBR statement later said that two Inland Revenue Service officers - one in BS-20 and the other in BS-19 - had been suspended, while two other IRS officers in BS-20 had been repatriated to FBR Headquarters for further investigation over an unauthorised press statement and a call to halt official work.

PESHAWAR: The Peshawar High Court (PHC) on Tuesday sought replies from the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government and senior police personnel, including the inspector general (IG), regarding non-functional provincial chief executive Sohail Afridi’s detention.
Afridi has not been seen since the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency in his province on Oct 11.
His whereabouts remained unknown on the day governor’s rule was imposed and a federal minister confirmed a day later that he and some of his cabinet members were in preventative custody.
The PTI has also alleged the detention and arrests of several of its other members, including lawmakers and ministers.
Their whereabouts have not been disclosed by the government so far.

Multiple pleas have been filed in the PHC in this connection, and a bench comprising Justice Syed Arshad Ali and Justice Farah Jamshed fixed them for hearing on Nov 3, when the respondents were told to submit their replies.

Apart from Afridi’s detention, the petitions pertain to the disappearance of KP Assembly Speaker Babar Saleem Swati, MNAs Junaid Akbar and Dr Amjid Ali, provincial minister Amjid Ali Khan, MPAs Ikramullah and Aurangzeb Khan, former chief minister of Gilgit-Baltistan Muhammad Khalid Khursheed and several other PTI leaders.
Afridi’s brother Muhammad Aamir filed one of the petitions, alleging that Afridi was “abducted” from the Chief Minister’s House on the night that the emergency was imposed in the province.
He had approached the PHC last week.

Aamir sought directives for the respondents, including the KP IG, the Peshawar capital city police officer (CCPO) and others to immediately take all lawful and effective measures to trace and recover his brother.

He also sought that if Afridi was found to be in custody, the PHC order that he be produced so that the legality of his custody could be examined in accordance with Article 199(1)(b)(i) of the Constitution.

The article states that a high court may direct that a person in custody within its territorial jurisdiction be brought before it, “so that the court may satisfy itself that he is not being held in custody without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner”.

The petitioner sought directives for the respondents concerned to submit a comprehensive report regarding the whereabouts, present condition and legal status of Afridi, as well as the details of steps taken to trace and recover him.

He also requested the court to direct the CCPO to submit a detailed report concerning the alleged Oct 11 incident at the CM House — “including the circumstances in which the abductee was allegedly taken away, the security arrangements in place, the people present and the action taken immediately thereafter”.

Presenting his arguments at the hearing on Tuesday, Aamir’s lawyer, Bashir Vazir, claimed that on Oct 11, at approximately 2pm, Afridi was “illegally detained” in the CM House and later on was abducted from the premises, in the presence of the Peshawar CCPO, by “certain unknown armed and masked individuals”.

He contended that Afridi’s detention and disappearance was “wholly illegal, unlawful, without lawful authority and of no legal effect” as the respondents had “not disclosed any lawful order, warrant, abduction order or other legal authority” under which Afridi was taken into custody.
Swati’s cousin, Waqar Ahmad Khan, has also filed a similar petition.
His lawyer is also Vazir, who requested the court at Tuesday’s hearing to issue directives for Swati’s recovery.
He claimed that on Oct 11 at approximately 7pm, Swati was “abducted” from the KP Assembly in the presence of the CCPO by “certain unknown armed and masked individuals”.

He stated that the precise sequence of events, the identities of the persons involved and the circumstances in which Swati was taken away required “immediate verification through the relevant official record, eyewitness accounts and other available evidence”.

In both cases, the petitioners prayed that the court direct the respondents to ensure the preservation and lawful examination of all relevant CCTV footage, security logs, entry and exit registers, duty rosters, vehicle access records and other material relating to the incidents.
Furthermore, they sought the registration of a first information report and a prompt, impartial and effective investigation into the alleged abductions, disappearances and detentions.

They contended that the whereabouts and present condition of PTI leaders needed to be immediately ascertained through lawful means, and requested the PHC to issue directives for their release if they were found to be in unlawful custody.
Junaid Akbar’s nephew, Nadir Shah, and Khalid Khursheed’s brother, Hanif Ullah, have also filed pleas, requesting the court to order the recovery and production of the two politicians.
In almost identical petitions, they challenged their “abduction” on the night of Oct 11.

France: Macron rejects interior minister Nunez resignation after nationwide riots President Emmanuel Macron rejected Interior Minister Nuñez's resignation after the October 17 riots, demanding transparency over security planning failures French President Emmanuel Macron has officially declined Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez's offer to resign following the severe, nationwide riots and widespread civil unrest that swept across Paris, France.
Beyond the capital, violence erupted in cities like Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, and Limoges—where a historic 19th-century town hall was largely destroyed by a deliberately set fire.
President Emmanuel Macron and top government officials condemned the extreme violence as "unacceptable," deploying heavy security forces using tear gas and water cannons to restore order.
The Elysée Palace stated that keeping Nuñez in office is essential to maintaining an unbroken chain of command within the police and security forces during an active national crisis.
While rejecting the resignation, President Macron explicitly criticized planning and intelligence "failures" that allowed the demonstrations to erupt into widespread arson, looting, and clashes.
As reported, the widespread protest has been sparked by public anger over rising living costs, faltering public services and also the state of schools.

In response, Macron has ordered Nuñez to rapidly implement new operational methods and security frameworks to better handle looters and ensure full transparency regarding the security lapses that preceded the weekend's violence.

As reported, nationwide demonstrations erupted into riots on Saturday, October 17, with a town hall torched, shops pillaged and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities.
More clashes also broke out in Paris and Marseille on Sunday, where riot police intervened to prevent attempts to ransack businesses.
Dell releases new 14S laptop featuring Intel Wildcat Lake chips and budget options - By Kumail Shah - - Oct 19, 2026 Dell has just launched the newest version of its Dell 14S laptop.
Earlier this year, the company released the Dell 14S DS14260 in May, which used Intel Panther Lake processors.
In September, Dell introduced the Dell 14S DS14270 with updated Wildcat Lake chips.
Dell originally planned to launch the updated Dell 14S in the fall for the Northern Hemisphere.
At that time, the company did not share pricing details.

However, it did confirm that the Dell 14S DS14270 would use the same Core 5 320 and Core 7 350 processors found in the more affordable XPS 13, which we reviewed earlier this year (currently $839 on Amazon).
The company has now begun selling its new 14-inch laptop worldwide without any prior announcement.
In the US, the DS14270 starts at $649, making it more than 50% cheaper than the DS14260.
Prices in other regions are AUD 1,271.60 in Australia, CAD 899.99 in Canada, €821 in the Eurozone, and £721.20 in the UK.
Part of the $750 price difference is because the DS14270 has half the RAM and storage of the DS14260.
The Dell 14S DS14270 starts with 256 GB of PCIe Gen 3 storage and 8 GB of LPDDR5x-7467 RAM in single-channel mode.
Dell also offers versions of the laptop with 512 GB or 1 TB PCIe Gen 4 SSDs and 16 GB of RAM, though these still use single-channel mode.
You can also choose an 1800p IPS display with a 120 Hz refresh rate and 450 nits of brightness instead of the standard 1200p, 60 Hz, 300-nit screen.
Every version of the laptop comes with a 3-cell, 61.2 Wh battery, which helps keep the weight at 1.15 kg.
Reports say the battery can last up to 21 hours when streaming Netflix at 150 nits on a 1200p display.
For more information, visit Dell’s website.

Parliament holds exclusive right to amend Constitution: minister Chaudhry criticises sections of judiciary, saying Constitution will reflect parliament, not judges Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry on Sunday defended the federal government, saying only Parliament holds the exclusive right to amend the Constitution, responding to Supreme Court judges' criticism of the 27th Constitutional Amendment.
His statement came after two top court jurists, Mansoor Ali Shah and Athar Minallah, tendered their resignations following the enactment of the 27th Constitutional Amendment earlier this week.

Not only the top court, a Lahore High Court (LHC) judge, Shams Mehmood Mirza, also resigned a day ago, saying he was "not inclined as a matter of principle and in good conscience to continue as a judge" after the 27th Amendment.

The tweaks fine-tuned the structure of the newly established Federal Constitutional Court (FCC), clarified the titles and ranking of the country's top judges, and approved changes to the military command.
On Friday, President Asif Ali Zardari approved Shah and Minallah's resignations.
"Amending the Constitution is Parliament's exclusive right, and it will do so whenever it chooses," he stated while talking to journalists in Faisalabad today.
He stressed that judges "are not a political party" and only take an oath to uphold the Constitution.
Criticising sections of the judiciary, Chaudhry said that the Constitution will reflect the parliament and the people of Pakistan, not judges.
He added that the legislature "must be seen as Parliament", arguing that certain actors had "reduced it to a municipal corporation".
He further said that judges' salaries and "every single decision" ultimately came under Parliament's authority.
"These resignations [of judges] are political.
They remained partial," the minister said.
The ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz leader said that the country cannot afford any form of chaos or instability at this stage.
"At times, they dismissed prime ministers through suo motu, and at other times they paralysed elected governments," he said.
Chaudhry said it was not the judiciary's role to "oust whomever it wants and install whomever it prefers".
It is noteworthy to mention here that the SC jurists had criticised the 27th Amendment, describing it as a "grave assault on the Constitution of Pakistan".

Shah, in his 13-page resignation letter, called the recent constitutional tweak an assault on the Constitution that dismantles the Supreme Court, compromises judicial independence, and weakens the country's constitutional democracy.
Warning that judicial independence faces "the beginning of the end", he said nations lose their moral compass when justice is constrained.
Justice Minallah, in his resignation letter, rejected the 27th Amendment, saying the Constitution he pledged to defend "no longer exists” and now survives only as a shadow without its spirit.
He wrote that he had warned the chief justice before the amendment's passage, but his concerns were realised amid "silence and inaction".
Continuing in office, he said, would betray his oath and dishonour the Constitution's memory.

ISLAMABAD: Former AJK president and former ambassador Masood Ahmed Khan on Monday stressed that diplomacy remains the only viable solution to resolve the ongoing tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan, urging Islamabad to prioritise diplomatic engagement to address outstanding disputes.

Masood Khan, President of the Centre for Law and Security (CLAS) and TMUC, was speaking during a lecture organised by the Institute of Cost and Management Accountants of Pakistan (ICMA), where he discussed Pakistan-Afghanistan relations, the country’s economic potential and the evolving role of public diplomacy.
He said Pakistan had historically extended support to millions of Afghan refugees but had faced hostile policies from the Afghan government in return.
He emphasised that diplomatic engagement remained essential to resolving existing differences and improving bilateral relations.
Khan said the government was making serious efforts to improve diplomatic ties with Afghanistan.

He also referred to reports that the National Defence University had invited the Afghan ambassador to Pakistan, describing diplomatic engagement as an important avenue for addressing bilateral challenges.
Highlighting Pakistan’s economic potential, the former ambassador referred to a World Bank report indicating that the country had the potential to become the world’s 10th-largest economy.
He said this reflected the scale of opportunities available to Pakistan if its economic potential was effectively realised.
He also highlighted the potential role of Zakat in poverty alleviation, observing that nationwide enforcement of a 2.5 percent Zakat system could help address poverty.
Speaking about public diplomacy, Khan said technological advancements and the widespread use of digital communication platforms had transformed traditional diplomatic practices.
Platforms such as WhatsApp and other social media networks had enabled diplomats to communicate directly with their counterparts abroad, changing the way international engagement was conducted.
He noted that Pakistan’s population of approximately 250 million included around 210 million mobile phone users and 160 million broadband subscribers.
This extensive digital connectivity, he said, had transformed society and increased the influence of social media on decision-making.
In the evolving environment of public diplomacy, every individual mattered in shaping global engagement and influencing perceptions, he added.
Khan also stressed the need for agricultural reforms, calling for more effective utilisation of foreign direct investment to strengthen the sector and support economic growth.

He underscored Pakistan’s longstanding role at the United Nations and its engagement at the level of the UN secretary-general, describing the country as an important player in regional and international affairs. “Pakistan is one of the most consequential states in West Asia,” he said, highlighting its substantial economic potential.

He added that as Washington sought more diversified supply and value chains across Eurasia, Pakistan should be viewed as a developing hub for trade, energy, transport and broader regional connectivity.
Former diplomat said Washington had publicly acknowledged Pakistan’s contributions to promoting peace across South and Central Asia.

He further noted that Pakistan had enjoyed the confidence of both Washington and Tehran in efforts to broker a ceasefire, facilitate direct talks and secure a memorandum of understanding providing a framework for negotiations.
Although the process had not progressed further, Pakistan continued to pursue all available avenues to bring the war to an end, he added.
ICMA President Muhammad Yasin and Ghulam Mustafa Qazi also spoke on the occasion.

Published October 20, 2026 US President Donald Trump's approval rating fell to a record low as Americans worried about high gasoline prices and appeared ready to punish his Republican Party in the November 3 congressional elections, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on Monday.
Some 31% of Americans approve of Trump's performance in office, down a percentage point from two weeks earlier and the lowest level in either of his presidential terms, the four-day poll showed.

Asked which party they would vote for if the congressional elections were held today in what is known as a "generic ballot" question, some 47% of registered voters in the nationwide poll picked Democrats and 35% chose Republicans.
The 12-point Democratic advantage was the widest over the current election cycle and could bolster Democratic hopes of seizing control of the US House of Representatives and the US Senate.
For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump's agenda in the last two years of his term.
Generic ballot polls are national polls that provide an overall view of which party poll respondents want to see in charge in Congress.

While these polls provide a view of national public sentiment, they do not capture all the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the Senate and House, contests in which Republicans hold some structural advantages.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll two weeks earlier showed Democrats leading Republicans by 7 points, 44% to 37%.
Much of the drop in support for Republican congressional candidates was due to a larger share of women saying they would pick Democrats.
Some 50% of female voters said they would vote Democratic, compared to 32% eyeing Republican candidates.
Men also favoured Democrats, but by a smaller margin.
Trump's popularity has suffered since he ordered military strikes on Iran in February alongside US ally Israel.
The war triggered a surge in gasoline prices, hitting household finances.
Some 68% of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy, including 37% of self-identified Republicans.
Voters in the poll picked Democrats over Republicans as the better stewards of the economy, by 40% to 33%.
The survey, which was conducted online, gathered responses from 1,679 US adults, including 1,279 registered voters.
The poll's results had a margin of error of 2 percentage points for all respondents and 3 percentage points for registered voters.

The price of disorder Pakistan’s roads reflect the broader dysfunction of its governance system: disorganised, improvised and reactive.
Every few months, a new chief traffic officer (CTO) assumes office in Lahore or Karachi, promising reform, digitisationand discipline.
Yet despite these recurring campaigns, little changes in the experience of daily commuters.
Traffic remains chaotic, enforcement is inconsistent and citizens are caught in a system where fines have increased but compliance mechanisms remain inaccessible.
The result is a model of governance that prioritises appearances over systemic reform.

The latest wave of fine increases began in Karachi, where the city’s traffic police announced a sharp rise in penalties for common violations, including lane indiscipline, signal breaking and helmetless riding.
These measures were justified as deterrents to reckless driving and as a means to ‘restore civic discipline’.
Yet the reforms have exposed a deeper flaw: the lack of a functioning, accessible system for payments and compliance.
In both cities, citizens report malfunctioning online challan portals, unresponsive helplines and long queues at manual counters.
The online Fine Payment App frequently crashes or fails to register payments, while integration with mobile banking platforms remains unreliable.
For many motorists, especially delivery riders and daily-wage workers, paying a fine can mean losing a day’s income or relying on informal agents to process challans.
These inefficiencies turn deterrence into an administrative ordeal.
A fine can only serve its purpose if it is accompanied by a transparent and functional system of compliance.
The dysfunction extends to the process of obtaining or renewing a driving license.
Despite efforts to digitise, licensing offices remain plagued by procedural confusion and a lack of infrastructure.
The surge in urban populations has outpaced institutional capacity, forcing provincial authorities to set up makeshift offices with minimal staffing and no standardised testing protocols.
Officers are often recruited without formal training in road safety, while the manual record-keeping system leaves room for both error and discretion.
In this environment, corruption is not an aberration but a symptom of structural neglect.
These operational gaps mirror a deeper absence of strategic continuity.
Pakistan’s traffic police departments remain reactive rather than policy-driven.
Lahore alone has seen more than six CTOs in five years; each launching short-lived enforcement drives, from helmet crackdowns to digital challan pilots.
Without institutional memory or long-term planning, reforms begin and end with the tenure of individual officers.
The lack of an overarching national road safety policy further isolates local efforts, making coordination between cities and provinces almost nonexistent.
Traffic departments receive only a fraction of the provincial police budget, less than 6.0 per cent in Punjab, according to the 2024 Public Expenditure Report.
Most funds are allocated to personnel costs, leaving little for technology upgrades, training or maintenance.
Many officers operate without radios, proper uniforms or designated patrol vehicles.
Field conditions are poor, and there are no clear career incentives for specialisation in traffic management.
This absence of institutional investment reinforces a cycle of inefficiency and low morale.
Accountability mechanisms, though present on paper, remain weak in practice.
Data from the Punjab Safe Cities Authority (PSCA) shows that nearly one-third of e-challans issued through automated cameras remain unpaid due to inadequate follow-up or administrative loopholes.
Manual ticketing leaves even more space for discretion.
In Karachi, enforcement relies on physical checkpoints and spot fines, allowing for arbitrary negotiation.
For many drivers, penalties have become negotiable inconveniences rather than deterrents grounded in law.
The consequences of this dysfunction are not limited to enforcement: they extend to how cities are planned and governed.
There is almost no coordination between the traffic police, transport authorities and municipal departments responsible for road design.
Infrastructure projects such as underpasses, flyovers and bus corridors are often planned without consulting enforcement data or traffic flow studies.
This disconnect results in roads engineered for volume rather than regulation.

Karachi’s corridor system and Lahore’s signal-free routes have increased driving speeds but not compliance, revealing how infrastructure expansion without parallel enforcement reform only amplifies risk.
Public perception of the traffic police reflects these contradictions.
For most citizens, traffic regulation is viewed not as a public service but as an unpredictable encounter.
The absence of consistent public education campaigns or transparent data on fine collections has reinforced scepticism about intent.
The perception that fines are designed for revenue generation, rather than safety, undermines civic cooperation.
When citizens experience digital breakdowns and arbitrary enforcement simultaneously, compliance loses moral legitimacy.
To its credit, the Punjab Safe Cities Authority’s e-challan system remains a partial success.
Automating violations through camera networks has reduced direct human interaction and corruption opportunities.
However, its effectiveness remains limited to select urban zones and depends on functional integration with payment gateways.
Smaller districts, where manual enforcement still dominates, remain disconnected from this digital infrastructure.
Without a unified provincial or national traffic database, repeat offenders cannot be tracked, and penalties cannot be scaled with consistency.
Ultimately, Pakistan’s traffic policing crisis is a microcosm of its broader governance dilemma: institutions that function through ad-hoc fixes rather than coherent frameworks.
The recurring fine revisions and short-lived digital drives reflect a preference for visibility over capacity.
A meaningful solution requires continuity in leadership, institutional investment in personnel and technology, and alignment between traffic management and urban planning.
Until such reforms take root, the country’s traffic system will continue to illustrate a familiar paradox of governance: a state that enforces compliance without enabling it.
Fines will rise, campaigns will rotate and new CTOs will announce digitisation drives, but the experience on Pakistan’s roads will remain the same.
Order, like reform, will stay aspirational, suspended between rhetoric and reality.
The writer is a transnational educational consultant, freelance columnist and policy analyst based in Lahore.
