Mir Raza case: Commission recommends JIT with ISI, Rangers, NCCIA representatives - By Sanjay Sadhwani - - Oct 20, 2026 KARACHI: The judicial commission investigating the death of Mir Raza Ali has raised serious questions about the police investigation, the handling of medical and digital evidence, and the initial conclusion that he died by suicide.
The commission has recommended a new joint investigation team (JIT) to conduct a comprehensive investigation into all aspects of his death.
The 70-page report, headed by Justice Umar Sial, was submitted to the Sindh chief minister on October 15.
The commission held 20 meetings between August 27 and October 7 and recorded statements from 50 witnesses.
According to the report, the police initially declared Mir Raza’s death a suicide on the basis of the preliminary post-mortem report.
His family challenged that conclusion, citing marks of violence on his body and other evidence.
The police surgeon identified shortcomings in the initial post-mortem report and recommended another examination.
Mir Raza’s body was re-examined on August 8.
The final report identified a bullet wound entering from the back as the cause of death.
The commission said it was not appropriate to conclude that the death was a suicide while ignoring contradictions in the medical evidence.
It criticised the police for maintaining their initial position despite conflicting medical findings and failing to meet basic investigative requirements.
JIT recommended to investigate all aspects of death The commission recommended that the Sindh government establish a JIT to investigate all aspects of Mir Raza’s death.
Representatives of the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), Rangers and the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) should be included in the team.
It also called for further investigation into possible blackmailing or a revenge killing.
The commission stressed that the available material was not sufficient to reach a final conclusion about an organised cover-up or criminal responsibility.
The report recommended further investigation into suspicious vehicles and individuals present at a guest house.
It also raised questions about the leadership and supervision of DIG Amir Farooqi and DIG Farukh Ali Lanjar.
Police criticised over digital evidence The commission raised serious concerns about the handling of CCTV footage, mobile phones, an Apple Watch and other digital evidence.
According to the report, police failed to take important CCTV recordings into legal custody through the proper procedure.
Instead, footage displayed on monitors was recorded using mobile phones.
The original digital video recorders were not secured in accordance with legal requirements.
The report also identified gaps in the record of evidence transfers and noted that some actions were not entered in the daily police diary.
Police statements about obtaining and preserving footage contained contradictions.
The commission questioned the procedures used to take custody of the phone, obtain digital data and access information stored on the Apple Watch.
Attempts to enter unauthorised passcodes made the phone’s data inaccessible and caused difficulties in retrieving information from the watch, affecting the investigation.
It also questioned how some digital evidence reached the media.
The commission asked why private messages and financial information were disclosed, potentially damaging the family’s reputation.
Financial difficulties not enough to establish cause of death The commission examined the police position that Mir Raza’s alleged financial difficulties could have led him to die by suicide.
The report said the police referred to statements from creditors and business partners regarding outstanding liabilities.
However, the commission stressed that financial problems alone do not establish that a person would die by suicide or that financial pressure was the cause of death.
It said the available material did not justify treating financial difficulties as the definitive cause.
The commission called for an independent investigation into Mir Raza’s behaviour and circumstances despite the reported financial pressure.
A message to Sarem bin Tahir referring to Rs30 million was also mentioned in the report.
The commission treated the possibility of blackmail as a matter requiring further investigation.
Dr Osama Sheikh’s conduct criticised The judicial commission strongly criticised medico-legal officer Dr Osama Sheikh, describing his conduct as extremely immature, childish and unprofessional.
The report said his behaviour was not appropriate for a medical professional.

The commission recommended that Dr Osama should not be assigned medico-legal duties for at least two years and should undergo proper academic and practical training before being given such responsibilities again.
It also observed that his conduct gave the impression that he might have been acting under someone’s influence.
The commission’s observations came amid questions over the initial post-mortem report prepared by Dr Osama, which was later challenged over discrepancies in the medical findings.
The final post-mortem report identified a bullet wound entering from the back as the cause of Mir Raza Ali’s death.
The commission also praised head clerk Zeeshan for his conduct, describing him as the only police official who brought credit to the Sindh Police in the case.
It recommended that he receive recognition and further training.
Questions over changes to the medical board The commission also questioned the sudden change in the medical board constituted to examine Mir Raza’s body.
According to the report, an eight-member board was formed under Karachi Police Surgeon Dr.
On August 7, the health department reduced its membership to five and included doctors from Hyderabad and Jamshoro.
The family rejected the revised composition.
The change delayed the process of exhuming the body.
Following public pressure and a legal notice, the original eight-member board was restored, and the examination was completed on August 8.
The commission described the sudden change as unusual, unclear and legally questionable.
It also raised questions about the role of the relevant health department officials.
Commission examines August 9 meeting at Chief Minister’s House The report also discussed a meeting held at the Chief Minister’s House on August 9, which prompted speculation about its purpose.
The commission said it found no evidence that the meeting was intended to pressure Dr Osama Sheikh or secure a report favouring the police.
It acknowledged that the chief minister had the authority to receive a briefing on a matter of significant public interest.
However, the commission said inviting the police surgeon to the meeting would have been appropriate in the interests of transparency.
Action recommended against police officials The commission criticised the performance of several police officers and recommended departmental and criminal proceedings where warranted.
It recommended a comprehensive inquiry against SHO Adeel Afzal, along with his interim suspension.
Departmental action and interim suspension were also recommended against Sub-Inspector Shabbir Laghari.
The commission further recommended departmental action against SHO Kamran Qureshi and his removal from the post.
The report called for further scrutiny of the relevant health department officials and an investigation into the possible loss of important evidence.
The commission said shortcomings in the initial police response and subsequent investigation had damaged public confidence.
It warned that serious failures in preserving evidence could affect legal proceedings.
It stressed that further investigation was necessary to establish responsibility and examine the possibility of a cover-up or other criminal conduct.
The commission said justice and the restoration of public trust would remain difficult without addressing the identified failures.
The severe disruption of the Strait of Hormuz since US-Israeli airstrikes began the war in February has pushed energy prices to multi-year highs, allowing trading desks to profit from the volatility.

In a sector notorious in the past for boom and bust, the majors have all promised this time to refrain from losing control of costs in what is one of the highest-earning years for global oil producers in recent memory.
Shell, BP, and TotalEnergies all expect refining margins to increase three- to fourfold in the third quarter from a year ago, with Shell guiding for a record high of $42 a barrel.
TotalEnergies expects cash flow from its refining and chemicals business to double to around $4 billion from the previous quarter.
Exxon signalled higher refining margins in the quarter could boost downstream profit by $4.5 billion versus the previous quarter.
ARE MAJORS ADAPTING THEIR SPENDING PLANS?

As majors report third-quarter results at the end of the month, investors are asking whether they will stick to their existing spending plans in times of exceptional earnings, wrote RBC Capital Markets analyst Biraj Borkhataria in a research note.
So far Chevron and Exxon have used the money to pay down debt.

Investors in Chevron will monitor investment in Venezuela and its progress toward extending its contract to operate the TCO joint venture in Kazakhstan, which is developing the country’s largest oilfield, analysts said.
HSBC expects Shell to announce a $3.5 billion buyback for the fourth quarter, after it reduced the pace of its buyback programme to a quarterly $3 billion earlier this year.
BP’S FORTUNES TURN After the major’s trading update last week, investment bank TPH called BP its favourite name among European majors.
Citi data shows BP’s net debt to operating cash flow falling from 1.7 times at the end of 2025, the highest of the five biggest majors, to an expected 0.8 times by the third quarter.

BP is likely to discuss its future capital allocation during its third-quarter earnings, HSBC said, as BP hits a target to reduce its net debt about a year early, also helped by pausing its buyback programme this year.

BP has flagged a strategy update on December 15. “We believe the priority will remain firmly on deleveraging, with stable capex and no buyback resumption before 2028,” said HSBC’s Kim Fustier and Sadnan Ali in a note.
Shell and Total are due to report on October 29 while BP, Chevron and Exxon are due on October 30.

KARACHI: Sindh Minister for Local Government, Housing and Town Planning Syed Nasir Hussain Shah has said that the restoration project of the Khiyam Canal in Clifton, along with the diversion of sewage water, will be completed within two months, helping reduce foul odour, minimise health risks and improve the overall environment of the area.
He expressed these views during his visit to Khiyam Canal, where he inspected the ongoing development work following complaints from local residents regarding commercial construction activities.
Shah said he had visited the site to review the concerns raised by residents living around the canal, adding that the Chief Minister of Sindh had also taken notice of the matter.

He clarified that the project was being undertaken by the Sindh Local Government Department and involved covering the drain and diverting sewage water to address sanitation-related problems in the area.
He said the initiative was aimed not only at improving the drainage system but also at restoring Khiyam Canal and enhancing the area’s overall appearance.
Shah said a clean-water canal was also being developed as part of the beautification plan, while greenery and tree plantation would be introduced along its surroundings.
He added that the completion of the project would help address problems caused by foul odour and unhygienic conditions, providing residents with a cleaner and healthier environment.
Addressing concerns regarding construction and possible commercial activities around Khiyam Canal, the minister categorically stated that no encroachment or unrelated construction was taking place.
He further clarified that no commercial activities had been authorised or were being permitted as part of the project.
Shah said the primary objective of the initiative was to facilitate the public, improve environmental conditions and ensure the restoration of Khiyam Canal.
He reiterated that the project would be completed within the stipulated two-month period, bringing improvements in sanitation, greenery and the overall appearance of the area for local residents.

Hegseth meets Netanyahu in unannounced visit to Israel, source says - By Reuters - - Oct 20, 2026 JERUSALEM: US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, a person familiar with the matter said, as tensions flare between the US and Iran.
The person did not say what the two men discussed during the meeting, first reported by Axios.
The Israeli prime minister’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Hegseth said in a social media post that he had visited US service members in the Central Command area of responsibility, which covers the Middle East, northeast Africa and parts of Asia.
Israel’s Army Radio reported his meeting with Netanyahu took place at an air force base in Israel’s southern desert.

Hegseth’s visit comes amid rising tensions in the Middle East war as tensions flare between the U.S. and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz and as Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis intensify their attacks on Saudi Arabia.

It also came a day after US President Donald Trump endorsed Netanyahu in next week’s parliamentary election in Israel, the country’s first ballot since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on southern Israel.
US and Israeli forces launched joint strikes against Iran in late February, setting off the wider Middle East war.
Netanyahu told Israeli media this month that he’s not seeking to attack Iran before the October 27 Israeli election.
Trump has said he will not attack Iran before US midterm elections in November.

RAWALPINDI: Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lt-General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry has reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to reducing regional tensions through diplomatic engagement with Iran while warning that any threat to Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity or Islamic holy sites would face a collective response under the Makkah Defence Alliance.

In an Interview with Independent Arabia, Lt-Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said that “the concern about escalation is always present because we are witnessing a recurring cycle of de-escalation and escalation, then de-escalation and escalation again,” explaining that Pakistan and its partners in the region continue to engage with the relevant parties to try to break this cycle.

He added, “We constantly emphasise to them that this cycle is not good, and it does not serve the interests of the region, nor the interests of the parties involved in the conflict itself,” stressing that Islamabad will continue its diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions.
The military spokesperson said Pakistan was maintaining communication with Tehran and other regional stakeholders to prevent further escalation and pursue peaceful solutions to ongoing conflicts.

He also confirmed that the collective deterrence mechanism established under the Pakistan-Saudi Arabia-Türkiye defence arrangement was already being implemented, describing it as a defensive framework intended to discourage aggression and preserve regional stability.

Discussing Pakistan’s communication with Iran, the ISPR DG said the country’s political and military leadership had maintained contacts with Tehran for several months, focusing on restraint and preventing further escalation.
He explained that Pakistan’s engagement with the relevant parties was aimed at narrowing differences and encouraging negotiated solutions rather than allowing the conflict to expand.
He said Pakistan and its regional partners were working to prevent the conflict from expanding geographically or intensifying militarily.
When asked whether Islamabad had conveyed a direct warning to Tehran following the attacks on Saudi Arabia, he neither confirmed nor denied such communication.
However, he emphasised that Pakistan’s diplomatic exchanges remained focused on reducing tensions.

The military spokesperson also warned that continued regional confrontation would not serve the interests of the countries involved, stressing the importance of negotiations and diplomatic engagement.
The ISPR DG reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to protecting Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and the security of the Two Holy Mosques.
He said Pakistan was already providing the necessary support to Saudi Arabia and would continue doing so under its existing defence commitments.
While declining to disclose operational details because of military confidentiality, he maintained that Islamabad remained prepared to employ the means available to fulfil its security obligations.
His remarks came against the backdrop of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, which have raised concerns about regional security and the protection of Islamic holy sites.
The DG ISPR said the attacks had generated anger among Pakistan’s political and military leadership and the wider public, reflecting the importance attached to the security of Makkah and Madinah.

Explaining the Pakistan-Saudi Arabia-Türkiye defence arrangement, Lt-Gen Chaudhry described the Makkah Alliance as a defensive mechanism grounded in the right of self-defence under Article 51 of the United Nations Charter.
He said the alliance was not directed against any particular country and had no offensive objectives.
Instead, its purpose was to strengthen collective security, discourage aggression and support regional peace.
According to the ISPR DG, any direct or indirect war against one of the three member countries would trigger a collective response under the alliance’s commitments.

He also highlighted progress in the alliance’s institutional development, including the establishment of its secretariat and a strategic political and defence committee involving senior officials from the three countries.
Lt-Gen Chaudhry said the arrangement built upon longstanding defence cooperation and historical relations among Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye.
He further clarified that the alliance did not replace existing bilateral defence agreements or security partnerships.

Addressing those responsible for attacks against Saudi Arabia, the military spokesperson said Pakistan’s defence commitments were intended to send an unmistakable message to both the perpetrators and those supporting them.
He stressed that the collective deterrence framework was designed to demonstrate the willingness and capability of member countries to respond to threats.

Referring to Pakistan’s experience in dealing with non-state armed groups, Lt Gen Chaudhry argued that such organisations often operated differently from states and could be difficult to deter through conventional diplomatic signals alone.
He maintained that clear and decisive security commitments were necessary to discourage further attacks and prevent militant groups from exploiting regional instability.
The ISPR DG also cautioned that expanding military confrontation would harm regional interests and complicate efforts to reach negotiated settlements.
Discussing the future of the Makkah Alliance, Lt-Gen Chaudhry said the arrangement was not necessarily limited to its three founding members.
He indicated that countries sharing its objectives of regional stability and collective security could potentially become part of the framework.

However, he did not confirm reports concerning the possible inclusion of other countries, explaining that decisions about membership rested with the political and strategic leadership of the existing member states.
The military spokesperson reiterated that the alliance was intended to promote peace and security rather than create confrontation with any particular regional actor.

The ISPR DG also discussed maritime security challenges in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, highlighting the importance of international cooperation to protect shipping routes and regional trade.
He referred to Pakistan’s participation in multinational maritime security arrangements and said regional countries were increasingly recognising the importance of collective security cooperation.

Milan on high alert as Italy deploys 500 troops following days of riots and looting Police detained 271 people after groups of masked youths set bins on fire, smashed windows and looted shops Italy will deploy 500 soldiers to Milan following days of violent protests over rising living costs that led to clashes with police, vandalism and widespread looting.
According to The Guardian, Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government has promised tougher security measures as the city prepares for further demonstrations on Saturday.
Police detained 271 people after groups of masked youths set bins on fire, smashed windows and looted shops during protests over the weekend.
Of those detained, 32 were arrested, including 23 minors.
Police used tear gas and water cannons to disperse violent groups.
Several luxury retailers, including Chanel, Tiffany and Dior, removed merchandise from their windows amid fears of further unrest.

Deputy Prime Minister Antonio Tajani warned that the government would take stronger action. “The government will respond firmly to these attacks on the state, including through measures aimed at curbing violence by minors,” he said.
Proposed security measures reportedly include tougher penalties for youth gangs, restrictions on public gatherings and extended preventive detention for minors.
Meanwhile, a protest movement called 17 October has announced plans for weekly demonstrations across major Italian cities.
Similar protests have also taken place in Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo and Turin, where police arrested 28 demonstrators.
Published October 19, 2026 Activists detained at Delhi's Jantar Mantar protest site.

An Indian court said on Monday that two "Cockroach" movement leaders would stay in prison for two more days, local media reported, after they were detained last week for demonstrating at a historic protest venue in violation of a ban.

Cockroach Janta Party leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were among 14 people who scaled barricades on Tuesday to enter the Jantar Mantar observatory, a day after it was removed from a list of designated protest sites.
They unfurled the Indian flag and chanted slogans demanding the chief election commissioner's resignation before police detained them, with a court later sending them to prison for five days.
On Monday evening, a local court extended their judicial custody by two days after Delhi Police requested more time to question them, local media reported.
Delhi Police did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
"This is an absolute mockery of the judicial system," the group's legal head, Ratna Singh, told reporters outside the court, adding they would challenge the order in a higher court.

The youth-led CJP, opposition parties and left-wing student organisations have held near-daily protests this month demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over a revision of voter lists that they say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party.

The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol, while the BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, student leaders and several of their supporters were also detained on Friday as hundreds poured into central Delhi for a protest in support of Das and Ranka.
The 'Cockroach' movement has emerged as one of the biggest political challenges to Modi and his BJP in his 12 years in power.
A weeks-long sit-in by the group and its supporters earlier this year forced the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over exam paper leaks.

The latest demonstrations erupted after the Indian Express newspaper reported that Kumar's two deputies had raised concerns internally about voter list changes, registration procedures and digital systems.

The 130 million names that were removed from voter lists starting last year — equivalent to more than the population of Japan — included 28 million people who have died, 63 million who have relocated and 30 million who could not be traced, according to the Election Commission.

The doctrine of necessity is the basis on which extraordinary actions by administrative authority, which are designed to restore order or uphold fundamental constitutional principles, are considered to be lawful even if such an action contravenes established constitution, laws, norms, or conventions.

The maxim on which the doctrine is based originated in the writings of the medieval jurist Henry de Bracton, and similar justifications for this kind of extra-legal action have been advanced by more recent legal authorities, including William Blackstone.
In a controversial 1954 judgment, Pakistani Chief Justice Muhammad Munir validated the extra-constitutional use of emergency powers by Governor General, Ghulam Mohammad.

In his judgment, the Chief Justice cited Bracton's maxim, 'that which is otherwise not lawful is made lawful by necessity', thereby providing the label that would come to be attached to the judgment and the doctrine that it was establishing.
The doctrine of necessity may also refer to the necessity of a judge with a reasonable apprehension of bias continuing to decide a matter if there is no alternative to that judge.
The Supreme Court of Canada applied this doctrine in the 1998 Reference re Remuneration of Judges (No 2) case.

International law In international law, the exception is allowed by the UN's International Law Commission (ILC) to be used by a state facing "grave and imminent peril": Under the law of State responsibility, necessity is one of the circumstances precluding the wrongfulness of conduct that would otherwise constitute a breach of an international obligation.

The doctrine is recognised in Article 25 of the International Law Commission's Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts, which reflects customary international law as recognised in international practice and judicial decisions.
The defence is exceptional and may be invoked only in limited circumstances.
Under Article 27 of the ILC Articles, the invocation of necessity does not terminate the underlying international obligation.
Once the circumstances giving rise to necessity cease to exist, the obligation resumes and must again be performed, unless it has otherwise come to an end under international law.

In any case, necessity may not be invoked by a State as a ground for precluding wrongfulness if: (a) the international obligation in question excludes the possibility of invoking necessity; or (b) the State has contributed to the situation of necessity.
Therefore, an obligation of customary international law or an obligation granted under a bilateral investment treaty may be suspended under the doctrine of necessity.

It is "an exception from illegality and in certain cases even as an exception from responsibility." In order to invoke the doctrine of necessity: The invoking State must not have contributed to the state of necessity, Actions taken were the only way to safeguard an essential interest from grave and impending danger.
Historical development The medieval English jurist Henry de Bracton is frequently cited as an early proponent of the doctrine, who presented it in the form of a maxim.
He was followed by the 18th-century jurist William Blackstone, who used it to justify various laws enacted by the English parliament.
The doctrine of necessity developed from earlier concepts of self-preservation in international law.

During the nineteenth century, several writers treated self-preservation as an inherent right of states that could, in exceptional circumstances, justify conduct inconsistent with international obligations.

In the course of the International Law Commission's work on the law of State responsibility, necessity was formulated as a distinct circumstance precluding wrongfulness and codified separately from broader theories of self-preservation.
The 1837 Caroline incident is frequently cited in discussions of the historical development of the doctrine.
During the Canadian Rebellions, British forces entered United States territory and destroyed the American vessel Caroline, which had been transporting personnel and supplies to Canadian insurgents.

In the subsequent diplomatic correspondence, United States Secretary of State Daniel Webster stated that any departure from international law required a necessity that was "instant, overwhelming, leaving no choice of means, and no moment for deliberation".
The correspondence between the two governments later became a frequently cited statement of the conditions governing necessity in international law.
The doctrine was subsequently considered in international adjudication.

In the Russian Indemnity arbitration (1912), the tribunal accepted that necessity could, in principle, affect the performance of an international obligation where compliance would endanger the existence of the state, although it rejected the plea on the facts of the case.

In his separate opinion in Oscar Chinn (1934), Judge Dionisio Anzilotti stated that necessity could excuse the non-observance of an international obligation but concluded that the conditions for invoking it had not been established in that case.
The International Law Commission examined the doctrine during its codification of the law of State responsibility.
Its Special Rapporteur, Roberto Ago, proposed draft provisions on circumstances precluding wrongfulness, including necessity.
Draft Article 33 was adopted on first reading in 1980.
Following further consideration and revision, the provision was adopted as Article 25 of the Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts in 2001.

The International Court of Justice recognised the doctrine in the Gabčíkovo–Nagymaros Project case (1997), holding that necessity is recognised under customary international law as a ground for precluding the wrongfulness of an internationally wrongful act.
The Court also stated that the conditions for invoking necessity are exceptional and cumulative.

The Court subsequently referred to Article 25 in its advisory opinion on the Legal Consequences of the Construction of a Wall in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (2004), where it found that the conditions for invoking necessity had not been satisfied.
Examples The doctrine of necessity has been invoked in a number of countries.

Pakistan, 1954 On 24 October 1954 the Governor-General of Pakistan, Ghulam Mohammad, dissolved the Constituent Assembly and appointed a new Council of Ministers on the grounds that the existing one no longer represented the people of Pakistan.
Stanley de Smith argues that the real reason for the dissolution was because Mohammad objected to the constitution which the Assembly was about to adopt.

The President of the Constituent Assembly, Maulvi Tamizuddin, appealed to the Chief Court of Sindh at Karachi to restrain the new Council of Ministers from implementing the dissolution and to determine the validity of the appointment of the new Council under Section 223-A of the constitution.
In response, members of the new Council of Ministers appealed to the court saying that it had no jurisdiction to approve the request of the President to overturn the dissolution and appointments.

They argued that Section 223-A of the constitution had never been validly enacted into the Constitution because it was never approved of by the Governor-General, and therefore anything submitted under it was invalid.

The Chief Court of Sind ruled in favour of President Tamizuddin and held that the Governor-General's approval was not needed when the Constituent Assembly was acting only as a Constituent Assembly and not as the Federal Legislature.
The Federation of Pakistan and the new Council of Ministers then appealed to the court, the appeal was heard in March 1955 (Federation of Pakistan v Maulvi Tamizuddin Khan).

In the appeal hearing under Chief Justice Muhammad Munir, the court decided that the Constituent Assembly functioned as the 'Legislature of the Domain' and that the Governor-General's assent was necessary for all legislation to become law.
Therefore, the Chief Court of Sind had no jurisdiction to overturn the Governor General's dissolution and it was held as valid.

However, the ground of which the court found in favour of the Federation of Pakistan called into question the validity of all legislation passed by the Assembly, not to mention the unconstitutionality of the Assembly itself since 1950.
To solve this problem, the Governor-General invoked Emergency Powers to retrospectively validate the Acts of the Constituent Assembly.

An appeal was filed against the Governor-General for invoking emergency powers and the Chief Justice had to determine the constitutionality of invoking the Emergency Powers and whether the Governor-General could give his assent to legislation retroactively.

The Court held that in this case the Governor-General could not invoke emergency powers because in doing so he validated certain laws that had been invalid because he had not assented to them previously.
Justice Munir also ruled that constitutional legislation could not be validated by the Governor General but had to be approved by the Legislature.
The lack of a Constituent Assembly did not transfer the Legislature's powers over to the Governor-General.
The Court was referred to for an opinion.
On 16 May 1955 it ruled: The Governor General in certain circumstances had the power to dissolve the Constituent Assembly.

The Governor-General has during the interim period the power 'under the common law of civil or state necessity' of retrospectively validating the laws listed in the Schedule to the Emergency Powers ordinance.
The new Assembly (formed under the Constituent Convention Order 1955) would be valid and able to exercise all powers under the Indian Independence Act 1947.
In his verdict, Munir declared it was necessary to go beyond the constitution to what he claimed was the Common Law, to general legal maxims, and to English historical precedent.
He relied on Bracton's maxim, 'that which is otherwise not lawful is made lawful by necessity', and the Roman law maxim urged by Ivor Jennings, 'the well-being of the people is the supreme law'.

Grenada, 1985 In a 1985 judgment, the Chief Justice of the High Court of Grenada invoked the doctrine of necessity to validate the legal existence of a court then trying for murder the persons who had conducted a coup against former leader Maurice Bishop.
The court had been established under an unconstitutional "People's Law" following the overthrow of the country's constitution, which had subsequently been restored.

The defendants argued that the court before which they were being tried had no legal existence under the restored constitution, and they were therefore being deprived of their constitutional right to a trial before a "Court established by law".

The High Court acknowledged that the lower court "had come into existence in an unconstitutional manner", but "the doctrine of necessity validated its acts." On this basis, the murder trials were allowed to proceed.

Nigeria, 2010 A related (although non-judicial) use of the doctrine took place when, on 9 February 2010, the Nigerian National Assembly passed a resolution making Vice President Goodluck Jonathan the Acting President and Commander in Chief of the Armed Forces.

Both chambers of the Assembly passed the resolution after President Umaru Yar'Adua, who for 78 days had been in Saudi Arabia receiving medical treatment, was unable to formally empower the vice president to exercise full powers as acting president, as provided for in Section 145 of the country's constitution.

No provision of the Nigerian constitution empowering the National Assembly to pass any such resolution, causing Senate President David Mark to assert that the Senate had been guided by the "doctrine of necessity" in arriving at its decision.

United Kingdom, 2022–2023 On 13 June 2022, United Kingdom Foreign Secretary Liz Truss introduced the Northern Ireland Protocol Bill in the House of Commons, which, if enacted, would allow the UK government to unilaterally "disapply" (the word used) parts of the Northern Ireland Protocol that it had signed up to, a part of the Brexit withdrawal agreement.

The UK government conceded that the bill would mean breaching its obligations under international law but said that its position was justified, explicitly invoking the doctrine of necessity and saying that having to uphold the Protocol was placing unacceptable levels of strain on institutions in Northern Ireland and that there was "no other way" of safeguarding the UK's interests.
On 15 June, vice-president of the European Commission Maroš Šefčovič said that there was "no legal nor political justification" for the bill and that it was illegal.

He also announced that the Commission would re-open the infringement proceedings against the UK government which had been started in March 2021, including two new counts where it was alleged the UK breached the Protocol.

In a session of the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee on 21 June 2022, Lorand Bartels, Professor of International Law at Trinity Hall, Cambridge, and Malgosia Fitzmaurice, Professor of Public International Law at Queen Mary University of London, were questioned about the use of the doctrine of necessity.

Fitzmaurice said that necessity is the "most contentious and controversial" of circumstances which allow treaty terms to be disregarded; she stated that using necessity as a justification "should be very carefully considered" seeing as action could instead be taken using Article 16 of the protocol.
Bartels suggested that the necessity doctrine could only be used to breach some parts of the protocol.

During the leadership election during the summer of 2022, Rishi Sunak said his preference was a negotiated settlement with the EU while Liz Truss, who was the minister responsible for introducing the Protocol Bill, supported it as a method to "[break] the deadlock in a legal way".
Although Truss won that leadership election, she resigned soon after amid a government crisis and Sunak became prime minister.

The UK government and the European Commission made a joint statement on 27 February 2023 announcing the Windsor Framework, a legal agreement which addressed concerns around the Northern Ireland Protocol.
As a result, the Northern Ireland Protocol Bill was withdrawn and allowed to lapse at the end of the 2022-23 session of parliament.
Bangladesh, 2024 On 5 August 2024, Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina was facing mass protests has submitted her resignation to the President of Bangladesh and subsequently fled to India.
General Waker-uz-Zaman has temporarily took control of the government.
On 6 August 2024, the President followed the wishes of protesters, dissolving the Jatiya Sangsad and installing Muhammad Yunus, a Nobel laureate, as leader of the interim government.
While there is no constitutional basis for a caretaker government, Bangladeshi courts have upheld the legitimacy of the government under the doctrine of necessity.
Court rulings have held that Hasina's resignation created a situation for which there was no constitutional remedy.
Hence, the urgent need to manage state affairs made the appointment lawful.

Application in international investment treaty tribunals The doctrine of necessity has been invoked in investment treaty arbitration by states seeking to justify measures adopted during periods of economic, political, or security emergencies that are alleged to have breached obligations under bilateral or multilateral investment treaties.

Investment tribunals have considered the customary international law defence of necessity reflected in Article 25 of the International Law Commission's Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts, as well as treaty provisions containing essential security interests clauses where applicable.
The doctrine has been considered in a number of arbitral proceedings involving measures adopted in response to financial crises, armed conflicts, and national security concerns.

Investment treaty tribunals have considered both the conditions for invoking the customary doctrine of necessity and the relationship between Article 25 and treaty provisions permitting states to adopt measures for the protection of their essential security interests.

Where both forms of defence have been invoked, tribunals have examined the wording of the applicable treaty alongside the requirements of customary international law in determining whether the challenged measures were justified.
The doctrine was considered extensively in a series of arbitrations arising from Argentina's 2001–2002 economic crisis.

Tribunals in these cases reached differing conclusions on the relationship between the treaty-based defence and the customary-law defence, and on whether Argentina had met the strict conditions of Article 25.
In CMS Gas Transmission Co. v.

Argentina, the tribunal treated the Treaty's essential-security-interests provision and Article 25 as effectively coextensive, and found that Argentina's measures did not meet the customary-law requirement that the act be the "only way" to safeguard an essential interest, since other, less drastic responses to the crisis remained available.
By contrast, the tribunal in LG&E Energy Corp. v.

Argentina held that Argentina's conduct during the acute phase of the crisis, from December 2001 to April 2003, was justified under the state of necessity contemplated by both Article XI of the Treaty and general international law, and accordingly exempted Argentina from liability for that period, while still awarding compensation for breaches occurring outside it.
The tribunal in Continental Casualty Co. v.
A subsequent illustration of the relationship between treaty-based essential-security-interests clauses and the customary doctrine arose in CC/Devas (Mauritius) Ltd. v.
India, concerning the annulment of a satellite-spectrum agreement that India said was necessary to meet its security needs.

The tribunal held that the essential-security-interests clause of the applicable treaty, which stated that its protections should "not in any way limit" the state's right to act for such interests, was not to be read restrictively by importing the conditions attached to the customary necessity defence under Article 25.

It reasoned that a treaty's general "preservation of rights" clause, which merely preserves protections investors might otherwise enjoy under international law, was analytically distinct from the customary necessity defence, which is available to states rather than conferring rights on investors, and that India in any event was invoking the treaty clause rather than the customary defence.
The tribunal noted that this conclusion was consistent with the approach taken by the tribunal in Continental Casualty and by the ad hoc committee in the CMS annulment proceeding.

Insurance canary As the cost of insuring our houses escalates around the United States and the world, it appears that property insurance is acting like a canary in a coal mine.
Canaries used to be taken into coal mines because they served as an early warning system if dangerous gases were building up.
Since the canaries were more sensitive to these gases than people, they protected the miners from life-threatening conditions.

When the canary dropped dead, the miners could still get out Like the canaries, the actuaries who interpret data for insurance companies are more sensitive than most individual people to changes going on in the world.
Actuaries earn big salaries because the financial health of their employers depends on them.

Things have already gotten so bad that the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) recently sponsored a webinar panel discussion: “Extreme Weather Events and Insurance: Households, Homeowners, and Risk.” (This link will take you to a video of the event.) The panelists were located in the United States (Washington, DC and Madison, Wisconsin) and England (London and Cambridge).
Climate changes are not limited to the United States, nor is awareness that we need to do something about them if we can.
The panelists were not grinding particular political axes.

They were discussing the measured fact that an increasing number of extreme weather events are destroying valuable property – housing, commercial buildings, streets, bridges, etc. – requiring insurance company payouts to policyholders.
These insurance payouts must be financed by the premiums charged to people who are insuring their property.
As damages increase, the premiums also have to increase.
Although premiums may be regulated by state regulators, if they do not allow the needed increases insurance companies will pull out of doing business in that state.
As insurance companies pull out, it may become more and more difficult – perhaps even impossible – for people to insure their houses.
But if a house cannot be insured, banks won’t finance a mortgage on it, and if it cannot be financed the owner may be unable to sell it.
For many people, their home is their primary investment, and they cannot afford to live in it if they cannot insure it.
If it burned down or was otherwise destroyed, they would be wiped out financially.
But if they cannot sell it, then the homeowner is a real pickle.
Disrupted housing markets can produce disastrous results for a country’s economy in general, as we Americans discovered during the recession beginning around 2008.

The impact of a world that is heating up is not being felt as much in the United States as in many other countries in Europe, Africa, and Asia which are suffering from unusually long bouts of very hot weather, flooding downpours alternating with extreme droughts, forest fires, etc.
Excerpted: ‘Property Insurance Is the Canary in the Climate Coal Mine’.

Minister for Energy (Power Division) Awais Leghari, while speaking at a ceremony in Dera Ghazi Khan on Monday, revealed the government’s plan to introduce modern technology to combat power theft and curtail line losses.

According to him, the APMS will identify specific transformers in high-theft areas, enabling targeted disconnections so that thousands of paying consumers on an entire feeder are not penalised for the actions of electricity thieves.
The minister reiterated that loadshedding will continue on feeders reporting 30 percent or higher losses, emphasising that no leniency will be shown toward electricity thieves or chronic defaulters.

According to power experts, the APMS will enable more targeted identification of high-loss consumers, improve energy accounting, enhance operational visibility, and support equitable load management through data-driven decision-making.

As the Power Planning and Monitoring Company (PPMC), the technical arm of the Ministry of Energy (Power Division), is playing a central role in supporting the planning, design, and effective implementation of this sector-wide reform, the APMS will serve as a key enabler in achieving these objectives through transformer-level monitoring, analytics, digital oversight, and enforcement mechanisms across Discos.

The APMS works alongside Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) and Automated Meter Reading (AMR) rollouts, enabling two-way communication and remote cutoff capabilities. “The APMS pilot project is all set to be launched in Lahore and Kasur soon, as the necessary work is underway by the Lahore Electric Supply Company (Lesco).
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif will inaugurate this pilot project soon,” confirmed an official source in Lesco while talking to Dawn.

Talking about the background and launch of the APMS, he said the Discos have been implementing, for the last few years, the Power Division’s policy under which loadshedding is observed, keeping in view the loss category of 11kV feeders.
According to him, loadshedding (both scheduled and forced) is being observed at loss-making feeders categorised as 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5.
So this system will soon be in place, gradually, to protect the rights of law-abiding consumers,” he explained.
He said that under the new arrangement, the APMS would be installed on transformers of various capacities currently placed on poles.
After the APMS installations, the existing conventional electricity meters would be replaced by AMI meters (smart meters).

After replacement, the APMS would be synced with the smart meters and start monitoring the real-time consumption of electricity users. “Suppose there are 200 consumers receiving power from one transformer in any area.
The APMS at each transformer will record the total number of units received from the power distribution system and the actual number of units used by the consumers.
If the units received from the system are 100,000 and the number used by the consumers is less than that, it would mean that the remaining units have been stolen through unfair means.

In this way, it will be easy for the Discos to detect power-stealing consumers,” he explained. “At present, it is difficult to detect power thieves in a vast area (2,000 to 3,000 consumers or even more) covered by a feeder.

With the APMS, the area would be narrowed from the feeder to the transformer (150 to 200 consumers),” he said, adding that this would help Lesco stop power theft and reduce line losses more effectively.

According to another Lesco officer, the APMS would be installed in a 2/4-foot iron box at transformers. “The APMS would automatically report the theft, line losses, etc. to the officials concerned, enabling them to respond quickly to fix the issue,” he maintained.
Similarly, he said, if someone touched the AMI meter with the intention to tamper with it and steal electricity, the meter itself would report to the system monitored by the officials.

Supreme Court rejects Google challenge to patent office review policy: Here's why By declining to hear the appeal, the high court preserves a controversial rule that restricts administrative challenges to older patents.
Supreme Court has declined to hear an appeal from Alphabet Inc.’s Google, leaving in place a federal patent office policy that restricts administrative reviews for older patents.
Core Dispute: The dispute stemmed from a software patent infringement case involving developer which accused Google of infringing upon its server technology.
The legal battle centered around a software patent infringement dispute between Google and a developer named VirtaMove, which accused Google of infringing on its server software technology.
Google's stance: In response, Google sought to challenge the validity of the patent through the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB), an administrative tribunal housed within the U.S.

However, the agency declined to initiate the review by applying its "settled expectations" practice, a framework under which the board more frequently rejects petitions to review patents that have been active for more than six years.
The patent office argues that older patents have built up "settled expectations" for their owners in the marketplace, making them less appropriate for administrative cancellation procedures.
In response, Google argued in its Supreme Court appeal that the patent office exceeded its statutory authority by imposing artificial time restrictions that were never established by Congress.
By refusing to hear the case, the Supreme Court left lower-court rulings intact without issuing a detailed opinion.

Broader context: Previously, Lower courtsrejected Google's challenge, and with the Supreme Court opting not to intervene, the policy remains active, dealing a notable setback to major technology companies that routinely rely on these administrative procedures to contest questionable patents.
For tech giants like Google, Apple, and others—who frequently rely on PTAB reviews to invalidate overly broad or suspect software and hardware patents—this decision is a notable blow.
It solidifies the patent office's power to gatekeep administrative challenges, leaving tech firms with fewer avenues to clear out older patents they are accused of infringing.

Abdul Samad Tariq ISLAMABAD, Oct 18 (APP):For children turning neighborhood streets into cricket grounds, students seeking affordable sports facilities and young athletes striving to develop their talent, the Capital Development Authority’s (CDA) planned Rs952 million multi-sport arenas could open new avenues for recreation, training and competition across Islamabad.
The projects reflect the authority’s efforts to expand the capital’s sports infrastructure and bring modern recreational facilities closer to residents.

By developing … From street cricket to state-of-the-art arenas: Islamabad’s sporting transformation Abdul Samad Tariq ISLAMABAD, Oct 18 (APP):For children turning neighborhood streets into cricket grounds, students seeking affordable sports facilities and young athletes striving to develop their talent, the Capital Development Authority’s (CDA) planned Rs952 million multi-sport arenas could open new avenues for recreation, training and competition across Islamabad.
By developing complexes at three locations, the CDA aims to create more opportunities for people to participate in sports, pursue healthy lifestyles and develop their athletic potential.
The authority plans to establish multi-sport complexes in D-12/1, G-11/3 Markaz and F-8 Markaz.

The proposed facilities include indoor swimming pools, gyms, futsal courts, cricket practice cages, padel courts, basketball facilities and multipurpose sports halls, offering a range of activities for sports enthusiasts and aspiring athletes.
The projects could also reduce the need for residents to travel across the city in search of suitable venues.
For families, students and amateur players, access to facilities within their communities could make regular participation in sports more convenient.
A CDA spokesperson told APP that operational arrangements would be finalized after construction was completed and the facilities became operational.
The authority has yet to announce the fee structure, concessions for students and registered sports clubs, or whether the complexes would be managed directly or through private operators.
These arrangements will be important in determining how residents use the facilities and how effectively the investment supports grassroots sports.
Affordable memberships, transparent booking procedures and designated training sessions could help attract a wider range of users.
Existing facilities illustrate the range of costs involved in organized sports.

Membership packages at the Pakistan Sports Complex, operated by the Pakistan Sports Board, have included registration charges ranging from Rs5,000 to Rs30,000 and monthly fees of Rs1,500 to Rs5,000, depending on the sport and package.
Commercial padel courts have reportedly charged around Rs2,000 an hour, while booking charges for some CDA-managed cricket grounds have reached approximately Rs15,000 a day for matches.
These rates vary by venue and booking category and do not indicate what the new complexes will charge.
The proposed arenas will have their own operational requirements, including staffing, maintenance, utilities and safety arrangements, which will influence their long-term management.
The proposed complexes could also widen opportunities for girls and women to participate in physical activity.
Convenient timings, reasonable fees, suitable facilities and effective safety arrangements would help make regular sports participation more accessible.

A female student said affordable facilities could encourage more girls to take part in sports, provided the venues offered convenient timings and a safe environment. “Many girls would like to take part in sports, but access to suitable facilities, the cost of regular sessions and family commitments can become barriers.
If these arenas offer affordable rates, convenient timings and appropriate facilities for women, more girls could benefit,” she said.
Residents have also welcomed the prospect of having sports facilities closer to their homes.

Murad Khan, a resident of D-12, said the complex planned for his sector could provide local residents with a convenient alternative to travelling across the city or paying private-club rates, provided the facilities remained affordable.
According to available project details, the D-12/1 complex will cover approximately 4.2 acres at an estimated cost of Rs327 million.
The G-11/3 facility will occupy around 3.5 acres and cost Rs317 million, while the F-8 Markaz complex will cover about 3.2 acres at an estimated cost of Rs307 million to Rs308 million.
The combined estimates amount to approximately Rs951 million to Rs952 million, making confirmation of the final approved allocation important.
The projects are to be financed through CDA resources and awarded through open competitive bidding.
Construction is expected to take about a year after work begins, according to the project information available for this report.
Once completed, the complexes will require regular maintenance, trained staff, proper sanitation and effective safety procedures, particularly for swimming pools and specialized sports facilities.
Sustainable management will be essential to maintaining service standards while ensuring that the venues remain useful to local communities.
Student concessions, group booking options and designated training slots for registered clubs could further expand participation.
Clear information about membership fees, opening hours and booking procedures would also help residents plan their use of the facilities.

The investment offers an opportunity to strengthen Islamabad’s recreational infrastructure while creating spaces for young people to develop their skills, build confidence and engage in healthy competition.
With effective management and accessible arrangements, the proposed arenas could become active community hubs that support grassroots sports and encourage a more physically active population.
Ultimately, the value of million investment will extend beyond the construction of courts, pools and sports halls.
Its lasting contribution will depend on how effectively these facilities serve Islamabad’s residents and help nurture the next generation of sporting talent.

Australian telecom shares tumble as SpaceX moves closer to direct-to-cell market Regional carrier shares tumble across Australia and New Zealand as investors reprice long-term satellite competition risks following a multi-billion-dollar spectrum acquisition.

Major telecommunications stocks across Australia and New Zealand fell sharply on Monday, echoing a global sell-off triggered by fears that SpaceX's expansion into direct-to-device mobile services could challenge traditional telecom operators.
Australia's Telstra dropped 2.5% to a six-week low, while TPG Telecom fell 4.9%, its steepest daily decline since early June.
New Zealand's Spark lost 1.8%, while smaller regional players, including Superloop and Aussie Broadband, also declined.

The sell-off followed SpaceX's agreement last week to acquire a nationwide low-band spectrum portfolio in the United States, strengthening Starlink Mobile's direct-to-cell capabilities and bringing Elon Musk's satellite venture closer to competing with established wireless carriers.

Low-band frequencies travel longer distances and penetrate buildings more effectively than higher-frequency airwaves, potentially allowing satellite-based services to challenge traditional mobile networks.
The deal has raised concerns among investors in the US and Europe about growing competition from satellite-based mobile services.
"Investors fear the U.S. is just the first market, and that incumbents' biggest advantage, coverage, is losing its value," said David Tuckwell, CIO at ETF Shares in Sydney.

Sindh’s struggle for survival The Sindh Rural Support Organisation (SRSO) has quietly become one of Pakistan’s most effective engines of resilience.
In a country where bureaucracy often confuses motion with progress, the SRSO has distinguished itself through the rare combination of compassion and competence.
It began modestly, with the idea that communities – especially women and the poor – should not merely receive help but shape it.
Over two decades, it has turned that principle into practice across Sindh’s flood-prone districts.
When the province was submerged in 2022, the SRSO turned its field offices in Shikarpur, Jacobabad, Larkana, Khairpur and Sukkur into lifelines.
They distributed food and medicine, but also wages and dignity. 'Cash-for-work' schemes rebuilt roads and morale.
Women artisans revived embroidery clusters that became symbols of both income and identity.
Even housing reconstruction acquired a climate-conscious twist: elevated eco-homes designed to resist the next deluge rather than commemorate the last one.
The publication of ‘Mausamyati Tabdili Ain Sindh’ (Climate Change and Sindh) marks the SRSO’s entry into the intellectual arena.
The 152-page volume is less a vanity project than a statement of intent: that the climate debate must be written and read in Sindhi if it is to matter.
In that, it continues the SRSO’s evolution from a relief agency to a knowledge institution – one that translates floodwater into public policy.
The volume’s compiler, Zubair Soomro, embodies the bridge between activism and analysis.
A development worker turned editor, he understands that people are more likely to act on ideas they understand.
Hence his insistence on linguistic ownership: climate literacy, he argues, cannot survive translation into bureaucratese.
The essays he curates draw their imagery from the Indus delta, the Kotri barrage, the Thatta mangroves and the brittle rhythms of fishing and farming life.
The result is a body of writing that feels lived rather than borrowed.
Soomro’s editorial hand ensures diversity without dilution.
The 17 contributions range from scientific exposition to moral argument.
They avoid the twin traps of despair and technocracy that often plague environmental writing.
Instead, they weave empirical evidence with cultural intuition – what might be called Sindh’s environmental vernacular.
This, more than anything, is Soomro’s quiet triumph: turning climate change from a donor-driven slogan into a people’s conversation.
No such conversation would be complete without Naseer Memon, the province’s most persuasive chronicler of rivers and rights.
His career – spanning civil society, journalism and research – has made him both witness and conscience.
Memon’s writings have long argued that the Indus Delta’s decline is not an act of nature but of neglect.
His notion of the 'right of rivers to exist' predates global debates about ecological personhood and makes a philosophical claim with practical urgency: if the Indus dies, so does Sindh.
In ‘Mausamyati Tabdili Ain Sindh’, Memon contributes three essays that distil decades of thought.
He reimagines the river as a living being, dissects the politics of Pakistan’s flood mismanagement and explores how the erasure of land erodes identity itself.
Few writers connect hydrology to history with such clarity.
Together, Soomro and Memon have forged an intellectual alliance that transforms climate anxiety into cultural critique.
Where one edits from within the development sector, the other writes from the margins of power.

Between them, they map a new moral geography for Sindh – one where environmentalism is as much about justice as it is about weather. 'Mausamyati Tabdili Ain Sindh' opens with forewords by Durrani and Kalhoro, both of whom anchor the collection in lived experience rather than abstract concern.
They remind readers that climate change, in Sindh, is not a forecast but is yesterday’s floodwater still standing in today’s fields.
The first essay, ‘Sarhadan Kaan Azad Mausam’ ('Climate Without Borders'), by Ali Tauqueer Shaikh, stretches the reader’s horizon beyond the provincial.
Shaikh, a veteran climate strategist, examines compound extreme weather events – the deadly cocktail of heatwaves, droughts and floods that increasingly defines South Asia.
His central message is that adaptation must be as borderless as the atmosphere.
The essay links Sindh’s fate to regional cooperation – a hard sell in a neighbourhood addicted to rivalry, but a necessary one.
Next comes M Ehsan Leghari, whose essay on the Indus’s lower Kotri stretch introduces a chilling idea: ecocide.
A biologist and conservationist with decades of experience in Sindh’s irrigation ecology, Leghari documents the loss of fish species, the intrusion of seawater and the collapse of delta ecosystems.
He reminds readers that biodiversity is not aesthetic but existential.
His writing bridges science and ethics, turning ecological decline into an indictment of state apathy.
The Indus, he implies, is being murdered in instalments.
The book then widens its scope.
Imdad Hussain Siddiqui, the Sindh ombudsman, contributes a thoughtful piece titled 'Climate Change and the Leadership Role of the Sindh Ombudsman'.
A career jurist and administrator, Siddiqui argues that climate adaptation is as much a question of governance as of geography.
His essay shows how oversight institutions – often dismissed as ceremonial – can enforce climate accountability by ensuring that local officials protect the rights of affected citizens.
He frames environmental justice as a constitutional duty, not a bureaucratic favour.
In a province where redress is rare, his voice lends moral authority and administrative realism.
Equally compelling is 'Sindh and the Climate Crisis' by Nasir Ali Panhwar, an environmental policy expert and executive director of the Centre for Environment and Development.
Panhwar’s career has long intertwined research and advocacy; his focus on water management and urban resilience makes him one of Sindh’s most informed commentators.

In this essay, he traces the historical evolution of Sindh’s vulnerability – from colonial canal construction to modern urban sprawl – and argues that climate policy must move from reaction to foresight.
His prose is spare but sharp: If we continue to treat the river as a pipe and the desert as waste, we will have neither.
Together, Siddiqui and Panhwar remind readers that climate change is not only a scientific concern but a political one.
Where Leghari writes as a naturalist, Siddiqui speaks as a reformer, and Panhwar as a planner.
Their essays, distinct in tone but united in urgency, reveal a spectrum of Sindh’s intellectual response – from the courtroom to the delta, from the policy bench to the field trench.
A cluster of other articles turns to adaptation, agriculture, and the gendered experience of crisis.

Several authors – teachers, journalists and development workers – offer firsthand observations from flood-affected villages, proposing micro-solutions such as floating gardens, seed banks and women-led disaster committees.
Yet it is again Memon’s trilogy that gives the book its spine.
In one essay, he declares that rivers possess an existence beyond their economic use; in another, he skewers the flood empathy cycle, where sympathy peaks after catastrophe and ebbs with the waters.
His third essay reflects on cultural displacement – the drowning of memory when geography disappears.
What sets the collection apart is its accessibility.
The Sindhi prose is clean, the layout elegant, and the tone serious without self-importance.
Citations from the IPCC and COP meetings coexist with local proverbs.
The mix is refreshing – a reminder that sophistication need not be foreign.
As a whole, 'Mausamyati Tabdili Ain Sindh' is both a document and a diagnosis.
It records the human cost of climate change in a province already living its future and it exposes the institutional lethargy that allows disaster to repeat itself.
More importantly, it establishes Sindhi as a language of environmental scholarship.
The SRSO and its collaborators have done something rare in Pakistan: they have created a book that belongs equally on an academic’s desk and in a villager’s home.
It argues, persuasively, that adaptation begins not with infrastructure but with understanding – and that understanding grows best in the language of the people.
In that sense, 'Mausamyati Tabdili Ain Sindh' is not merely a book about climate change.
It is a reminder that the struggle for survival, like the Indus itself, flows from the same source: memory, dignity and the refusal to surrender to the tide.
The writer holds a PhD from the University of Birmingham, UK.

Surgical sponge found in woman’s abdomen after one year of operation - By Web Desk - - Oct 20, 2026 MUZAFFARABAD: Prime Minister of Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) Iftikhar Ali Gillani has taken notice of a severe medical negligence case at the District Headquarter (DHQ) Hospital in Bagh, ARY News reported.
It was revealed that a surgical bandage was left inside a woman’s abdomen for an entire year following an operation at the facility.
Reports indicate that approximately 200 grams of bandages were subsequently removed from the patient’s body.
Taking swift notice of the incident, the AJK Prime Minister ordered the Director General (DG) of Health to conduct a transparent and thorough investigation into the matter.
He also instructed the authorities to identify those responsible and submit a detailed inquiry report to him immediately.
Earlier, the federal government has decided to restructure the administrative framework of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), ARY News reported on Wednesday, citing sources.
Sources said an administrative structure based on the Medical Teaching Institution (MTI) model would be introduced at PIMS, requiring amendments to the existing PIMS Act.
Under the proposed reforms, PIMS will be administered through a Board of Governors comprising individuals from various fields, according to Ministry of Health sources.
The sources said the chairman of the PIMS Board of Governors would be appointed from the market.
A committee headed by Federal Health Minister Mustafa Kamal has also been constituted to oversee administrative reforms at PIMS.
The committee includes the law minister, vice chancellors of medical universities and health experts, sources said.
The committee has been tasked with presenting its recommendations for amendments to the PIMS Act within 15 days.
Sources said a special committee has already submitted its report and recommendations regarding PIMS to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

The decisions concerning administrative reforms at PIMS were taken in light of the special committee’s recommendations, while the prime minister has issued directions regarding the hospital’s administrative affairs, sources added.
A 20-member PIMS Reform Committee was constituted on the directives of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
The committee comprised prominent health experts from both the public and private sectors, according to sources.

Idlib pomegranate farmers seek new markets to sell surplus harvest - By Web Desk - - Oct 19, 2026 IDLIB: Syrian pomegranate farmers in the town of Darkush, in northwestern Idlib province near the Turkish border, are struggling to bring an expected strong harvest to market amid rising production and transportation costs, low prices and limited export opportunities.
According to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA), the challenges are squeezing farmers’ incomes despite expectations of a good harvest this season.
Pomegranate cultivation is a key source of livelihood for farmers in Darkush, which lies in a valley in the Orontes River basin, at the foothills of the Syrian Coastal Mountain Range.
Farmers are calling for affordable agricultural supplies, cold storage facilities and access to new markets to help them sell their produce and improve their earnings.
Pomegranate orchards cover more than 250 hectares in Darkush, according to the local Agricultural Extension Division.
The harvest of early varieties began in the second half of September, with production expected to be good this season.

Mohammad Dada, an agricultural supervisor at the Darkush Agricultural Extension Division, said field visits were being conducted to advise farmers on harvesting, packaging and controlling pests, including aphids and fungal diseases.
More than 70 per cent of farmers in the area depend on pomegranate cultivation, Dada said.
However, current selling prices are insufficient to cover rising costs of pesticides, labour, packaging and transportation.
Producing one kilogramme of pomegranates costs around 50 Syrian pounds, equivalent to $0.41, he said, calling for subsidised fertilisers and pesticides to ease the financial burden on farmers.
Farmer Mohammad Sharif said pomegranate cultivation was deeply rooted in Darkush’s heritage.
Some varieties are used to produce pomegranate molasses and juice, enabling producers to diversify their products and make better use of the harvest.
Farmer Nima Adeeb Nima said five main pomegranate varieties were grown in Darkush: Nab Al-Jamal, Asfouri, Al-Helu, Al-Laban and French.
Early varieties are harvested from mid-September to early October.
However, limited export opportunities and restricted access to foreign markets have hurt sales, while domestic markets are unable to absorb the entire harvest, he said.
Trader Samer Bakro said transportation costs, particularly fuel prices, had made it more expensive to ship pomegranates to Damascus and other provinces.
Renting a vehicle costs around $130, he said, adding that more export channels were needed to sell surplus produce, which also faces limited storage options.
Expanding export opportunities and improving storage facilities could help farmers and traders reduce losses, reach new markets and secure better returns from the harvest.

Beluga whale Cyprus dies in California months after leaving Ontario's Marineland The aquarium said a full necropsy would be conducted to determine the cause of death A nine-year-old beluga whale rescued from the now-closed Marineland in Ontario has died at SeaWorld San Diego, becoming the latest animal to die following a mass relocation.
The whale, named Cyprus, arrived at the California aquarium on August 22 and had reportedly been adjusting well to his new surroundings.
However, SeaWorld said Cyprus stopped eating on Friday, and an ultrasound revealed that his intestinal tract was not functioning normally.
The aquarium said a full necropsy would be conducted to determine the cause of death.
Cyprus was among 30 belugas and four dolphins transferred from Marineland in Niagara Falls after the facility said it could no longer afford to care for its remaining animals.
His death follows several others involving animals relocated from the Canadian park.
Earlier this month, Shedd Aquarium in Chicago confirmed the death of Caspian, a 27-year-old female beluga.
Two other belugas, Peekachu and Rain, also died at the aquarium.
A beluga named Jelly Bean and a dolphin named Echo died after being transferred to Oceanogràfic Valencia in Spain.
SeaWorld said its two remaining rescued belugas were in stable condition and continued to receive close monitoring. “As we have indicated, this process will take a considerable amount of time.
Our commitment to the health, well-being and care of these belugas, like every animal we rescue, continues,” SeaWorld said in a Facebook post on Sunday.

Australia, NZ dollars firm as French fallout pressures euro - The Aussie was flat at $0.6977, having risen 0.5% overnight and away from a recent 15-week trough of $0.68945 SYDNEY: The Australian and New Zealand dollars held firm on Tuesday helped by gains on European currencies following riots in France, while investors awaited developments on domestic interest rates.
The Aussie was flat at $0.6977, having risen 0.5% overnight and away from a recent 15-week trough of $0.68945.
Near-term resistance comes in at $0.6993 and $0.7015.
It also bounced on the euro, sterling and the Swiss franc as political concerns hit bonds across the continent.
The kiwi dollar stood at $0.5665, after edging up 0.1% overnight.
Major support lies at the recent 17-month low of $0.5566, with resistance at $0.5675 and $0.5750.

The next domestic hurdle for the Aussie will be an appearance by Reserve Bank of Australia Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser on Wednesday where he is likely to field questions about the chance of a fifth hike in rates this year.

Speaking on Monday, the RBA’s head of financial markets acknowledged that the labour market might be loosening a little faster than expected, but also highlighted the importance of third-quarter consumer price data due on October 28.
Analysts see a risk core inflation could rise a hefty 1.0% in the quarter to keep the annual pace at 3.6% and well above the RBA’s target range of 2% to 3%.
Indeed, analysts at Westpac think core inflation could also rise by a chunky 0.9% this quarter, putting annual inflation at 3.5% compared to the RBA’s forecast of 3.3%.
Central bank officials will have an opportunity to respond live to the Q3 numbers as Governor Michele Bullock and her team are appearing before lawmakers on the same day and at almost the same time.
Markets imply a one-in-three chance of a hike in the 4.60% cash rate in November, rising to 56% for December.
Also on October 28, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand will announce whether it is lifting rates for a third time this year, with investors pricing in an 89% probability of a quarter-point move to 3.0%.
Markets also imply rates could reach 3.75% or more next year, far above the RBNZ’s own projection of 3.20%.
