Pakistan and the new Middle East The global economic landscape is undergoing a profound transformation and the Middle East – long defined by oil rents and labour imports – is now emerging as a dynamic hub of diversification, investment, and innovation.

Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030, the UAE’s technology-led expansion and Qatar’s logistics and green transition strategies together signal a clear pivot: this region no longer trades in oil alone; it trades in opportunity.
For Pakistan, this transformation is a lifeline.
The Middle East has always been central to Pakistan’s economic story, accounting for over 60 per cent of its remittances and nearly one-fifth of total trade.
But for decades, the relationship has remained transactional – limited to labour exports and energy imports.

As the Gulf economies diversify away from oil and toward knowledge, technology and sustainability, Pakistan faces a critical question: will it adapt fast enough to join this transformation, or will it remain a bystander?
The good news is that Pakistan holds strategic and economic advantages that few countries in the region can match.
It has one of the world’s largest labour forces, vast agricultural potential, proximity to the Gulf and strong cultural and religious ties with Saudi Arabia and other GCC nations.
Yet, despite this, Pakistan’s trade with the Gulf remains underdeveloped and its investments in human capital and knowledge exchange remain far below potential.
In this shifting landscape, a new era of partnership appears to be emerging.

On September 17, 2025, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed a Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement (SMDA) – a historic accord committing both nations to treat any act of aggression against one as an attack on both.
While this agreement primarily focuses on defence, it also lays the foundation for a deeper, multidimensional partnership.
It symbolises trust and interdependence, creating the political and institutional space to expand cooperation into trade, technology, agriculture and human development.

If both countries use the SMDA as a platform to align economic and strategic priorities, Pakistan can transform its role from a peripheral partner into a central player in the emerging Middle Eastern growth story.
The Middle East is opening new windows of opportunity for regional cooperation and Pakistan must learn to navigate through them.
The shift from aid to partnership, from remittances to revenue and from labour exports to knowledge exports must now form the core of Islamabad’s economic diplomacy.
Three sectors can anchor this transformation.
The Middle East imports nearly 85 per cent of its food, with Saudi Arabia and the UAE together spending over $60 billion annually on food imports.
Pakistan, with its fertile plains, water resources and proximity advantage, is uniquely positioned to become a regional food supplier.
This requires moving beyond raw commodity exports to high-value agro-processing.

A ‘Pakistan–Saudi Agro Corridor’ could be developed – jointly financed through Gulf sovereign funds and Pakistani agribusiness groups – to build cold chains, logistics hubs and modern storage facilities.
Exporting fresh produce, halal meat and processed foods could bring in billions annually, while creating rural jobs and enhancing agricultural resilience.
With the right investment in infrastructure and certification systems, Pakistan could supply up to 10 per cent of the Gulf’s food import needs within five years.
Over four million Pakistanis work in the Gulf, contributing more than $25 billion in remittances annually.
Yet, these workers are overwhelmingly low-skilled.

As Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 redefines its economy around technology, energy diversification and high-end services, the demand for engineers, health professionals, data analysts and technicians is growing rapidly.
Pakistan needs to evolve from exporting labour to exporting skills.
This calls for a new generation of Skill Mobility Partnerships with the Gulf states, co-designed with the private sector.
Technical and vocational education programs should be aligned with the Gulf labour markets, focusing on renewable energy, logistics, construction technology and healthcare services.
By exporting skilled human capital instead of low-wage labour, Pakistan can both increase remittances and enhance its global competitiveness.
The new Middle East is building futuristic digital cities – NEOM in Saudi Arabia, Masdar in the UAE and Oxagon on the Red Sea.
These projects are not just about construction – they are about creating knowledge ecosystems.
Pakistan’s IT and tech sectors have grown rapidly, with annual exports now exceeding $3 billion.
Yet, this remains a fraction of the potential.
Through a ‘Pakistan–Gulf Innovation Bridge’, Pakistan can position its tech entrepreneurs, universities and start-ups to collaborate with Middle Eastern innovation hubs.
This bridge could facilitate joint research centres, venture capital funds and technology transfer programmes.
Gulf investors, flush with liquidity, are actively looking for scalable technology ventures; Pakistan’s young, English-speaking workforce could be their most cost-effective and innovative partner.
But for this partnership to succeed, Pakistan must undertake institutional reforms at home.
First, trade diplomacy needs a reset.
The country’s embassies in Riyadh, Dubai and Doha should function as business facilitation centres rather than ceremonial offices.
Pakistan should establish a Pakistan–Middle East Economic Council (PMEC), tasked with identifying investment opportunities, streamlining procedures and coordinating private sector partnerships.
Second, the government should revive domestic investment in export-enabling infrastructure.
Pakistan’s high energy tariffs, inconsistent tax policies and bureaucratic hurdles have made local industries uncompetitive.
The cost of doing business must come down before any meaningful integration with Gulf value chains can occur.
Third, Pakistan should accelerate the development of Special Economic Zones (SEZs) and Village Economic Zones (VEZs) linked to regional trade corridors.
These can act as localised export hubs for agriculture, textiles and light manufacturing.
Gulf investors could be offered land and tax incentives in these zones, allowing production for re-export to Middle Eastern markets.
Saudi Arabia remains central to this new regional growth dynamic.
With over $3 trillion in investment projects under Vision 2030, Riyadh is actively seeking partners for food security, green energy, mining and digital innovation.

The Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement provides the trust and framework to now translate this security alliance into a Strategic Economic Partnership (SEP) – anchored in mutual growth, energy cooperation and shared prosperity.
To make this partnership sustainable, Pakistan must offer predictability.
Investors need policy continuity, not constant course correction.
This means insulating economic diplomacy from political cycles and ensuring that agreements signed today are honoured tomorrow.
Beyond trade and investment, the region’s stability itself depends on greater economic interdependence.
The Middle East’s transformation will not be complete without South Asia’s participation, and Pakistan is the natural bridge.
With 250 million people, a young workforce and access to the Arabian Sea, Pakistan can become the Middle East’s gateway to Central and South Asia.
As regional alliances evolve, the coming decade could well define Pakistan’s economic future.
The Middle East is no longer merely a source of remittances – it is an engine of regional reinvention.
If Pakistan continues to think small, it will remain a subcontractor in a changing world order.
But if it thinks strategically, it can become a co-architect of regional growth.
The time has come to stop viewing the Middle East through the narrow lens of labour export or financial assistance.
It is time to see it as a partner in building shared prosperity.
Pakistan’s exports of agriculture, knowledge and human capital are pathways to resilience and renewal.
In a rapidly changing world, nations that trade ideas, not just goods, will define the next century.
For Pakistan, that century starts with the Middle East.
The writer is associate professor at the Pakistan Institute of Development Economics (PIDE).

Published October 18, 2026 Saudi Arabia said on Saturday that it had intercepted a fresh wave of drones, as its ally Egypt weighed helping the kingdom defend against repeated attacks by Yemen's Houthis.
Riyadh leads a military coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government in its war against the Houthis.
A military spokesman for the Iran-backed group said on Saturday that dozens of Saudi strikes over the past day had killed and wounded "numerous" people.
A spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition said on Saturday that it had "intercepted and destroyed four drones over the past few hours in the regions of Riyadh, the Eastern Province, and the South".
"I'm not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone," he said.
"We are speaking only about defence." Although Egypt is a member of the anti-Houthi coalition, its role has largely focused on Red Sea maritime security rather than the fighting in Yemen.
Egypt and Saudi Arabia have historically close relations and strategic economic ties.
Egypt's parliament will hold an emergency session on Sunday at Sisi's request.
The repeated Houthi strikes have prompted foreign embassies to warn their citizens against using Saudi airports or travelling to the kingdom altogether.
Saudi Arabia's Education Ministry on Saturday announced an extension of remote learning measures for students in Riyadh and nearby Diriyah.
Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis' recent escalation, a charge Tehran denies.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday that Tehran supported a "comprehensive political process as the only practical and sustainable way to resolve" the conflict on the Arabian Peninsula.
He also reiterated Iran's offer to mediate between the two sides.
Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh previously said Riyadh had not responded to Iran's offer.
However, Yemeni Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba rejected the proposal in a statement on X on Saturday, saying "the Tehran regime is a party to the war against Yemenis, not a mediator".
The Houthis are part of Iran's "Axis of Resistance" against Israel and the United States, but both the group and Tehran insist that the Houthis act independently.
Saudi Arabia has carried out daily airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen, where government forces are seeking to reverse gains made by the group in a lightning offensive in September.
On Saturday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Riyadh had carried out 53 strikes in the capital, Sanaa, and six other provinces over the past 24 hours, causing "numerous dead and wounded".

ISLAMABAD, Oct 20 (APP):Minister for Finance and Revenue Senator Muhammad Aurangzeb on Tuesday said Pakistan’s twin deficit had declined from a cumulative 12.5 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) to 2.6 percent, reflecting progress in macroeconomic stabilization and fiscal consolidation.

Addressing a two-day high-level workshop on “Reforms for a Modern and Growth-Friendly Tax System in Pakistan”, the minister said that the country had achieved a 22-year low fiscal deficit in the last fiscal year and recorded primary surpluses for three consecutive years.

The event was organized by the Ministry of Finance and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which bring together senior government officials, representatives of the IMF and World Bank, international tax experts, academics and private-sector leaders to discuss priorities for modernizing Pakistan’s tax system and strengthening its contribution to sustainable economic growth.

Senator Muhammad Aurangzeb said that the Federal Board of Revenue’s (FBR) tax-to-GDP ratio had increased from 8.8 percent to 10.3 percent, while tax revenues had risen by 40 percent over the last two fiscal years.

The minister attributed the improvement to stronger enforcement measures and new tax policy initiatives, explaining that 0.9 percentage points of the 1.5-percentage-point increase in the tax-to-GDP ratio over the last two and a half years had come from enforcement, while 0.6 percentage points resulted from new policy measures.
The government would further strengthen enforcement, curb revenue leakages and broaden the tax base to improve revenue mobilization, he added.

The minister highlighted the ongoing FBR transformation program, covering human resources, processes and technology, which he said was being led by the prime minister and monitored through weekly reviews.

He said that the taxation reforms remained a critical component of the government’s broader structural reform agenda, alongside reforms in the energy sector, state-owned enterprises (SOEs), privatization, public finance, pensions and tariffs.

Emphasizing the need to move from economic stabilization towards growth, Aurangzeb said Pakistan’s economy had recovered from a contraction of 0.3 percent and returned to a positive growth trajectory.

However, he stressed that the country needed sustainable, export-led growth rather than liquidity-driven, consumption-based expansion, which had contributed to boom-and-bust cycles in the past. “We will not let that repeat,” he said, underscoring the government’s commitment to ensuring that future growth was sustainable and supported by stronger economic fundamentals.

The finance minister also pointed to improvements in the country’s external position, saying foreign exchange reserves had recovered from a level equivalent to around two weeks of import cover to more than three months, reaching a record high.
He said the quality of reserves was as important as their volume, noting that the recent improvement had not been accompanied by a comparable increase in external debt.

Aurangzeb said Pakistan’s external debt stock had increased by around $4 billion over the preceding four years, compared with an annual increase of $6 billion to $7 billion during the 2015–2022 period, when external liabilities had risen from around $55 billion to more than $100 billion.
He said the government would continue designing tax policies around economic value and competitiveness rather than focusing solely on meeting revenue targets.

Referring to the previous budget, he said the government had undertaken recalibrations relating to exports and export-oriented industries and would build on these measures to support export-led growth.
The minister identified broadening the tax base, simplifying the taxation code and ensuring policy predictability and continuity as key priorities for the ongoing reform process.

He said frequent and unexpected tax changes could undermine private-sector investment, stressing that businesses needed a predictable policy environment to support long-term planning and economic expansion.
Aurangzeb identified political consensus, stronger institutions, improved taxpayer trust and clear communication as essential enablers of successful tax reforms.

He said cooperation between the federal and provincial governments was particularly important, while rebuilding trust and credibility in the tax authority was necessary to improve compliance and strengthen the relationship between taxpayers and the state.
The minister acknowledged the need for better communication to demonstrate progress on structural reforms and explain the measures being taken to increase revenue collection and improve its quality.
He expressed the hope that discussions during the conference would help assess progress on ongoing reforms and develop a roadmap for advancing from stabilization to sustainable economic growth.
He said effective tax policy design and administration would remain critical to strengthening the private sector’s role in economic development and ensuring durable economic stability.

He said the government’s reform agenda, supported by the IMF through its Extended Fund Facility (EFF), aimed to raise productivity, strengthen the private sector and create better economic opportunities for Pakistan’s younger generations.

Referring to the IMF’s Regional Economic Outlook, he said stronger policy frameworks and buffers had helped countries cushion external shocks, but inflationary pressures, fiscal constraints and financing needs were becoming increasingly evident.

He said a stronger, broader, fairer and more predictable tax system could improve fiscal sustainability while reducing distortions that discourage investment, productivity, business expansion and formal job creation.

Azour outlined four key themes for the workshop including credibility, growth, fairness and implementation, adding that Pakistan needed to preserve its hard-won stabilization gains by continuing to meet fiscal and external objectives, strengthening resilience and ensuring that reforms were sustained and firmly embedded in institutions.

Tax policy and tax administration, he said, must advance together, noting that a simpler policy framework makes administration easier, while effective administration lends credibility to policy reforms.

ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) issued notices on appeals filed by human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari and her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha, challenging an anti-terrorism court’s (ATC) decision to dismiss their pleas against the framing of charges and the inclusion of terrorism-related provisions in a case registered against them.

A division bench of the IHC comprising Justice Raja Inaam Ameen Minhas and Justice Shahrukh Arjumand on Monday heard the matter while Riasat Ali Azad, Zainab Janjua and other lawyers, representing Imaan and Chattha, appeared before the court.
At the outset of the hearing, Justice Minhas asked whether the accused had received copies of the relevant documents.
Counsel Riasat Ali Azad replied in the negative and said he wanted to examine how the charges had been framed.
The counsel argued that the ATC had passed the impugned order without the requisite authority to do so.
He said the case had remained pending before the court of Judge Abual Hasanat Mohammad Zulqarnain from March 12, 2025, until recently.
Citing the precedent in the Zulfikar Ali Bhutto case, Azad argued that the court in which the challan was submitted was the one authorised to hear the case.

He further contended that the accused had not been provided with copies of the relevant documents and that the charges had not been read out in their presence, as they were not physically present in the courtroom at the time.
The counsel argued that the legal proceedings cannot move forward in the absence of the accused, adding that the charges must be framed in the presence of the accused.
He also alleged a violation of a decision of the National Judicial Policy Making Committee.
Describing the charge as the foundation of a trial, Azad maintained that any defect in its framing would undermine the legality of the subsequent proceedings.
Justice Minhas asked whether the trial was being conducted through a video link.
The counsel replied that the proceedings had initially taken place through a video link but had shifted to a jail trial at the most recent hearing.
The judge also inquired whose signatures appeared on the charge document.
Azad said the document bore his signature, but lacked those of the accused, which, according to him, were legally required.

Justice Minhas questioned whether the proceedings could not be conducted through a video link, observing that the accused had been connected through the facility and that their attendance had been recorded when the charges were framed.
The counsel, however, insisted that the accused were not present when he signed the documents and requested the court to summon the video recording of the proceedings.
He also said the copies had not been delivered to the accused in jail, and that an affidavit had been submitted to this effect.
Justice Minhas remarked that it appeared the defence had not intended to accept the copies.
Azad responded that every application filed by the defence before the ATC had been rejected.
He said the defence had requested both the case record and the video recording of the proceedings.
The judge subsequently asked where it was stipulated that the accused must be physically produced for the framing of charges.

Azad reiterated that the appeals also challenged the inclusion of anti-terrorism provisions in the case and repeatedly urged the high court to halt the trial. “We shall see; we will let you know,” Justice Minhas remarked.
Justice Minhas said the court would issue an order and inform the parties accordingly.
He concluded that notices had been issued, and the court would decide how to proceed once the responses were received.
Published October 19, 2026 On January 12, when Farhan Chishti landed at Islamabad airport in the afternoon, the MQM MNA’s phone was dead.
He could neither call nor receive a message.
He thought there might be a network failure, but when it did not restore for many hours, he went to a service centre of the cellular company to report the problem.
There he learnt that a duplicate SIM, which he had never requested, had been issued against his number, disabling his original connection.
Staff told him it had been issued in Karachi’s Malir area.
Disabling it was possible only from the company’s headquarters, which was closed for the day and would reopen in the morning, he was told.
By then, the damage was already underway.
The person holding his number had registered Chishti for online banking, although he had never used electronic channels.

The same person raised his withdrawal limit, set the password “Saeen Sarkar,” and moved Rs1.5 million out of his account to that of one Sakina Bibi, herself a victim whose account had been opened without her knowledge, and to other accounts opened in the names of women in South Punjab and Sindh.
Chishti complained to the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA).

Investigators questioned the owner of the point of sale in Khokhrapar (Malir), who said a man had approached him claiming his mother, who needed a duplicate SIM, was too weak to leave the car, and asked for the biometric device to take her thumbprint there.
How they obtained Chishti’s thumbprint remains unexplained.
The man who used the duplicate SIM was from Nawabshah.
Investigators believe bad actors harvest biometrics in bulk from leaked data or from places where fingerprints are not mandatory for routine services, then load them onto software and misuse them.
The case went to the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA), which fined the cellular company Rs77.8 million.
The company argued that a third party had deceived the retailer.
The PTA rejected this, citing Regulation 4(4) of the Subscribers Regulations, under which any SIM sold by any means is the operator’s sole responsibility.
It found failures in monitoring, said the company’s later remedial steps did not cure the initial lapse, and noted that similar violations keep surfacing despite repeated instructions.
Another MNA, Shaharyar Mahar, lost Rs2 million in another episode.
Karachi businessman Sunny Kumar also fell victim.
A duplicate SIM was issued in his name on September 29, 2025, at a retail outlet in Dhabeji, Thatta.
Incidentally, Kumar and Chishti are customers of the same cellular company.
As much as Rs8.5 million was taken from Kumar’s account.
The investigation into the case revealed an insider at the bank.
A branch service officer in Mardan had viewed Kumar’s account before the SIM was issued.
The same officer had accessed around 30 accounts, after which funds were withdrawn or restrictions applied, with suspected fraud of about Rs25 million.
He first said he was helping a friend with a balance inquiry, then admitted sharing customers’ details with that friend, saying he was under pressure.
Phone records showed him also seeking customer data from an employee of another bank, and offering payment to a Nadra employee, who later refused to provide the information.
A PTA order in this case imposed the same Rs77.8 million fine in Kumar’s case.
Kumar recovered his money from the bank.

A source privy to the details said a similar pattern, including the involvement of bank insiders, was observed in the other two cases, but the investigation did not proceed because the complainants were keen only on recovering their stolen funds.
This is not limited to these three cases.
Such incidents have also occurred in other provinces as well.
While the telecom company was penalised in both cases, the only action against the banks was an order to return the victims’ money.

Beyond the 27th The push by Pakistan’s ruling structure to amend the constitution for the 27th time fails to impress on a key front-the welfare of the people.
The entire exercise appears aimed primarily at a further consolidation of power while extending patronage, through steps like enlarging the induction of ministerial rank advisers.
While the present ruling structure reassures itself of becoming unassailable after the latest constitutional amendment, the future of Pakistan remains surrounded by uncertainty.
In the past two years, members of the ruling clan have repeatedly commended themselves for steering Pakistan away from a default on its foreign debt repayments.
And yet, this success is easily overshadowed by unresolved questions over the plight of Pakistanis, notably more than 40 per cent of the population living below the poverty line.
This is indeed tragic and alarming.

Pakistan’s internal economic divide is a pressing reality that has powerfully and repeatedly reminded historians of the apt guidance by Hazrat Ali (a.s.), outlining a fundamental pillar of statecraft: “Society can survive with ‘kufr’ (infidelity) but not injustice”.
From thereon has flowed a precious lesson in the history of the world, notably the fate of empires that crumbled under the weight of inner contradictions.
Taking the cue from this lesson of history, it must be mandatory for members of Pakistan’s ruling structure to redouble their campaign for narrowing the country’s internal divide.
In this background, the 27th Amendment must be followed with two interrelated initiatives at the federal and provincial levels, notably Punjab.

The battle against climate change and reversal of the downturn surrounding Pakistan’s agriculture will be fought and won or lost in Punjab, where evidence of recent policy failures has pushed down farm incomes by a large margin.
First, key players in Pakistan need to agree on a revival of the economy, anchored primarily on lifting the badly sagging farm incomes.
The federal government’s recent announcement of guaranteeing a minimum purchase price of wheat stocks from the next crop fails miserably to reverse the damage already done.
Just weeks after the provincial government of Punjab came to power in early 2024, it abruptly reversed its promise to purchase stocks from the new crop in spring that year at Rs3900 per maund.
Within days, the returns to farmers crashed by at least one-third below their expectations.
That failure has been followed by widely reported evidence of rising rural poverty at a pace seldom witnessed before.

Meanwhile, the Punjab government’s recent announcements to support farmers through means such as providing loans for new tractors or credit for inputs of crops fail to compensate for the damage already done.
In effect, Pakistan’s entire chain of food supplies remains dangerously stretched.
This year’s heavy rainfall and floods have only caused further aggravation to the livelihoods of rural dwellers.
And there is more to come with forecasts of heavier rainfall next summer triggered by climate change.
Any further deviation from the central cause of securing Pakistan’s threatened food supply will amount to one of the worst blunders in the history of Pakistan.
Second, it is vital to work aggressively towards reviving the existing economy, notably the industrial sector, which also faces a continuing downturn.
Pakistan suffers from a lethargic economy in a slowdown mode whose future rests upon a complete overhaul of the existing policy framework.
An honest beginning towards a new future must tackle Pakistan’s political discord, which has sharpened in the wake of the February 2024 elections.
Imran Khan remains in jail while his party leads the opposition.
On the streets, the PTI remains popular.
But that popularity remains intact due to the government’s failure to create fresh opportunities for low-to-moderate-income Pakistanis across the board.
It is this outcome which helps explain the popular mood across the country.
Going forward, the revival of the popular mood must be led by responding to the public’s needs where it matters the most.
For months, the Punjab government has repeatedly promised to oversee fancy new development projects.
In an ideal world, Pakistan could have embarked upon such initiatives, provided the country was able to afford them.
But the challenges which surround Pakistan’s outlook require an urgent change of direction.
On its own, the 27th Amendment may have faced passing criticism if the country were surrounded by fewer challenges and fast-rising opportunities.
But the scale of the challenges that now engulf Pakistan requires an uninterrupted focus of the kind never seen before in the country’s history.
The writer is an Islamabad-based journalist who writes on political and economic affairs.

The successful IBOs come as armed forces have intensified efforts to eradicate terrorism under the Azm-e-Istehkam operation.
Terrorist attacks have seen a sharp increase in Pakistan, particularly in the bordering provinces of KP and Balochistan, since 2021, when the Afghan Taliban regime came into power.
A police report noted that KP alone recorded over 600 terror incidents, in which at least 79 police personnel were martyred alongside 138 civilians, during the first eight months of 2025.

The violence spread to other regions of the country, including Islamabad, where a suicide bombing on November 11 resulted in the martyrdom of 12 and 36 others were injured, among them lawyers and petitioners.
Islamabad has repeatedly urged Kabul and the international community to address the presence of terrorist safe havens in Afghanistan, including those of the outlawed Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).
Despite Pakistan’s efforts to engage the Taliban regime on the issue of cross-border terrorism, Kabul has remained largely unresponsive to its concerns.
The recent talks, mediated by Qatar and Turkiye, about regional peace ended without a result due to what Islamabad said were the Taliban's "illogical arguments" and their views far from reality.
Pakistan's position on terrorism emanating from Afghanistan also received support from the head of the UN Security Council's Daesh and Al-Qaeda Sanctions Committee.

Denmark's Deputy Permanent Representative to the UN, Sandra Jensen Landi — who also serves as the committee's chair — presented a report to the UNSC, stating that the TTP carried out multiple high-profile attacks in Pakistan from Afghan soil.

She termed the TTP "a serious threat" emanating from the region, saying that the terrorist group was receiving constant logistical and substantial support from the "de facto" authorities in Afghanistan.

The Jinnah Muslim League (JML) was a Pakistani political party founded in 1949 as a breakaway faction of the Muslim League by the first ever Chief Minister of Pakistani Punjab, Iftikhar Hussain Khan Mamdot.
The party's founder, Mamdot was a close confidant and ally of Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan.
Mamdot played a key role in the Pakistan Movement and therefore was granted the position of the first chief minister of West Punjab following the Independence of Pakistan.

He retained the position of chief minister until he was sacked by the ruling Muslim League in 1949 after Jinnah's death due to issues in Mamdot's provincial government and because of Mamdot's relations with Muslim League top leaders worsening after Jinnah's death.
Following this, Mamdot left the Muslim League to found the Jinnah Muslim League between 1949 and 1950.
The party's ideology was not clear, as Mamdot was the only prominent leader in the party.
Mamdot himself would be a stern disciplinarian.
He advocated for the policies of his Punjab provincial ministry (1947–1949) and was a close advocate of Jinnah's.
The party was founded to also contest against Mamdot's arch-rival, Mumtaz Daultana of the Muslim League.
The party joined hands with Hussein Shaheed Suhrawardy and his Awami League and formed the All-Pakistan Awami League to contest in the 1951 Punjab provincial election, Punjab's first election.
The Muslim League defeated Mamdot and the Awami League coalition, following this, Mamdot became Leader of the Opposition in the Provincial Assembly of the Punjab under the JML.
The JML did not dissolve until 1953, when Mamdot quit and rejoined the Muslim League, while the All-Pakistan Awami League remained a party until the creation of Bangladesh.

Netflix faces scrutiny over user engagement ahead of Q3 report Facing mounting pressure over plateauing viewing hours and rising domestic churn, the streaming giant heads into high-stakes financial results As Netflix prepares to report its third-quarter earnings, investors are focusing on slowing user engagement, rising domestic churn and intensifying competition for viewers’ attention.
According to a Nielsen report, the streaming giant faces a fundamental shift in entertainment consumption as lower-cost, creator-led videos increasingly compete with premium scripted content.
YouTube, the leading streaming platform in the US by viewing share, commands nearly twice Netflix’s viewing time, underscoring the growing challenge from digital video competitors.
Analysts warn that slowing viewing hours and intensifying competition could test Netflix’s growth narrative.

Ted Sarandos, the company’s co-CEO, recently acknowledged that Netflix “is not growing as fast as I want us to,” while suggesting that live programming could provide an opportunity to accelerate growth.
Market data also points to pressure on viewing time per member compared with previous years, partly reflecting a lighter content slate and competition for consumer attention.
Meanwhile, research firm Apptopia reported that Netflix’s US user churn rose 16.6% year over year in the third quarter, roughly twice the pace recorded in each of the previous three quarters.
Downloads across the US and Canada also fell 20%, pointing to potential challenges in attracting and retaining users.
Netflix has also taken steps to strengthen its cost discipline.
The company cut about 6% of its workforce, a move that eMarketer analyst Ross Benes said reflected the streaming industry’s broader shift toward profitability.
Separately, the company underwent a content leadership change, with longtime content head Bela Bajaria leaving and former Disney executive Peter Rice taking over.

With subscriber growth maturing, investors are expected to scrutinize Netflix’s advertising-tier monetization and cost-management strategy for signs that these measures can offset slowing engagement and support profit margins.
According to data compiled by LSEG, Netflix is forecast to post its slowest third-quarter revenue growth in three years, with sales expected to rise 11.8% to $12.87 billion.
The results, due Tuesday, will offer investors a clearer picture of whether the company can sustain growth amid rising churn, shifting viewing habits and mounting competitive pressure.

To combat current economic challenges, he stressed the need for deeper cooperation in emerging sectors such as artificial intelligence (AI), the digital economy, and green energy development.
The Chinese finance chief reaffirmed Beijing's dedication to implementing comprehensive economic reforms and maintaining high-standard openness to support both regional and global market stability.
China, the world's second-largest economy, would continue comprehensive economic reforms, he said, without elaborating.

A plastic bag picked up after a shopping trip may seem harmless, but thousands of such choices are adding to Islamabad’s growing waste problem.

The renewed “Plastic-Free Islamabad” campaign is seeking to raise awareness about the environmental impact of single-use plastics and encourage residents and businesses to adopt reusable and environmentally friendly alternatives.

Islamabad’s renewed plastic-free push puts everyday habits under scrutiny Abdul Samad Tariq ISLAMABAD, Oct 5 (APP):A plastic bag picked up after a shopping trip may seem harmless, but thousands of such choices are adding to Islamabad’s growing waste problem.

The Capital Development Authority (CDA) and Islamabad administration have launched the “Plastic-Free Islamabad” initiative on the directions of Interior Minister Syed Mohsin Raza Naqvi and CDA Chairman and Chief Commissioner Islamabad Sohail Ashraf.

The campaign, being supervised by Additional Deputy Commissioner (General) Dr Anam Fatima, will focus on markets, commercial areas, food outlets, educational institutions, parks, recreational sites and other public places.
Assistant commissioners have been tasked with monitoring activities in their respective areas.

While the authorities are seeking greater public cooperation, the initiative also highlights a practical challenge: reducing plastic use requires changes not only in consumer behaviour but also in the way shops, restaurants and other businesses package and sell everyday goods. “As a longtime resident of Islamabad, I’m tired of seeing plastic bags littering our beautiful parks and streets.
Switching to reusable bags would make such a difference in keeping our city clean and green for everyone,” said Naseem, a housewife in Sector G-7.

For retailers, however, the transition can be more complicated. “As a shopkeeper in Islamabad, I’ve noticed most customers still prefer plastic bags because the reusable ones cost more and some people forget to bring them.

The Plastic-Free Islamabad campaign is a good idea, but it will only work if alternative bags are made cheaper and easily available for small shops like mine,” said Raheem, a local vendor at Aabpara Market in G-6.

The issue is equally relevant to younger residents, who authorities hope will adopt environmentally responsible habits as part of their daily routines. “As a student in Islamabad, I’ve started carrying a reusable bag everywhere so I don’t have to take plastic ones from shops.
If more of us do the same, our parks, campuses and streets will stay much cleaner,” said Sawaira, a BS Media Studies student at NUML University.

Food businesses face another set of challenges, particularly because takeaway packaging has to meet requirements related to hygiene, convenience and customer expectations. “Running a small restaurant in Islamabad, I’ve tried switching to paper and biodegradable packaging, but the higher cost is tough when customers still expect cheap takeaway.
Practical alternatives only work if suppliers make them affordable and people are willing to pay a little extra for a cleaner city,” said Asif, a restaurant owner in F-10.
The renewed campaign is not being launched in a regulatory vacuum.

The Pakistan Environmental Protection Agency (Pak-EPA) said the Single-Use Plastics (Prohibition) Regulations, 2023, already prohibit the manufacture, import, sale, distribution, storage and use of polythene bags and other banned single-use plastics across the Islamabad Capital Territory.

A Pak-EPA spokesperson said the agency’s enforcement would continue through regular market inspections, confiscation of banned materials, sealing of non-compliant outlets and legal action against violators.
According to the spokesperson, penalties range from Rs5,000 for individuals to Rs10,000–50,000 for shopkeepers, while manufacturers and wholesalers can face penalties of up to Rs500,000.

The agency said limited exemptions were available for authorised industrial packing, municipal waste, hospital waste and hazardous waste, subject to prior approval from Pak-EPA. “Our enforcement priority is clear and ongoing: regular market inspections, confiscation of banned materials, sealing of non-compliant outlets and legal action against violators,” the spokesperson said.
The agency also urged businesses to shift towards affordable reusable and biodegradable alternatives and called on citizens to carry their own bags and cooperate with enforcement efforts.
The campaign’s effectiveness, however, is likely to depend on how easily consumers and businesses can make the transition.
While awareness about the environmental impact of plastic is increasing, convenience and cost continue to influence the choices of both consumers and businesses.
For a household, carrying a reusable bag may be a relatively simple change.
For a small retailer, replacing thousands of plastic bags can add to operating costs.
Restaurants face similar concerns when replacing plastic containers and other disposable packaging with more expensive alternatives.
For many small businesses, the availability of affordable alternatives could therefore determine whether the campaign succeeds in the long term.

If reusable and biodegradable products remain significantly more expensive, shopkeepers and restaurant owners may find it difficult to make the switch without passing the additional cost on to customers.
Consumers, meanwhile, may also need to change established habits.
Many shoppers accept plastic bags automatically when making purchases, particularly for small or unexpected purchases.
Carrying reusable bags regularly could reduce demand for single-use alternatives and make environmentally responsible choices part of everyday life.

The authorities have said the campaign is intended not only to discourage single-use plastic but also to create greater awareness about its environmental impact and encourage responsible waste disposal.

CDA Chairman and Chief Commissioner Islamabad Sohail Ashraf has described making Islamabad plastic-free as a shared responsibility rather than merely an enforcement exercise, stressing the need for cooperation among residents, traders, businesses, educational institutions and government agencies.
The administration is also seeking to link the campaign with broader cleanliness and waste-management objectives.
Officials say reducing plastic waste can help keep roads, markets, parks and public spaces cleaner and reduce the amount of plastic entering drainage systems.
Plastic waste can be particularly visible in Islamabad’s green spaces, where bags and disposable packaging can accumulate around roadside areas, parks and markets.
During rainfall, improperly discarded plastic can also enter drains and contribute to blockages, adding another challenge for the city’s waste-management system.

For Islamabad, a city whose identity is closely associated with its green spaces, the issue is increasingly visible in everyday life from plastic bags caught in roadside vegetation to disposable packaging accumulating around markets and public areas.
The challenge now is to turn the campaign from an enforcement exercise into a sustained change in consumption habits.
Regular inspections and penalties may discourage businesses from using banned materials, but lasting results will require consumers to change their behaviour as well.

That could mean a resident remembering to carry a reusable bag, a student refusing unnecessary packaging, a shopkeeper finding an affordable alternative or a restaurant absorbing or sharing the additional cost of environmentally friendly packaging.
Schools, universities and other educational institutions could also play an important role by encouraging students to avoid unnecessary plastic and promoting reusable products.
Similarly, businesses could help by making alternative packaging more visible and accessible to customers.

Ultimately, the success of the “Plastic-Free Islamabad” campaign may depend on whether these small individual choices become routine and whether affordable alternatives are available to make those choices practical for both consumers and businesses.
The fight against plastic will not end with inspections or fines.
It will be won through everyday choices.
If residents, businesses and authorities act together, Islamabad can protect its green identity and build a cleaner future for generations to come.

Red flag warning Antarctica has moved to “the front of the line” as a global warming threat that’s already well beyond expectations, and it’s happening fast.
Based upon statements by polar scientists over the past 18 months, it warrants a Red Flag Warning, meaning higher than expected risks of catastrophic meltdown within current lifetimes.

This meets criteria for the latest international concern surrounding climate change: “When is enough, enough” for world leaders to take to heart the risks of ecosystem failures and take extraordinary, drastic, unprecedented measures in unison to hopefully head off the onset of a maniacal worldwide climate system.
There are people of stature who believe it (climate change) is already over the top, meaning “it’s too late.” But this is not universal belief.

Antarctica may be the catalyst that tips the scales enough to scare the daylights out of world leaders, but will this be recognized early enough for extreme mitigation measures to hopefully take hold well before EVs, with electron sparks flying, are left floating on city streets throughout the world?

Antarctica has been commanding more public attention as the principal ogre of global warming’s impact on sea levels simply because it is the biggest monster in the room, and it’s starting to move, a lot.

Increasingly, the science that once, not so long ago, thought of Antarctica as an issue for the distant future, has turned tail as the rapidity of global warming has changed the entire complexity of the continent’s future.
Its future is now, not a hundred years from now.
The risk of massive sea level rise flooding coastal megacities has jump-started from a distant hundred years hence, or more, to today’s generation, right now.
After all, 13 feet doesn’t suddenly happen in the year 2099.
And this is the first time such a projection (13’) has gone public.

And this is the first time a group of polar scientists has stated “catastrophic sea level rise within our lifetimes.” Now, a new study has discovered evidence of Antarctica mimicking Greenland’s meltdown dynamics, which are pervasive: Ruth Mottram, et al, The Greenlandification of Antarctica, Nature Geoscience, October 2025.
Indeed, this study adds a new layer to outcries by scientists that a very big problem is about to burst loose with Antarctica’s meltdown phase.

X faces pressure to reject Turkey’s broad requests to block accounts The groups urged X to carefully examine blocking requests from Turkish authorities On Tuesday, journalism groups called on social platform X not to comply with government takedown orders directed at journalists and media outlets in Turkey that occur outside the course of regular judicial proceedings.

In a joint declaration, the International Federation of Journalists, the European Federation of Journalists and the Turkish Journalists Union reported a surge in access limitations and said X was reportedly complying with demands that lacked adequate judicial oversight.

The groups urged X to scrutinize blocking requests by Turkish authorities to ensure they are supported by independent and clear court decisions and to rebuff overbroad or excessive requests while increasing transparency regarding limitations.

OPEC+ agrees to keep November oil targets steady amid market uncertainty An agreement has been reached in principle to maintain oil output targets for this November OPEC+ has reportedly agreed in principle to keep its November oil production targets unchanged ahead of the group’s meeting scheduled for Sunday.

The geopolitical tensions have also delayed the productivity evaluation review essential for reviewing members; 2027 output quotas because they have clouded future production outlooks.
A source close to the talks said that the OPEC+ group including the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia concurred in theory to maintain baseline objectives.
OPEC+ has been raising output targets for much of the year 2026 following years of production cuts but most of the increases stayed on paper due to the Middle East conflict.
According to OPEC data, the seven core OPEC+ members’ output reached 25 million barrels per day in August, though it was still roughly 5 million bpd below prewar levels in February.

There are almost 25 million bpd of output cuts in place covering most members but a workload assessment is needed to determine how to allocate rises and structural adjustments and any changes to output are unlikely before 2027.
Furthermore, the group’s seven core members meeting on Sunday include Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman.

ISLAMABAD: The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) has launched an investigation into the initial public offering (IPO) of SE Fruits and Vegetable Limited after an anonymous complaint revealed major financial discrepancies in the company’s audit report, officials said.

text: The commission is also looking to strengthen the Audit Oversight Board after discrepancies were detected in the company’s audit report.
The inquiry will examine whether any gaps, omissions or negligence occurred during the IPO approval process and determine responsibility where warranted.
The inquiry follows an anonymous complaint received on Sept 11, two days after the SECP approved the company’s prospectus based on its audited financial statements.

A preliminary review flagged differences between reported sales and sales tax returns for 2022-26, local sales that were not reflected in the company’s 2024 income tax return and a gap between reported sales, after accounting for closing receivables, and bank credits.

The inquiry will examine the information and explanations provided to determine whether the differences resulted from inaccurate disclosures, accounting treatment or other factors.

The investigation will review the Pakistan Stock Exchange’s role as a front-line regulator, the consultant to the issue’s due diligence, its role in preparing the prospectus and certifying its accuracy, and the auditor’s examination of the company’s financial statements.

Australian employers using AI to track workers without their knowledge, report warns The report highlighted cases including a fast-food chain allegedly using cameras in changing rooms Australian employers are increasingly using AI and surveillance technology to monitor workers, raising concerns about employee privacy and workplace rights.

According to The Guardian, a new report from the University of Technology Sydney's Human Technology Institute warns that companies are tracking employees through CCTV cameras, keystroke monitoring, office access cards and workplace messaging platforms.
The report highlighted cases including a fast-food chain allegedly using cameras in changing rooms to prevent staff from using their phones.
Another case involved a supermarket cashier receiving a final written warning after an AI system detected an error rate of just 0.18 percent, roughly one mistake every 533 items scanned.
Researchers also raised concerns about Microsoft Teams, which can automatically update employees' office locations when they connect to workplace Wi-Fi.
A March 2026 survey found that only nine percent of Australians knew monitoring was happening in their own workplace.
The institute is calling for stronger workplace privacy laws, including new rules requiring employers to justify surveillance and consult employees.
The report also recommends banning surveillance technologies that pose unacceptable risks to employees' rights.
